documents.title: Beach Mulloway – How to Land the Silver Ghost from the Sand
documents.description: The Elusive Mulloway (Jewey)

sections.heading: Beach Mulloway – How to Land the Silver Ghost from the Sand
sections.text: The Elusive Mulloway (Jewey) If you’ve ever stayed up all night on a lonely stretch of beach, rod in hand, eyes on the stars, and hope in your heart — you’re not mad. You’re beach fishing for Mulloway! Also known as jewfish, these elusive silver slabs are the holy grail of Aussie beach fishing. And while they’re notoriously tricky to land, they’re absolutely catchable with the right rig, timing, and a bit of mongrel. Why Beach Mulloway Fishing is a Challenge! Mulloway don’t muck around. They hit like freight trains and fight like they've got somewhere to be. The challenge? They’re picky, they’re nocturnal, and they love a sloppy gutter with just enough water to hide in.

sections.heading: Best Rig for Mulloway off the Beach
sections.text: Want to dive deeper into Mulloway rigs used across beaches, estuaries and rock ledges? See our Best Mulloway Rigs in Australia guide for a full breakdown of proven setups in different conditions. You want strong, simple, and stealthy. Our go-to? Snapper & Jewfish (Mulloway) rig - Hook: 2x 6/0 snelled hooks (top hook sliding) - Leader: 60lb abrasion-resistant monofilament, for those rocks & head shakes - Mainline: Use 20–30lb braid or monofilament (we prefer mono due to its great abrasion properties, especially if fishing rocky areas) - Sinker: Star sinker on a sliding weight clip Pro tip: Use a luminous bead to protect the knot that ties the mainline to the rig. (The knot will be protected from the sliding weight clip.) If you're unsure whether this setup suits your local beach conditions, our Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide explains how to match rigs to species, structure and surf conditions across Australia.

sections.heading: Best Baits for Beach Mulloway
sections.text: - Live mullet or tailor (small to mid-sized) - Fresh squid strips or whole squid Mulloway are sniffers. They’ll cruise through a gutter multiple times before committing. Give ‘em something to come back for. Choosing the right rig presentation makes a big difference when fish are following a bait more than once. If you'd like to understand why hook spacing and leader strength affect mulloway hook-ups in surf conditions, see Why the Right Rig Matters in Australian Fishing. These ghosts of the surf show up when: - The tide’s pushing in or topping out - There’s decent swell or movement in the wash - It’s after dark, ideally around new or full moons - You’ve had a good bit of rain in the estuary (bait flushes into the surf) Be patient — they often show up in the last hour before you're ready to pack it in. Look for deep gutters with nearby structure like rocks or sandbanks. If you're unsure how to identify productive gutters before dark, see our guide on How to Read a Beach: Spotting Gutters, Banks & Breaks Like a Pro → You can also use our Rig Finder to quickly narrow down proven mulloway setups based on where you're fishing and local conditions. Some proven SE QLD beach haunts: - South Stradbroke (surf side) - Fraser Island (moonlit mission material) - Broadbeach Gutter Zones - Lennox Head (NSW border bonus)

sections.heading: Don't Forget the Right Gear
sections.text: - Long rod (12ft+) with a soft tip for easy bite recognition and long casts - Sturdy sand spike (you’ll need both hands) - Headlamp and patience. Lots of patience. (and new batteries!)

sections.heading: Our Mulloway Rig Range
sections.text: We offer a dedicated Beach Mulloway Rig, as mentioned earlier, although several of out rigs are suitable for catching Mulloway, all our rigs are hand-tied with premium mono and quality hooks. These rigs are tried and tested and ready to handle any serious fish in serious surf. 📦 To Browse our Mulloway Rigs click the link below Snapper & Jewfish (Mulloway) rigs For a full breakdown of mulloway rig types across beaches, estuaries, and rock ledges, see our Best Mulloway Rigs in Australia guide →

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Mulloway Setup for Your Beach
sections.text: Different beaches fish differently depending on gutter depth, sweep strength and structure nearby. If you’re fishing unfamiliar water, our Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide helps match rigs to conditions across surf, estuary and rock locations so you can start with a setup that’s already proven to work. For a species-specific breakdown across environments, see Best Mulloway Rigs in Australia. Beach mulloway fishing isn’t for everyone — but it’s unforgettable. And when it happens… it’s magic. documents.title: Choosing the Right Fishing Hook- (Why Most Fishos Get It Wrong)
documents.description: The correct fishing hook is not determined by a species name or a number printed on a packet.

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Fishing Hook- (Why Most Fishos Get It Wrong)
sections.text: The correct fishing hook is not determined by a species name or a number printed on a packet. It must fit the bait, operate properly with the way the rig is being fished, penetrate under the pressure being applied and remain strong enough for the complete setup. Most hook problems begin when one of those requirements is overlooked. The point becomes buried in bait, the fisho strikes a circle hook like a J hook, the wire gauge does not suit the expected load, or the hook starts the fight without being fully engaged. This guide explains how to make those choices in the correct order and how to diagnose a hook problem without automatically blaming sharpness, brand or bad luck.

sections.heading: Start with the Bait, Not the Fish
sections.text: The baited hook is what the fish encounters. That makes bait size, thickness, length and toughness the first considerations. A hook that looks suitable when bare may become too small once it passes through a thick squid strip or fish bait. If the point or gape becomes buried, the hook may not make proper contact when the fish takes it. An unnecessarily large hook can also create problems. It may crowd a small bait, split softer bait or make it difficult to rig the bait straight. After baiting, check that: The hook point remains completely exposed The gape is not packed with bait The bait sits straight and securely The hook is positioned in a firm section of bait The hook arrangement covers enough of a longer bait A long bait may need ganged hooks, a fixed twin-hook rig or an adjustable sliding-snell arrangement rather than one hook at the front. See Sliding Snell Rigs Explained for adjustable hook spacing along different bait lengths.

sections.heading: Hook Numbers Are Only a Starting Point
sections.text: Numbered hook sizes become larger as the number decreases. Ought sizes begin at 1/0 and become larger as the first number increases. The important limitation is that hook sizes are not an exact universal measurement. Two hooks marked 6/0 may use different gapes, shank lengths, point shapes and wire gauges. Do not choose from the number alone. Compare the actual hook with the bait and inspect how much point and gape remain clear after it is rigged. The companion guide Fishing Hooks Explained—Types, Sizes & Materials covers the main hook patterns, numbering system, gauge, materials and finishes.

sections.heading: Choose a Hook Pattern That Suits How You Fish
sections.text: The hook and the fisho must be working by the same method.

sections.heading: Recurve Circle Hooks
sections.text: A recurve circle hook has a point turned back towards the shank. As the fish moves away and steady pressure comes onto the line, the hook is designed to travel towards the edge of the mouth and rotate into the jaw corner. Allow the line and rod to load, then increase pressure smoothly. A hard strike can pull the hook away before it has rotated. The point and gape must remain clear of bait. A correctly chosen circle hook cannot operate properly if both are packed with squid, pilchard or bait elastic.

sections.heading: J Hooks and Beak Hooks
sections.text: A conventional J hook is commonly used when the fisho detects the bite and actively sets the hook. A beak hook has a point curved inward towards the shank. Beak describes the hook shape; it is not another name for every J hook, suicide hook or octopus hook. Many conventional beak hooks are fished actively, but the word “beak” alone does not determine the hook-setting method. Check the actual point shape and the intended use of that hook. Actively set hooks suit rigs and fishing methods where the fisho controls when pressure is applied. The required timing depends on how the fish takes the bait and whether the bait is being held, moved or carried away. Circle hooks and actively set hooks each suit different jobs. Problems begin when one is used as though it operates like the other.

sections.heading: A Hook Can Feel Solid Without Being Fully Engaged
sections.text: Initial contact is not the same as complete penetration. This becomes particularly important with sharks and other fish that have tough skin or heavy cartilage around the jaw. A circle hook may roll towards the jaw corner, but the point can still be only partly engaged. If the hook has not seated properly, the load may act against a shallow section of the point and create additional leverage through the bend. Under sustained pressure, that can help open a hook that may otherwise have held its shape. Once the circle hook has rolled and the line is loading, apply a firm, controlled increase in pressure so the point can penetrate and the hook can seat correctly. This is not a wild strike. A straightened hook does not prove that the brand or material was weak. Incomplete engagement, unsuitable wire gauge, excessive drag pressure, prior damage and a mismatch elsewhere in the setup must also be considered. For more information about heavy hook and trace selection, see Shark Fishing Rigs Explained.

sections.heading: Match Hook Gauge, Leader and Drag Pressure
sections.text: Hook gauge is the thickness of the wire. It is separate from the hook-size number. Fine-wire hooks require less force to penetrate and add less weight to small or soft baits. They also have less resistance to opening under heavy load. Heavy-wire hooks resist opening more effectively but require greater force to penetrate. A heavy hook that is blunt, partly buried or only lightly engaged may not seat properly. The hook, leader and drag must work as one system. A very heavy leader and high drag pressure do not compensate for a hook that is too light for the load. An excessively heavy hook does not improve a light setup if the bait and applied pressure cannot make it penetrate. Why the Right Rig Matters in Australian Fishing explains how the hook, leader, sinker and complete rig change with the fishing ground and conditions.

sections.heading: The Same Species May Need a Different Hook
sections.text: A species chart cannot account for every bait, rig and location. The same fish may be targeted with a small bait on a lighter estuary rig, a long bait in surf wash or a larger bait beside reef and structure. Each change can alter the required hook size, arrangement and wire gauge. Choose for the actual bait and setup being used that day. The target species remains important, but it does not make the other decisions for you.

sections.heading: Diagnose the Problem Before Changing Hooks
sections.text: When a hook-up is missed or a fish is lost, inspect what comes back. If the point is buried, change how the bait is rigged or use a larger hook If the bait has folded around the gape, straighten and secure it before the next cast If the point is dull, sharpen a suitable reusable hook or replace it If the hook has opened, assess engagement, gauge, drag pressure and previous damage If a circle hook repeatedly fails to connect, check the baited gape and how pressure is being applied Changing brands without finding the cause may simply reproduce the same failure. Common Fishing Rig Mistakes—And How to Fix Them covers other mismatches that can appear to be hook problems.

sections.heading: A Practical Hook-Selection Order
sections.text: Choose the hook in this order: Select the bait and decide whether it needs one hook, two hooks or a gang Choose a hook pattern suited to how the rig will be fished Check the actual hook size against the bait Make sure the point and gape remain exposed Match the wire gauge to the expected load, leader and drag pressure Inspect the point, shape, eye and surface condition before use Use the Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide to compare the main rig systems, or use the Rig Finder to narrow complete rigs by species, bait, fishing location and conditions. The best hook is the one that fits the bait, operates by the intended hook-setting method and has the correct gauge for the complete setup. Keep the point and gape exposed. Apply pressure in the way the hook pattern requires. If something fails, inspect the evidence before blaming the hook. Once those decisions match, hook choice becomes much simpler—and the hook has a much better chance of doing its job properly. BAIT UP. CAST IN. HANG ON.

documents.title: Common Fishing Rig Mistakes (And How to Fix Them)
documents.description: Fishing rig problems usually begin with a mismatch somewhere in the setup.

sections.heading: Common Fishing Rig Mistakes (And How to Fix Them)
sections.text: Fishing rig problems usually begin with a mismatch somewhere in the setup. The hook may not suit the bait, the leader may be too light for the ground, the sinker may not control the rig in the current, or the rig layout may allow the bait trace to twist and tangle. These mistakes can lead to: • Missed hook-ups • Baits spinning or folding during the cast • Bite-offs and leader damage • Twisted or tangled bait traces • Sinkers repeatedly snagging • Rigs failing when a better fish is hooked The correct fix depends on what is going wrong. A rig that casts badly requires a different change from one that tangles in current, snags during retrieval or loses fish around structure. This guide explains the most common fishing rig mistakes and the practical changes that help Australian fishos avoid them. Not sure which rig style suits your target species, fishing location and conditions? Start with the Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide

sections.heading: 1. Using a Rig That Does Not Suit the Job
sections.text: The same species can require very different rigs depending on where and how it is being targeted. A running-sinker rig may allow a bait to move naturally across clean estuary ground, while a paternoster rig provides greater control in current and holds the bait above the seabed. A long-cast pulley rig keeps the bait close to the sinker during flight when additional casting distance is needed. A wire bite trace becomes important when tailor, mackerel, sharks or other toothy species may take the bait. Before choosing a rig, consider: • The target species • The bait being used • Water depth and current • Sand, reef, rock, weed or other ground • The required casting distance • Whether toothy species are likely Choose the rig for the job it needs to perform, not simply because it has worked somewhere else. Use the Rig Finder Tool when you need to compare rigs against the target species, fishing location, bait and conditions.

sections.heading: 2. Matching the Hook to the Fish but Not the Bait
sections.text: Hook size is often chosen solely from the target species. The bait must also fit the hook correctly. A hook that is too small can become buried inside a thick bait. An unnecessarily large hook may make a small bait difficult to rig naturally. The hook point and gape must remain exposed after baiting. If either is buried, the hook may not make proper contact when a fish takes the bait. Longer baits may also require more than one hook. Ganged hooks, adjustable sliding-snell rigs and fixed twin-hook rigs provide different ways of positioning hooks along pilchards, whole fish, squid and strip baits. Match the hook arrangement to the bait’s length and thickness. • The bait sits straight • The hook point remains exposed • The hook gape is not packed with bait • Multiple hooks are spaced along the bait rather than bunched together • The hook style suits the way the rig will be fished Learn more in Fishing Hooks Explained – Types, Sizes & Materials

sections.heading: 3. Choosing Leader Strength from Fish Size Alone
sections.text: Leader strength must account for the ground as well as the fish. A smaller fish hooked beside oysters, reef, pylons or rocks can damage a light leader faster than a larger fish caught over clean sand. As practical starting points: • 20lb mono is commonly used for lighter estuary and whiting rigs • 40–60lb mono covers many surf and general coastal rigs • 60–100lb mono is more appropriate around reef, heavier structure and larger fish • Sharks and large toothy species require purpose-built wire bite traces and, where necessary, heavier mono rub leaders These are not fixed rules. Leader strength should increase when abrasion risk, structure, bait size or the expected fish demands it. Use enough strength and abrasion resistance for the ground being fished without automatically making every rig as heavy as possible. Inspect the leader regularly. A leader that was suitable when new may no longer be reliable after rubbing against reef, rocks, teeth or rough skin.

sections.heading: 4. Using the Wrong Sinker or Sinker Weight
sections.text: The sinker controls where the rig fishes and how the bait behaves. Too little weight allows the rig to wash away from the intended area. Too much weight can unnecessarily pin the bait in place and make the complete setup harder to cast and manage. Sinker style also matters: • Ball and bean sinkers suit running-sinker rigs where the line must move through or beside the sinker • Star and breakaway sinkers provide greater grip in surf and stronger current • Paternoster rigs use a sinker at the bottom to keep the baited hooks fishing above the seabed • Slide baiting requires a firmly anchored breakaway sinker so the trolley can travel down the tensioned mainline Some purpose-built rigs are supplied with a fitted sinker. On these rigs, changing the sinker normally requires cutting and rebuilding part of the setup. Use enough sinker weight to control the rig in the conditions while remaining within the rod and line rating. If the rig repeatedly moves away from the fishing area, increase the holding power. If the bait is unnecessarily pinned down in relatively calm water, a lighter or more mobile sinker arrangement may be more suitable.

sections.heading: 5. Rigging the Bait Without Checking Its Shape
sections.text: A bait that is folded, twisted or hanging loosely can spin during the cast and in the current. This creates drag, reduces casting distance and can twist the bait trace around the backbone. Long baits require the hooks to be positioned along their natural shape. Adjustable sliding-snell rigs allow the spacing to be changed for each bait, while ganged hooks support long fish baits such as pilchards and garfish. • Lay the bait straight along the hooks • Adjust the hook spacing to suit that individual bait • Keep every hook point and gape exposed • Trim loose sections that will flap or spin • Use a small amount of bait elastic where needed Bait elastic can help prevent softer or longer baits from folding, spinning or tearing away during the cast. See Sliding Snell Rigs Explained for adjustable twin-hook bait rigging.

sections.heading: 6. Ignoring the Cause of Repeated Tangles
sections.text: A tangled rig is not always caused by casting technique. Common causes include: • A bait trace long enough to wrap around the backbone • Paternoster arms or traces reaching each other • A folded or spinning bait • Excessive slack before or during the cast • Damaged mono retaining tight coils • A rig layout unsuited to the current Simply untangling the rig and casting it again does not correct the cause. Lay the rig out before casting and check whether the bait trace can reach the backbone, sinker or another hook. Keep the rig under controlled tension during the cast, streamline the bait and replace leader that remains heavily coiled or damaged. When using a paternoster, the arms and bait traces should hold the hooks away from the backbone without allowing them to overlap excessively. See Paternoster Rigs Explained for more information about sinker position, backbone layout and paternoster arms.

sections.heading: 7. Using the Correct Rig Incorrectly
sections.text: Some rigs only work properly when their operating parts are set correctly. • A running sinker must be able to move freely • The hook on a long-cast pulley rig must be seated correctly beneath the impact shield before casting • Sliding-snell hook spacing must be adjusted for each bait • A slide bait trolley must travel all the way to the stopper before fishing begins • Circle hooks need room to rotate and should not have the point or gape buried in the bait Buying the correct rig does not correct an incorrect setup. Understand how the rig is designed to work before casting it. Check every moving, sliding, locking or release component and confirm that the bait has not prevented it from operating. The Fishing Rigs Explained hub contains detailed guides covering the main rig systems and how each one works.

sections.heading: 8. Adding Components Without Knowing Their Purpose
sections.text: Floats, beads, luminous tubing and flasher material can all provide a genuine advantage when used for the right reason. Problems begin when components are added without considering what they change. A float can lift the bait above the bottom. Flasher material adds colour, reflection and movement. Luminous components provide contrast in low light. Beads may protect knots, space components or add attraction. None of them needs to be added automatically to every rig. Every component should have a clear job. Match added attraction to: • Water clarity • Available light • Current and bait movement • The required bait position • The species being targeted Use stronger colour and contrast when visibility is reduced, then use a more restrained setup when fish can inspect the bait clearly. Learn more in Using Colour and Contrast in Rigs to Trigger More Bites and When Should You Use Flasher Rigs?

sections.heading: 9. Reusing a Rig Without Inspecting It
sections.text: A rig may appear intact after landing a fish or retrieving it from rough ground, but small areas of damage can weaken it considerably. • Abrasion or flattened sections of mono • Kinks or broken coating on wire • Crimps that have moved or become damaged • Blunt, bent or corroded hooks • Swivels that no longer rotate freely • Clips that have opened or distorted • Knots showing movement or damage Pay particular attention to the section closest to the hook and any part that has contacted reef, rocks, teeth or rough skin. Run your fingers carefully along mono leaders and inspect wire, hooks and connections before using the rig again. Replace a damaged rig or component before the next cast. Finding the damage on the beach is much better than discovering it when the next fish loads the line.

sections.heading: Diagnose the Problem Before Changing the Rig
sections.text: Avoid changing the complete setup without identifying what actually went wrong. • The bait spins — straighten it, reduce loose bait and use bait elastic where needed • The rig tangles — check trace length, spacing, bait shape and casting tension • The sinker moves — increase its weight or holding power • The bait is unnecessarily pinned down — consider a lighter or running-sinker setup • The leader returns abraded — increase abrasion resistance and inspect the fishing ground • Toothy fish bite through the trace — use suitable wire bite protection • Fish take the bait without hooking up — inspect the baited hook point, gape, size and position • The rig snags during retrieval — reconsider the sinker arrangement and the rig style being used over that ground Correcting the specific problem is more effective than adding more components or changing everything at once. Most fishing rig mistakes are visible before the cast if you know what to check. Match the rig to the bait, species, current and ground. Keep the hook points exposed, use an appropriate sinker, inspect every connection and understand how the rig is supposed to operate. A fishing rig does not need to be complicated. It needs to perform the job required without creating another problem elsewhere in the setup. Not sure which rig suits your next trip? Use the Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide, explore the Fishing Rigs Explained guides or use the Rig Finder Tool to narrow the options. BAIT UP. CAST IN. HANG ON.

documents.title: Field Notes from Swains – What the Reef Taught Us
documents.description: Swains Reef is a teacher that doesn’t go easy on anyone. Every trip out there is a mix of chaos, adrenaline, and lessons you don’t forget.

sections.heading: Field Notes from Swains – What the Reef Taught Us
sections.text: Swains Reef is a teacher that doesn’t go easy on anyone. Every trip out there is a mix of chaos, adrenaline, and lessons you don’t forget. Over the years — and plenty of busted leaders later — we’ve learned what works, what doesn’t, and why your gear is the difference between a good story and a fish in the esky. The Swains Slayer Series™ was born from those lessons, but what we learned applies anywhere serious reef fish live around coral structure. Many of the ideas behind these lessons eventually shaped the Swains Slayer Series™ itself. If you're interested in how real encounters with trout, emperor and mackerel influenced the final rig designs, see Tested on the Reef: The Story Behind the Swains Slayer Series™. Here’s what the reef taught us. If you're unsure how offshore rigs change between reef systems and species, start with the Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide, which explains how rig design shifts across environments.

sections.heading: 1. Length Matters – Especially on Big Boats
sections.text: Most Swains trips are on large charter boats. That means you’re fishing from high gunwales with heavy braid. If your rig is too short, you’ll end up lifting big, angry fish with bare braid in your hands — and that’s a shortcut to sliced palms. That’s why Slayer rigs are built longer, so you can handline mono safely and control fish boatside instead of trusting your fingers to braided line under load. Pro tip: Even if you tie your own rigs, make sure you’ve got enough mono leader to safely reach your fish. It’s one of the simplest ways to avoid injury and lost fish.

sections.heading: 2. Braid is Brutal – Protect Yourself and Your Gear
sections.text: Braid is thin, sharp and unforgiving under tension. When reef fish hit hard in current, braid transfers shock instantly. One of the biggest lessons from fishing Swains was learning to let the rig absorb punishment instead of your hands doing it. Strategic mono and wire sections reduce direct braid contact during the fight and lift. Pro tip: Always carry gloves. Reef fish don’t care about your skin.

sections.heading: 3. Shock Absorption Saves Fish
sections.text: Swains current is relentless, and when a big fish smashes your bait the shock load on your gear can be enormous. Straight braid systems with no stretch lose fish surprisingly often during the first run. That’s why every Slayer rig includes mono sections that act as built-in shock absorbers. That small amount of stretch dramatically improves hook security when large trout, emperor and reef predators surge for cover. Pro tip: If your system has zero forgiveness, expect bust-offs. Add controlled stretch where it matters.

sections.heading: 4. Bright Days Call for Flash
sections.text: Clear blue reef water changes how fish respond to presentations. Some days subtle wins. Other days flash triggers instant reaction bites. That’s why skirts, flashers and glow beads appear on selected Slayer rigs. They aren’t decoration — they’re strike triggers tested under real reef conditions. Learn how colour and contrast influence strike behaviour in Using Colour and Contrast in Rigs to Trigger More Bites. Pro tip: Carry both plain and enhanced rigs. Let the fish decide which version they want.

sections.heading: 5. Wire Where It Counts
sections.text: Spanish mackerel, sharks and reef pests are part of life at Swains. Losing fish to bite-offs teaches expensive lessons quickly. That’s why wire is used only where needed in the Slayer rigs — enough protection to prevent bite-offs without compromising presentation. Pro tip: Cheap wire fails faster than people expect. Use quality trace wire or expect heartbreak.

sections.heading: 6. Preparation is Everything
sections.text: Swains Reef isn’t the place to experiment mid-session. The fishos who fish best arrive ready. Every Slayer rig is packed ready-to-fish because when reef fish switch on, time spent tying knots is time spent watching someone else wind up fish. Pro tip: Pack twice as many rigs as you think you’ll need. Sharks, coral and missed hooksets will burn through them fast. Swains Reef is one of Australia’s toughest and most rewarding fisheries. It doesn’t hand out easy wins, but prepared fishos who understand rig length, abrasion control and presentation mechanics consistently do better. Want to see how these lessons translated into specific rig layouts for coral trout, red emperor and reef predators? The Tested on the Reef: The Story Behind the Swains Slayer Series™ article walks through how each rig in the range earned its place. Fishing coral structure somewhere other than Swains? The same rig principles apply anywhere trout, emperor and reef predators live around hard reef edges. For a broader breakdown of reef-specific leader strength, sinker weight and rig layouts used across Australian coral systems, see the Best Reef Fishing Rigs in Australia guide → Explore the Swains Slayer Series™ to see how those lessons shaped the rigs. Not sure which offshore rig suits your conditions? Start with the Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide.

documents.title: Fishing Crimps Explained: Why Wire Rigs Fail — and How to Stop It
documents.description: A fishing crimp is a small load-bearing connection. If it slips, damages the trace or creates a sharp stress point, the strength of the hook and wire no longer matters.

sections.heading: Fishing Crimps Explained: Why Wire Rigs Fail — and How to Stop It
sections.text: A fishing crimp is a small load-bearing connection. If it slips, damages the trace or creates a sharp stress point, the strength of the hook and wire no longer matters. Crimp failures are rarely caused by the sleeve being inherently weak. They usually begin with a mismatch between the trace, sleeve, crimping tool and compression method. There is no universal crimp material, sleeve size or squeezing pressure that suits every wire rig. Reliable connections come from treating the complete crimping system as one matched set. This guide explains what must match, how common failures develop and what fishos should inspect before trusting a crimped wire trace.

sections.heading: What a Fishing Crimp Must Do
sections.text: A crimp sleeve secures the trace by applying controlled pressure over a specified length of line or cable. The connection must provide enough grip to prevent movement under load without crushing the wire, cutting individual strands or creating a sharp transition at the edge of the sleeve. More pressure does not automatically produce more strength. Too little compression may allow the trace to slip. Too much can deform the sleeve excessively, damage a coating or weaken the cable inside it. The aim is not to make the sleeve look as flat or tight as possible. It is to form the sleeve in the way intended for that trace, crimp and tool.

sections.heading: The Four Parts That Must Match
sections.text: A reliable crimped connection depends on four compatible parts: The trace material and construction The finished outside diameter of the trace The sleeve material, shape and internal size The crimping tool and correct die cavity Changing any one of these can change the finished connection. A sleeve that works on one uncoated cable may not suit a coated trace with a different finished diameter. A crimping die that forms one sleeve correctly may flatten or under-compress another. Choose components from their stated specifications rather than appearance alone.

sections.heading: Match the Sleeve to the Finished Trace Diameter
sections.text: The relevant measurement is the diameter that actually passes through the sleeve. On coated wire, that normally means accounting for the coating as part of the finished diameter unless the particular connection system specifically instructs otherwise. Forcing coated wire through a sleeve that is too small can scrape, cut or bunch the coating before crimping even begins.

sections.heading: When the Sleeve Is Too Large
sections.text: An oversized sleeve may still appear secure after being squeezed, but the tool may not close it evenly around the trace. Possible results include: The trace slipping gradually under load Uneven grip along the sleeve A loop changing size during use The connection holding during a light pull but moving under a stronger load

sections.heading: When the Sleeve Is Too Small
sections.text: An undersized sleeve can damage the trace while it is being assembled or compressed. Cut or distorted coating Compressed or displaced cable strands A sharp internal pressure point Damage hidden beneath the finished sleeve “Close enough” is not a useful sizing method. Use the trace diameter and sleeve specification together.

sections.heading: Copper, Aluminium and Other Sleeve Materials
sections.text: Sleeve material cannot be selected reliably from one rule such as “copper for heavy rigs” or “aluminium for everything else.” Fishing sleeves are produced in different materials and shapes for different mono, cable and wire systems. The correct choice depends on the trace construction, sleeve specification, crimping tool and intended load. Saltwater also makes material compatibility and corrosion important. Dissimilar metals can react in a wet, salty environment, but that does not make one sleeve material universally superior. The correct response is to use a specified compatible system, then inspect it for corrosion and damage. Do not substitute a sleeve simply because its colour or outside size looks similar. Two sleeves that appear alike may have different internal dimensions, wall thickness or forming requirements.

sections.heading: Single-Barrel and Double-Barrel Sleeves
sections.text: Single-barrel and double-barrel sleeves are different designs, not interchangeable shapes that should be squeezed however the tool happens to close them. A double-barrel sleeve keeps the outgoing and returning sections of trace in separate channels. A single-barrel sleeve carries both sections through one opening. Each design requires a matching die and the correct forming method. Some sleeves are intended to finish oval, while others have their own defined profile. The useful rule is not “round beats flat.” It is: preserve the intended sleeve shape and avoid sharp edges, cracked surfaces or uncontrolled flattening.

sections.heading: Why Ordinary Pliers Are Not Crimping Tools
sections.text: General-purpose pliers apply pressure wherever their jaws happen to contact the sleeve. They do not provide a matched cavity that controls the final shape and diameter. Flatten the sleeve unevenly Create sharp edges Leave one area loose and another over-compressed Cut or distort coated wire Produce a different result every time A dedicated fishing crimper uses sized die cavities to form compatible sleeves consistently. The marked die must match the sleeve system being used; choosing the cavity by guesswork defeats the purpose of the tool.

sections.heading: Compression Position Matters
sections.text: A crimp can use the correct sleeve and tool but still be damaged by poor compression placement. Crushing directly over the extreme edge of a sleeve can create a hard, sharp transition where the flexible trace exits the connection. Randomly overlapping compressions can also leave an uneven finished profile. Follow the sleeve and tool instructions for: The correct die cavity The number of compressions Their order and spacing The required distance from each end The correct finished profile Do not invent a universal compression pattern. A technique suitable for one sleeve length and tool may be wrong for another.

sections.heading: Loop Size and Trace Alignment
sections.text: The trace should enter and leave the sleeve cleanly without crossing, twisting or being forced against a sharp component. A loop that is unnecessarily large may allow excessive movement. A loop pulled hard against a hook eye or swivel can create an abrupt bend and concentrate wear. Before crimping, check that: Both sections of trace sit correctly inside the sleeve The loop suits the hook, swivel or attachment point The trace is not crossed or kinked The sleeve is positioned away from sharp edges The returning tag is long enough to remain securely captured

sections.heading: How Crimped Wire Connections Commonly Fail
sections.text: The trace moves through the sleeve because the sleeve is oversized, the die is too large, the compression is incomplete or the components are incompatible.

sections.heading: Damage Beneath the Sleeve
sections.text: Over-compression, an undersized sleeve or the wrong die damages strands or coating where the problem cannot be seen easily.

sections.heading: Failure Beside the Sleeve
sections.text: A sharp sleeve edge, compression too close to the end, a kink or a poorly aligned loop concentrates repeated bending at one point. Saltwater retained around the connection can attack the sleeve, trace or nearby hardware. Surface staining, pitting, swelling or a damaged coating requires closer inspection and usually replacement.

sections.heading: Fatigue and Previous Damage
sections.text: A connection may survive one heavy load and still be damaged. Snags, tooth contact, rough skin, reef and repeated flexing can reduce the reliability of a rig that still appears complete. For a wider fault-finding guide, see Why Fishing Rigs Fail at the Worst Possible Moment.

sections.heading: Inspect Every Finished Crimp
sections.text: A finished connection should be checked before it is trusted. Reject it if you find: A cracked, split or sharply flattened sleeve Cut, bunched or displaced coating Trace strands damaged beside the sleeve An uneven or incorrect finished profile Movement when the connection is loaded appropriately Corrosion, kinks or abrasion near the join Test a new combination of trace, sleeve and tool before using it in a fishing rig. Do not make the first trial connection on a rig intended for a large fish.

sections.heading: Check Crimps Before Reusing a Rig
sections.text: Inspect crimped wire rigs after a fish, snag or hard session and before the next cast. Pay attention to the section immediately beside each sleeve. Look for wire kinks, broken coating, corrosion, displaced strands and any change in the loop or tag position. A sleeve is not reusable. If a connection must be changed or there is doubt about its condition, rebuild it with a new compatible sleeve.

sections.heading: How Wiggle ya Worm Approaches Crimped Rigs
sections.text: On crimped wire rigs, the connection is treated as part of the load-bearing system rather than a finishing detail. Matching the sleeve to the trace system Using dedicated crimping tools and suitable die cavities Applying controlled, repeatable compression Checking trace alignment and the finished sleeve Rejecting connections that show damage or inconsistency The Shark Fishing Rigs Explained guide shows how the hook, wire bite trace, mono rub leader and complete rig layout work together for Australian land-based shark fishing. You can also browse the Wiggle ya Worm shark fishing rig range to compare coated wire, heavy mono and different hook sizes. A reliable fishing crimp is not created by squeezing harder. Match the trace, sleeve, tool and die. Follow the forming method intended for that system. Inspect the finished connection and replace it when damage or doubt appears. The crimp may be one of the smallest parts of a wire rig, but it carries the load between every component on either side of it. BAIT UP. CAST IN. HANG ON.

documents.title: Fishing Hooks Explained – Types, Sizes & Materials
documents.description: A fishing hook must suit the bait before it can work properly on the fish.

sections.heading: Fishing Hooks Explained – Types, Sizes & Materials
sections.text: A fishing hook must suit the bait before it can work properly on the fish. If the hook is too small for the bait, the point and gape can become buried. If it is unnecessarily large, a smaller bait may be difficult to rig straight and securely. The hook pattern then needs to suit how the rig will be fished. A circle hook works differently from a J hook, while a long bait may need ganged hooks or an adjustable twin-hook arrangement rather than one hook positioned at the front. This guide explains hook sizes, common bait-hook patterns, wire gauge, materials and finishes so fishos can choose by function instead of relying on a species name printed on a packet. For a closer look at bait fit, see Choosing the Right Fishing Hook—Why Most Fishos Get It Wrong.

sections.heading: How Fishing Hook Sizes Work
sections.text: Fishing-hook numbering runs in two directions. Numbered sizes become larger as the number decreases. A size 6 is larger than a size 10, and size 1 is larger again. Ought sizes begin at 1/0 and become larger as the first number increases. A 6/0 is larger than a 3/0 within the same hook pattern and range. Hook sizes are not an exact universal measurement. Two hooks marked 6/0 can have different shank lengths, gapes, wire thicknesses and overall dimensions when they come from different manufacturers or use different patterns. Use the size number as a starting point, then inspect the actual hook against the bait.

sections.heading: Match Hook Size to the Bait
sections.text: The hook must be large enough to pass through the bait while leaving the point and gape clear. The bait sits straight rather than folding around the hook The hook point remains completely exposed The gape is not packed with bait The bait is supported firmly enough to survive the cast The hook arrangement covers the useful length of a longer bait Worms, pipis and small prawn pieces generally need a different hook shape and wire gauge from squid strips, whole pilchards or large fish baits. Long baits may require ganged hooks, a fixed twin-hook rig or an adjustable sliding-snell arrangement. The Sliding Snell Rigs Explained guide shows how hook spacing can be changed to suit each bait.

sections.heading: Recurve Circle Hooks
sections.text: A recurve circle hook has a point that turns back towards the shank. As steady pressure comes onto the line, the hook is designed to travel towards the edge of the mouth and rotate into the jaw corner. Striking hard like a J hook can pull it away before it has rotated. Keep the point and gape clear of bait so the hook has room to turn. Circle hooks are widely used on paternoster, running-sinker, sliding-snell, reef and shark rigs where the fish can load the line. A J hook has a more open point and is commonly used when the fisho controls the hook set. It suits active fishing where a bite is detected and the hook is set by lifting or striking with the rod. The timing and force required depend on the bait, target fish and hook size. Beak hooks have a point curved inward towards the shank. They are strong general bait hooks used in many single-hook and twin-hook rigs. Beak describes the hook shape; it should not automatically be treated as another name for every J hook or octopus hook. Octopus hooks normally have a short shank, wide gape and an eye suited to snelling. The term describes the hook pattern, not one single point shape. Octopus-style hooks are available in conventional and circle-hook forms, so check the actual point and instructions rather than relying on the word “octopus” alone. The longer shank provides more room for threading worms, pipis, prawns and other narrow baits. It can also make a small hook easier to hold and remove. Long-shank hooks are not a substitute for a suitable wire trace when bite protection is required.

sections.heading: O’Shaughnessy and Ganged Hooks
sections.text: O’Shaughnessy hooks use a strong, relatively straight pattern commonly found in ganged-hook arrangements. Ganged hooks are several hooks linked together rather than one separate hook pattern. They support long fish baits such as pilchards and garfish while placing hook points along the bait.

sections.heading: Hook Gauge: Fine Wire or Heavy Wire
sections.text: Hook size and wire gauge are different measurements. Two hooks with similar overall dimensions may use very different wire thicknesses. Fine-wire hooks require less force to penetrate and add less weight to small or soft baits. Their lower strength must still suit the leader, drag pressure and expected fish. Heavy-wire hooks provide greater resistance to opening under high load. They also require more force to penetrate, making a sharp point and clear hook gape particularly important. Do not choose heavy wire simply because it looks stronger. Match the gauge to the bait, tackle, drag pressure, target fish and ground being fished.

sections.heading: Hook Materials and Finishes
sections.text: The base metal, heat treatment, wire gauge and finish all affect how a hook performs. The colour alone does not identify its strength.

sections.heading: Carbon-Steel Hooks
sections.text: Many fishing hooks are made from carbon steel because it can provide a strong, sharp hook in a wide range of wire gauges. Carbon steel can corrode when its protective finish is damaged or salt is left on the hook. Rinse reusable rigs with fresh water, allow them to dry and inspect the hook before the next trip.

sections.heading: Stainless-Steel Hooks
sections.text: Stainless steel provides greater corrosion resistance, but it is not maintenance-free. Salt deposits, damaged surfaces and crevices around the eye can still develop corrosion or pitting. “Chemically sharpened” describes how the point is finished; it is not a type of hook material and should not be used to compare carbon steel with stainless steel.

sections.heading: Coatings and Coloured Finishes
sections.text: Black nickel, tin, PTFE-style and bronze-coloured finishes are applied to steel hooks for purposes that may include corrosion protection, lower surface friction and colour. A hook described as bronze is normally a steel hook with a bronze-coloured finish, not a hook made from solid bronze. A finish can protect the surface, but its colour does not determine the hook’s strength or suitability.

sections.heading: How to Inspect a Hook
sections.text: Check the hook before baiting and again after contact with reef, rocks, fish teeth or hard ground. A dull point does not automatically mean the hook must be replaced. Larger, more expensive hooks—particularly heavy stainless-steel shark hooks—can normally be resharpened with a hook file or sharpening stone. Unlike some smaller factory-finished hooks, these larger hooks do not depend on a hardened surface point that would be removed by careful filing. After sharpening, check that the point has the correct shape, shows no cracks or serious pitting and catches readily against a fingernail. Replace the hook if the damage cannot be removed without substantially changing or shortening the point. Replace the hook or complete rig if: The point is rolled, bent, cracked or cannot be restored correctly The gape has opened or the shank is distorted Rust or pitting has developed The eye, join or connection is damaged The protective finish has broken away around a damaged section A hook that has opened under load should be replaced rather than bent back and trusted again.

sections.heading: A Practical Hook-Selection Order
sections.text: Choose the hook in this order: Select the bait and decide whether it needs one hook, two hooks or a gang Choose a hook pattern suited to how the rig will be fished Check the bait leaves the point and gape exposed Match the wire gauge to the expected load, leader and drag pressure Inspect the hook’s point, shape, eye and surface condition The Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide compares the main rig systems, while the Rig Finder matches complete rigs to the species, bait, fishing location and conditions. The hook-size number alone cannot tell you whether a hook suits the job. Look at the actual hook beside the bait. Check the pattern, gape, shank length and wire gauge, then make sure the point remains exposed after baiting. A well-matched hook holds the bait correctly, engages as intended and has enough strength for the complete setup without being unnecessarily heavy. BAIT UP. CAST IN. HANG ON.

documents.title: How Long Cast Pulley Rigs Really Work (And Why Some Cast Further)
documents.description: What a Long Cast Pulley Rig Is (Quick Recap)

sections.heading: What a Long Cast Pulley Rig Is (Quick Recap)
sections.text: A long cast pulley rig is built to cast farther than a normal bait rig. It does that by locking the hook and bait behind and in line with the sinker so they travel through the air as one compact unit. The streamlined rig is more aerodynamic, prevents the bait from helicoptering and reduces wind resistance. That is the main reason for using one—but it is not the only advantage. After the hook releases, the line can move through the pulley bead. When a fish is hooked and pressure comes onto the rig, that pulley action raises the sinker from the seabed and brings it into line during the fight and retrieval. The sinker is therefore less likely to trail below the fish and catch on reef, rock or other bottom structure. This guide explains both halves of the system: how a pulley rig casts and what the pulley action does after a fish takes the bait. See the complete Long Casting Pulley Rig Guide for the full setup, rig range and fishing uses.

sections.heading: Why a Pulley Rig Casts Further
sections.text: A normal bait rig may have the hook and bait hanging away from the sinker during the cast. As the rig accelerates, the bait can spin, swing or fold back against the airflow. That movement creates drag and wastes part of the casting force. On a long cast pulley rig, the hook is locked beneath the trigger arm of the impact shield. The bait sits behind and in line with the sinker during the cast, making the complete rig more aerodynamic and reducing wind resistance. This creates a much smaller shape in the air and reduces resistance throughout the cast. The difference is particularly useful with longer fish baits, squid and strip baits that would otherwise move around during flight. The weight of the sinker pulls down on one side of the pulley loop while the mainline pulls up through the pulley bead. That opposing force keeps the hook locked in the impact shield.

sections.heading: How the Pulley Loop Holds Everything Together
sections.text: The line passes through the pulley bead, allowing both sides of the loop to equalise automatically. As the sinker pulls downward, the hook side of the loop is drawn upward until the hook is held firmly beneath the impact-shield trigger arm. The hook and bait near the sinker The pulley loop under tension The complete rig straight during the cast The bait from spinning independently around the sinker

sections.heading: How the Impact Shield Releases the Hook
sections.text: The opening image shows the three stages of the Wiggle ya Worm impact-shield release: locked, releasing and released.

sections.heading: Stage 1: Locked for the Cast
sections.text: The hook sits beneath the trigger arm of the impact shield The hook sits in front of the leader line passing through the impact shield The sliding bead sits against the fixed crimp above the shield The sinker pulls down while the mainline pulls up through the pulley bead This tensions the pulley loop and keeps the bait, hook and sinker together during flight.

sections.heading: Stage 2: Releasing on Splashdown
sections.text: When the sinker hits the water, it slows sharply and the impact shield moves upward towards the fixed crimp. The sliding bead contacts the fixed crimp, forcing the bead and the leader line passing through it to move down the arm of the impact shield.

sections.heading: Stage 3: Hook Released
sections.text: As the bead and leader line move down the arm, the leader line mechanically pushes the hook off the trigger arm. The hook and bait are released, the pulley loop unlocks and the rig begins fishing normally.

sections.heading: Why Hook and Leader Position Matter
sections.text: The release depends on the hook sitting in front of the leader line that passes through the impact shield. When the sliding bead contacts the fixed crimp, it forces the leader line down the arm behind the hook. The leader line then mechanically pushes the hook off the arm. If the hook is placed behind the leader line, the leader cannot push it off the arm and the hook will remain locked in the impact shield.

sections.heading: Why Some Pulley-Rig Setups Cast Further Than Others
sections.text: The main difference is how much air resistance the complete baited rig creates. A straight bait held behind and in line with the sinker presents a smaller shape to the airflow than a bulky or loosely rigged bait. Less resistance allows more of the casting force to carry the sinker and bait forward. For the cleanest flight: Keep the bait straight along the hook or hooks Use bait elastic where needed to stop long or soft baits folding Remove loose sections that can catch the air Keep the bait behind and in line with the sinker The rig casts further because the bait and sinker remain in line and create less drag.

sections.heading: What Happens After a Fish Is Hooked
sections.text: Once the impact shield has released the hook, the line is free to move through the pulley bead. When a fish takes the bait and the mainline comes under pressure, the hook section pulls through the pulley bead. This shortens the sinker side of the rig and raises the sinker from the seabed. Instead of the sinker remaining below the fish and dragging along the bottom, it is brought up towards the pulley bead and into line with the rest of the rig. This gives the pulley rig an important advantage during the fight: The sinker spends less time dragging across the seabed It is less likely to wedge into rock, reef or other structure The fisho maintains a straighter connection to the fish The complete rig is easier to retrieve over rough or broken ground The same pulley action continues during retrieval, keeping the sinker raised and in line rather than allowing it to hang well below the hook trace.

sections.heading: Where a Long Cast Pulley Rig Is Most Useful
sections.text: Long cast pulley rigs are particularly useful when fish are holding beyond the comfortable range of a normal bait rig. Beyond an inside beach gutter On the far edge of a sandbank In deeper water reached from the beach or rocks Over rough ground where the sinker may snag during the fight When a longer bait must remain secure during a powerful cast The Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide compares pulley rigs with the other main bait-rig layouts used in Australian fishing.

sections.heading: Quick-Change Long Cast Pulley Rigs
sections.text: The Quick-Change Long Cast System uses the same pulley and impact-shield mechanics with a reusable backbone and interchangeable hook traces. The backbone continues to provide the casting and pulley action, while the hook trace can be changed to suit a different bait, hook arrangement, leader strength or target fish. This allows fishos to change the fishing end of the rig without replacing the complete long cast pulley system. A long cast pulley rig has two clear advantages. During the cast, it locks the hook and bait behind and in line with the sinker, reduces wind resistance and casts further than a normal bait rig. After a fish is hooked, the line travels through the pulley bead, raises the sinker from the bottom and brings it into line during the fight and retrieval. This reduces the chance of the sinker snagging below the fish. The impact shield provides the change between those two stages. It holds the hook during flight, then mechanically releases it on splashdown so the pulley rig can fish as intended. BAIT UP. CAST FURTHER. HANG ON.

documents.title: How to Clean & Cook Your Catch: Reef Fish Recipes & Techniques
documents.description: There’s nothing better than dropping a bait on the reef, feeling that hit, and hauling up a fish you’ll remember forever. But what happens after the photo? Knowing how to clean and cook your catch properly turns a great ...

sections.heading: How to Clean & Cook Your Catch: Reef Fish Recipes & Techniques
sections.text: There’s nothing better than dropping a bait on the reef, feeling that hit, and hauling up a fish you’ll remember forever. But what happens after the photo? Knowing how to clean and cook your catch properly turns a great fishing trip into an unforgettable meal. Whether it’s a coral trout, red emperor, sweetlip, or nannygai, here’s your quick guide to getting the most from your reef fish — from the cleaning table to the dinner plate.

sections.heading: Cleaning Your Catch – The Right Way
sections.text: Cleaning reef fish isn’t hard but doing it right makes a huge difference to the quality of your meal. Here’s how to do it like a pro:

sections.heading: 1. Bleed Your Fish Immediately
sections.text: The moment you’ve boated your fish, cut through the gills and let it bleed in a bucket of seawater. This simple step: Keeps the flesh firm and white. Reduces the “fishy” taste. Makes filleting cleaner and easier later.

sections.heading: 2. Ice Is Your Best Friend
sections.text: Get your fish onto ice as soon as possible. Cold fish = fresher taste, and it makes cleaning much easier when you’re back at the filleting table.

sections.heading: 3. Fillet with a Sharp Knife
sections.text: Use a flexible, razor-sharp filleting knife and follow these steps: Lay the fish flat and make a cut behind the gill plate. Run the knife along the spine toward the tail in one clean motion. Flip and repeat for the other side. Remove the rib bones and pin bones for boneless fillets. Pro tip: Keep your knife clean and sharp. Reef fish have tough scales and thicker bones than estuary species, so a dull blade will tear the flesh.

sections.heading: Cooking Reef Fish – Simple, Fresh, Delicious
sections.text: The beauty of reef fish like coral trout, red emperor, sweetlip, and snapper is their delicate, sweet flesh. You don’t need fancy recipes — just techniques that let the fish shine.

sections.heading: 1. Pan-Fried Fillets
sections.text: Perfect for coral trout, sweetlip, or small red emperor. Lightly coat the fillets in flour, salt, and pepper. Heat a little butter and olive oil in a pan. Cook for 2–3 minutes per side until just cooked through. Finish with a squeeze of lemon.

sections.heading: 2. Whole Baked Fish
sections.text: For larger fish like snapper or red emperor: Score the fish deeply on both sides. Stuff the cavity with lemon slices, garlic, and fresh herbs. Rub olive oil and salt into the skin. Bake at 180°C (350°F) for 25–40 minutes, depending on size. Pro tip: Whole-baked fish looks incredible at the table and keeps the flesh moist and flaky.

sections.heading: 3. Thai-Style Curry
sections.text: Perfect for firm-fleshed reef fish like nannygai or tuskfish. Cut fillets into chunks. Fry off a good curry paste in coconut cream. Add vegetables like capsicum and beans. Simmer the fish gently until cooked through. Serve with jasmine rice and lime wedges.

sections.heading: 4. BBQ Reef Fish Steaks
sections.text: Thicker cuts from larger fish can handle the BBQ. Brush with olive oil, garlic, and herbs. Grill for 2–3 minutes per side over medium heat. Avoid overcooking — reef fish dries out quickly.

sections.heading: Tips for Getting the Best Flavour
sections.text: Don’t overcook it: Reef fish cooks quickly — as soon as the flesh turns white and flakes easily, it’s done. Keep it simple: Fresh fish doesn’t need heavy seasoning. Use the frame: Don’t throw the frames away — boil them for stock or make a killer fish soup.

sections.heading: Species-Specific Highlights
sections.text: Coral Trout: Sweet, delicate flesh — perfect for pan-frying or steaming. Red Emperor: Firm, meaty fillets — brilliant baked or grilled. Sweetlip/Grass Emperor: Mild flavour — great for kids and versatile in recipes. Nannygai: Holds up well in curries and soups thanks to its firmer texture.

sections.heading: From Catch to Plate – Make It Memorable
sections.text: Cleaning and cooking your own reef fish is part of what makes a trip offshore so rewarding. With a little care at the cleaning table and simple techniques in the kitchen, you’ll turn every catch into a meal you’ll talk about for years.

documents.title: How to Read a Beach: Spotting Gutters, Banks & Breaks Like a Pro
documents.description: Successful beach fishing isn’t just about casting far — it’s about casting smart. Knowing where fish are feeding starts with understanding beach structure. Whether you're chasing whiting in shallow gutters or hoping for ...

sections.heading: How to Read a Beach: Spotting Gutters, Banks & Breaks Like a Pro
sections.text: Successful beach fishing isn’t just about casting far — it’s about casting smart. Knowing where fish are feeding starts with understanding beach structure. Whether you're chasing whiting in shallow gutters or hoping for mulloway near a deeper drop-off, learning to read the beach is one of the most valuable skills an Australian fisho can develop. If you're unsure how structure influences rig choice as well as fish location, start with the Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide, which explains how rigs change across surf conditions and target species.

sections.heading: What Does “Reading the Beach” Mean?
sections.text: Reading the beach means analysing visible features and water movement to locate likely fish-holding areas. It involves interpreting sand formations, water colour, wave patterns and currents to identify where species like bream, flathead, whiting, tailor and mulloway are most likely to be feeding. Structure tells you where fish are. Rig choice determines whether they eat your bait when they get there.

sections.heading: Key Beach Features to Identify
sections.text: Gutters are deeper channels running parallel to the beach, often bordered by sandbanks. They act as feeding highways and provide shelter from wave energy. Look for calmer, darker water compared to surrounding whitewater — especially at higher tide levels. Tailor regularly patrol these zones during feeding runs. See the Tailor Rig Guide. Deeper gutters are also prime mulloway territory, particularly during tide changes and after dark. See the Beach Mulloway Fishing Guide. Sandbanks are raised shallow areas where waves begin to break early. They help form gutters and concentrate bait movement along their edges. Fish often sit just behind these banks waiting for food to wash through the turbulence. Running sinker rigs and lighter surf presentations often work well along inside bank edges. See Master the Art of Selecting Fishing Rigs for how rig choice changes with structure depth. Breaks are gaps in sandbanks that allow water — and bait — to move between deeper and shallower areas. Predators frequently patrol these transition zones. Long cast pulley rigs are especially effective for reaching fish holding beyond inside banks or near outer gutter breaks. Learn more in How Long Cast Pulley Rigs Really Work. Rips are fast-moving channels that carry water back out to sea. While dangerous for swimmers, they create natural feeding funnels where fish intercept drifting bait. Casting alongside rip edges often produces better results than casting directly into heavy whitewater. These zones are ideal locations for targeting salmon and tailor during active feeding periods. See the Australian Salmon Rig Guide. Water colour reveals depth differences. Dark green or blue usually indicates deeper water lighter green or sandy tones suggest shallow banks Fish often patrol the transition edges between these zones.

sections.heading: Key Beach Features to Identify
sections.text: Whiting commonly feed along inside colour transitions where waves flatten before reforming. See the Best Whiting Rigs in Australia guide.

sections.heading: When to Read the Beach
sections.text: The best time to scout structure is during low tide. Sandbanks, gutter shapes and breaks become much easier to identify when water levels drop. Take mental notes or photos. These same features continue influencing fish movement as the tide rises. Fishos using drones can also use the live camera to identify gutters, sandbanks and deeper channels before deploying a bait. Learning to recognise these features from above can make bait placement even more accurate. Learn more in the Australian Drone Fishing Guide. Understanding structure early makes choosing the right rig much easier later. See Why the Right Rig Matters in Australian Fishing for how environment affects rig performance.

sections.heading: Tips for Spotting Productive Zones
sections.text: Look for sections where waves don’t break — these often indicate deeper gutters. Scan for V-shaped wave patterns pointing seaward — a sign of rips. Watch how foam and bubbles drift — they usually track current flow through gutters and channels. Fish where whitewater meets darker water — this is a reliable strike zone. Observe bird activity or bait flicking near the surface. Structure tells you where fish are holding. Presentation determines whether they commit to the bait.

sections.heading: What Species Prefer Which Structure?
sections.text: Whiting Shallow gutters and inside sandbank edges where waves flatten before breaking. See the Best Whiting Rigs in Australia guide. Bream Gutter edges and whitewater zones near structure. See the Best Bream Rigs in Australia guide. Flathead Drop-offs and sandy patches beside structure transitions. See the Flathead Fishing Guide. Tailor Deeper gutters and breaks near rips during feeding runs. See the Tailor Rig Guide. Mulloway Deep holes and outer gutters near breaks, especially at night or during tide movement. See the Beach Mulloway Fishing Guide. Matching structure to species behaviour improves hook-up rates immediately. That’s also why adaptable rig systems have become increasingly useful in surf fishing, allowing fishos to quickly change presentations as gutters, sweep, bait movement, and target species change during a session.

sections.heading: Use the Right Rig for the Zone
sections.text: Choosing the right rig matters just as much as choosing the right location. Long cast rigs help reach deeper gutters beyond inside banks, while running sinker rigs often present baits more naturally along sandbank edges. Paternoster rigs can help reduce tangles in moving surf and turbulent water. More adaptable modular systems can also allow fishos to quickly swap trace styles, hook sizes, and bait presentations as beach conditions change throughout a session. If you’re unsure which rig suits the structure you’re fishing, the Rig Finder Tool recommends proven setups based on species and location. Mastering beach reading is a genuine advantage in surf fishing. Observing structure, walking the beach at low tide and understanding how waves shape underwater terrain will consistently improve results. Combine good structure awareness with the right rig choice and you’ll find more fish — and better fish — much more often. Fishos wanting a more adaptable long cast setup can also explore the Quick-Change Modular Long Cast System, designed to allow faster trace changes and more flexible bait presentations without rebuilding complete rigs on the beach. Tight lines and clear skies.

documents.title: Master the Art of Selecting Fishing Rigs
documents.description: The best fishing rig is not the most complicated or the heaviest one available. It is the rig that performs the required job without creating another problem elsewhere in the setup.

sections.heading: Master the Art of Selecting Fishing Rigs
sections.text: The best fishing rig is not the most complicated or the heaviest one available. It is the rig that performs the required job without creating another problem elsewhere in the setup. Choosing that rig means looking beyond the target species. The same fish may be caught over clean sand, beside rock, in strong current or beyond a surf gutter. Each situation changes what the sinker, leader, hooks and complete rig need to do. Use the following seven questions before tying on a rig. They turn rig selection into a practical process based on the fishing conditions rather than habit or guesswork. If you first need to compare the main rig systems, start with the Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide.

sections.heading: 1. What Ground Are You Fishing?
sections.text: The seabed and surrounding structure determine how much abrasion resistance, sinker control and snag protection the setup requires. Clean sand and mud allow greater freedom to use moving sinkers and lighter leaders. Reef, rock, oysters and pylons can damage mono quickly and give hooked fish something to reach. Before choosing the rig, identify whether you are fishing: Surf gutters and banks Weed beds or broken ground Rock ledges and wash zones Reef, wrecks, pylons or other hard structure A leader selected only from the expected fish size may be unsuitable for the ground. A smaller fish beside reef can damage light mono faster than a larger fish hooked over clean sand.

sections.heading: 2. Where Does the Bait Need to Fish?
sections.text: Decide whether the bait should move along the seabed, remain close to one area, sit above the bottom or fish higher in the water column. A running-sinker or fish finder layout allows the bait and leader to move in relation to the sinker. This can suit clean ground where natural bait movement is useful. See Fish Finder Rigs Explained. A paternoster positions the baited hooks above a bottom sinker. It provides greater control in current and can keep baits fishing above reef, weed or the seabed. See Paternoster Rigs Explained. A float rig suspends the bait at a chosen depth, while specialist drone and balloon systems can place or suspend baits farther offshore. Choose the bait position first. The suitable rig systems become much easier to identify once you know where the bait needs to remain.

sections.heading: 3. What Bait Are You Using?
sections.text: The bait determines the required hook size, hook spacing and the amount of support needed during the cast. A small bait must not be overwhelmed by an unnecessarily large hook. A thick bait must not bury the hook point or fill the gape. Long fish, squid and strip baits need their hooks positioned along the natural shape of the bait rather than bunched together. Is the bait small, thick, long or fragile? Will one hook support it correctly? Can the bait be rigged straight? Will it fold or spin during the cast? Will the hook point and gape remain exposed? An adjustable sliding-snell rig changes the distance between two hooks to suit each bait. Ganged hooks provide another way of supporting long fish baits such as pilchards and garfish. For more detail about hook patterns and how bait size affects the choice, see Fishing Hooks Explained – Types, Sizes & Materials.

sections.heading: 4. What Must the Sinker Do?
sections.text: The sinker controls where the rig fishes and how much freedom the bait has. In relatively calm water, a ball or bean sinker may allow the bait to move across clean ground. In surf or stronger current, a star or breakaway sinker provides more holding power. On a paternoster, the sinker sits at the bottom of the rig and controls the baited hooks above it. Use enough weight and holding power to keep the rig in the intended area without automatically making the complete setup heavier than necessary. If the rig repeatedly washes away, the problem may be sinker weight or style rather than the complete rig. If the bait is unnecessarily pinned down in calm water, a lighter or more mobile arrangement may be more suitable.

sections.heading: 5. How Will the Bait Reach the Fishing Area?
sections.text: The deployment method changes the correct rig layout. For short and normal casts, the priority may be simple bait control and reliable spacing. When additional distance is needed, the bait must remain streamlined and protected through a harder cast. A long-cast pulley rig holds the bait close to the sinker during flight, reducing drag and helping prevent the bait from folding or tearing away. Slide baiting casts and anchors the sinker first, then sends the bait down the tensioned mainline on a trolley. This avoids casting a large or fragile bait through the air. Drone deployment introduces different requirements, including rig stability, payload, release reliability and sufficient clearance beneath the aircraft. See the Australian Drone Fishing Guide.

sections.heading: 6. What Can Damage the Leader?
sections.text: Leader strength must cover more than the pulling power of the target fish. Consider contact with: Reef, rocks, shells and oysters Jetty pylons and other structure Teeth, rough mouths and abrasive skin Heavy sinkers and repeated casting Mono provides different strength and abrasion options across general estuary, surf and reef fishing. Toothy species may require a purpose-built wire bite trace. Large sharks may also require a heavy mono rub leader to resist contact with rough skin and the tail. Increasing leader strength has trade-offs. Heavier leader is stiffer, more visible and harder to manage, so the aim is enough protection for the fish and ground rather than the heaviest leader available.

sections.heading: 7. Can You Set Up and Use the Rig Correctly?
sections.text: The fish do not care how experienced the fisho is, but the rig must be assembled and operated correctly. A running sinker must be free to move. A long-cast pulley rig must have the hook seated correctly beneath its impact shield. A sliding-snell must be adjusted for the individual bait. A slide bait trolley must reach the stopper before fishing begins. If a rig has a moving, sliding, locking or release component, check it before the cast. A suitable rig used incorrectly can perform worse than a simpler rig that has been set up properly. The Fishing Rigs Explained library provides detailed guides to the main rig systems and how each one works.

sections.heading: Put the Seven Answers Together
sections.text: Each answer narrows the choice. A light bait over clean estuary ground may suit a running-sinker layout with enough freedom for the bait to move. A bait that must remain above reef in current may suit a paternoster with stronger leader and a controlled bottom sinker. A long bait being cast toward a distant surf gutter needs suitable hook spacing and support during flight. A bait deployed for a toothy predator needs bite protection regardless of how clean the ground appears. The target species matters, but it is only one part of the decision. Ground, bait, sinker control, distance and abrasion risk complete the picture.

sections.heading: When More Than One Rig Could Work
sections.text: Fishing conditions rarely produce only one possible rig. A running-sinker and a paternoster may both catch fish over clean ground, but they control the bait differently. A sliding-snell and a long-cast pulley rig may both carry a long bait, but one prioritises adjustable hook spacing while the other also streamlines the bait for distance. When two rigs are suitable, decide which job matters most on that trip. Then change one part of the setup at a time if the rig is not behaving as expected. Use Common Fishing Rig Mistakes (And How to Fix Them) to diagnose tangles, poor bait shape, unsuitable sinker control, hidden hook points and leader damage.

sections.heading: Quick Rig-Selection Check
sections.text: Before tying on, confirm: The rig suits the ground and current The bait will fish at the required depth The hook size and spacing suit the bait The sinker provides the required movement or holding power The rig suits the casting or deployment method The leader can handle abrasion and teeth Every moving or release component is set correctly The hook points and gapes remain exposed after baiting

sections.heading: Use the Selection Tools
sections.text: Use the Rig Finder when you want products matched to the species, environment, bait, current and casting distance. Use Ask Wiggle when you have a direct fishing question or need to find the most relevant guide, explanation or product. Use the Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide when you want to compare rig systems across different fishing environments. Selecting a fishing rig is a process of matching jobs. Start with the ground and required bait position. Match the hooks to the bait, choose a sinker that controls the rig, account for casting distance and use enough protection for the structure and fish. When every part has a clear purpose, the rig becomes easier to choose, easier to troubleshoot and more reliable in the water. BAIT UP. CAST IN. HANG ON.

documents.title: Night Fishing from the Beach – Strategies for Success
documents.description: Night fishing opens up a completely different set of opportunities for beach fishos. Many prized surf species feed more confidently under low light, moving closer to shore and into gutters that are often quiet during the...

sections.heading: Night Fishing from the Beach – Strategies for Success
sections.text: Night fishing opens up a completely different set of opportunities for beach fishos. Many prized surf species feed more confidently under low light, moving closer to shore and into gutters that are often quiet during the day. With the right preparation, structure awareness and rig choice, night sessions can be some of the most productive fishing you’ll do from the beach. If you're unsure which rigs suit low-light surf conditions, start with the Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide, which explains how setups change across species and environments.

sections.heading: Why Fish at Night?
sections.text: Many beach species are naturally nocturnal or feed more aggressively under low light. At night: • fish move closer to shore under cover of darkness • shallow gutters become active feeding zones • competition from other fishos is lower • larger predators like mulloway and gummy sharks become more active See the Best Mulloway Rigs in Australia guide to match your setup to night beach conditions. Common night targets include mulloway, tailor, bream, whiting, gummy sharks and Australian salmon.

sections.heading: Essential Gear for Night Beach Fishing
sections.text: Night fishing requires a few additional items for safety and efficiency: • headlamp or LED torch (red light helps preserve night vision) • rod holder or sand spike • glow sticks or luminous beads for bite detection • reflective tape on rod tips • thermal gear and windproof clothing in colder months A simple trick is zip-tying a small glow stick to the rod tip.
