It makes subtle bites much easier to detect when fishing multiple rods. Keeping gear organised becomes far more important after dark.

sections.heading: Best Rigs and Baits for Night Fishing
sections.text: Night sessions favour rigs that present bait naturally and remain stable in deeper gutters. Effective options include: Paternoster rigs Ideal for holding position in deeper gutters and maintaining bait visibility above the bottom. If you're targeting mulloway specifically after dark, our Beach Mulloway Fishing Guide explains bait choice, tides and gutter positioning in detail. Running sinker rigs Excellent for subtle feeders like bream and whiting moving through inside gutters. Pulley rigs and slide bait rigs Best suited to larger predators like mulloway and sharks holding beyond inside banks or along deeper structure edges. Learn how pulley rigs improve surf presentation in How Long Cast Pulley Rigs Really Work, or explore larger bait deployment techniques in the Slide Bait Rig Guide.

sections.heading: Best Baits for Night Beach Fishing
sections.text: Fresh, oily baits perform especially well after dark: • fresh squid or octopus • live or fresh mullet • pilchards and bluebait • pipis, prawns or beach worms for whiting and bream Low-light predators rely heavily on scent and movement as well as visibility. Adding luminous beads or contrast elements can improve detection in deeper gutters. See Using Colour and Contrast in Rigs to Trigger More Bites for when these additions help most.

sections.heading: Safety Tips for Night Fishing
sections.text: • always tell someone where you're fishing and when you expect to return • fish with a mate if possible • avoid unstable footing or rock platforms after dark • bring a fully charged phone • carry spare batteries for headlamps • keep your tackle area tidy to prevent trips and tangles Preparation makes night sessions safer and more productive.

sections.heading: Tips for Success When Fishing After Dark
sections.text: • fish the last two hours of the rising tide or around high tide • target deeper gutters identified during daylight scouting • keep noise and light near the water to a minimum • use berley sparingly — oily mixes like pilchard mash work well • focus on structure transitions where gutters meet banks If you’re unsure how to identify productive gutters before dark, see How to Read a Beach: Spotting Gutters, Banks & Breaks Like a Pro. Night beach fishing offers quieter conditions, active predators and access to species that rarely feed confidently during daylight hours. Combining structure awareness, correct rig selection and simple low-light presentation adjustments can dramatically improve results. With the right preparation and a rig matched to the conditions, fishing after dark becomes one of the most effective ways to target larger surf species along Australian beaches.

documents.title: Tested on the Reef: The Story Behind the Swains Slayer Series™
documents.description: Swains Reef looks like paradise until the first bait hits bottom.

sections.heading: Tested on the Reef: The Story Behind the Swains Slayer Series™
sections.text: Swains Reef looks like paradise until the first bait hits bottom. Fish hit like freight trains. Sharks move in fast. Coral heads wait for mistakes. And anything not built for reef fishing gets exposed quickly. For years we fished these waters chasing red emperor, coral trout, Spanish mackerel and whatever else was willing to eat first. Just as often, we watched standard rigs fail — hooks opening, leaders snapping and connections giving way at the worst possible moment. Eventually the question became unavoidable: What if rigs were built to survive Swains Reef instead of just fish it? That question became the Swains Slayer Series™. If you want to see the practical lessons the reef taught us before these rigs existed, see Field Notes from Swains – What the Reef Taught Us.

sections.heading: From Chaos to Creation
sections.text: The Slayer Series didn’t come from a desk or a product catalogue. It came from lost fish. A red emperor showed us standard leader strength wasn’t enough — so heavier mono and wire went where lighter components used to be. A Spanish mackerel proved how quickly speed and shock loads destroy weak connections — so swivels, hooks and trace layouts were reinforced. A coral trout disappearing into structure forced changes to dropper spacing, hook positioning and presentation balance. Every failure shaped the rigs. Every success confirmed what stayed. Over time, trial and error became a system.

sections.heading: Meet the Lineup – Built for Purpose
sections.text: The Swains Slayer Series™ isn’t a random collection of offshore rigs. Each one exists to solve a specific reef problem. Drift Assassin™ & Drift Assassin II™ Built for controlled drifts across reef edges where predators sit waiting in ambush zones. Reef Reaper™ Designed for extracting large reef fish from structure before they reach coral cover. Depth Charger™ & Depth Charger XL™ Purpose-built for deep-water drops targeting heavyweight reef species holding below the main structure edges. Trout Crusher™ Configured specifically for coral trout behaviour around hard reef. Twin Strike™ Twin-hook configuration for aggressive feeding periods when fish are committing hard to larger baits. Bottom Flasher™ Adds colour and movement when reef fish are hesitant or conditions are bright and clear. Skirted Assassin™ Combines flash and stealth for pressured reef systems. Silent Assassin™ Minimal-profile presentation for cautious fish holding tight to structure. Learn how colour and visual triggers influence strike behaviour in Using Colour and Contrast in Rigs to Trigger More Bites. Forged in battle on the reef, every rig in the Series proved itself before earning its place as a Slayer rig.

sections.heading: Why These Rigs Matter
sections.text: There’s no shortage of rigs on the market. Most are designed to look neat in packaging. Few are designed for reef punishment. Reef fishing exposes weaknesses immediately: coral abrasion toothy by-catch shock loading current pressure structure lock-ups The Slayer Series was built as a response to those conditions, not as a variation of existing shelf rigs. When you're offshore and the fish of a lifetime hits, “good enough” disappears quickly. Confidence in your rig becomes everything.

sections.heading: Stories from the Swains
sections.text: One night, drifting in 60 metres, a prototype rig went down and came back with a trophy red emperor. That fish helped define what would become the Reef Reaper™. On another drift, a Spanish mackerel smashed a bait rigged on what became the Drift Assassin II™. It ran hard across current and structure, but the reinforced connections held. Other nights ended differently. Coral claimed leaders. Those weren’t wasted sessions. They were design sessions.

sections.heading: More Than Just Gear
sections.text: The Slayer Series isn’t just about landing fish. It’s about understanding what reef fishing demands from a rig. Length matters when lifting fish boatside. Shock absorption matters when braid meets current. Wire matters when predators move through the drift. Preparation matters when opportunities are short. If you're unsure which offshore rig layout suits your fishing conditions, start with the Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide. Swains Reef doesn’t reward average gear. It rewards preparation. The Swains Slayer Series™ grew out of repeated exposure to reef conditions where weaknesses show quickly and strong rig design makes the difference between landing fish and losing them. Not fishing Swains specifically? The same rig principles apply anywhere coral trout, emperor and reef predators hold tight to structure. For a broader breakdown of reef-specific rig layouts used across Australian coral systems, see the Best Reef Fishing Rigs in Australia guide → Explore the Swains Slayer Series™ to see how those lessons translate into ready-to-fish reef rigs.

documents.title: The Wiggle ya Worm Rig Education Project
documents.description: Choosing a fishing rig becomes much easier when you understand the job it needs to do.

sections.heading: The Wiggle ya Worm Rig Education Project
sections.text: Choosing a fishing rig becomes much easier when you understand the job it needs to do. A rig may need to hold a bait above reef, move naturally across clean sand, resist teeth and abrasion, prevent a long bait from folding, or keep the sinker and bait together during a long cast. Two rigs can look similar on a packet while behaving very differently once they enter the water. Hook style, leader strength, sinker position, trace length and the spacing between components all affect how the complete setup fishes. The Wiggle ya Worm Rig Education Project brings our fishing guides, practical articles and selection tools together in one place. Its purpose is simple: help Australian fishos understand what a rig does, choose one for the conditions and correct problems when a setup is not working properly.

sections.heading: What Rig Education Means
sections.text: Rig education is not about memorising dozens of knots or using the most complicated setup available. It is about recognising the decisions that change how a rig works: Where the bait needs to fish How much movement the bait should have Whether the sinker must hold firmly or move with the bait Which hook size and arrangement suit the bait How much abrasion or bite protection is required How current, water depth and casting distance affect the layout Once those jobs are clear, each part of the rig has a reason for being there. The Understanding Fishing Rigs guide explains how the hook, leader, sinker and rig layout work together as a complete fishing system.

sections.heading: Start with What You Need
sections.text: The education project has three main starting points. Choose the one that matches what you are trying to solve.

sections.heading: Ask a Fishing Question
sections.text: Use Ask Wiggle when you have a specific question or problem. You can ask in normal language, including questions such as: Why does my paternoster keep tangling? Which rig suits gummy shark fishing from the beach? How does water clarity affect flasher colour? What rig helps keep a long bait straight during the cast? Ask Wiggle searches the product range, fishing guides and blog articles, then separates the results so practical information is not buried beneath products.

sections.heading: Find a Rig for the Job
sections.text: Use the Rig Finder when you want products matched to the fishing job. Select the environment, target species, bait, current and required casting distance. The results narrow the range to rigs built for those conditions instead of expecting one all-round setup to work everywhere.

sections.heading: Compare Rig Styles
sections.text: Use the Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide when you want to compare the main rig systems before choosing one. It explains which layouts suit surf, estuary, reef, offshore and specialist fishing situations, and why the environment can change the correct choice even when the target species stays the same.

sections.heading: Learn How the Main Rig Systems Work
sections.text: The Fishing Rigs Explained library contains detailed guides to the main systems used by Australian fishos. A paternoster positions one or more baited hooks above a bottom sinker. The backbone, paternoster arms and sinker work together to control the baits in current and keep them fishing above the seabed. See Paternoster Rigs Explained.

sections.heading: Fish Finder and Running-Sinker Rigs
sections.text: These layouts allow the bait and leader to move in relation to the sinker. They are commonly used where a bait needs greater freedom across clean ground or when a fish should be able to take line without immediately moving the complete sinker. See Fish Finder Rigs Explained.

sections.heading: Sliding-Snell Rigs
sections.text: An adjustable sliding-snell changes the spacing between two hooks to suit the length of each bait. This helps longer fish, squid and strip baits sit straight while keeping both hook points correctly positioned. See Sliding Snell Rigs Explained.

sections.heading: Long-Cast Pulley Rigs
sections.text: A long-cast pulley rig holds the bait close to the sinker during flight, reducing drag and helping protect the bait during a powerful cast. The pulley action also changes the relationship between the sinker and hooked fish during retrieval. See Long Cast Pulley Rigs Explained. Slide baiting casts and anchors the sinker first, then uses a trolley to carry the bait down the tensioned mainline. It allows large or fragile baits to be deployed without casting them through the air. See Slide Bait Rigs Explained.

sections.heading: Drone Fishing Rigs
sections.text: Drone rigs must remain stable beneath the aircraft, deploy cleanly and then fish correctly after release. Rig length, payload, bait position and the sinker system all matter. See the Australian Drone Fishing Guide and the Wiggle ya Worm Drone Fishing System.

sections.heading: Choose Rigs for the Species and Conditions
sections.text: Species guides connect feeding behaviour with bait size, hook style, leader strength, fishing location and suitable rig systems. Start with the guide for the fish being targeted: Best Whiting Rigs in Australia Best Bream Rigs in Australia Best Flathead Rigs in Australia Best Australian Salmon Rigs Best Tailor Rigs in Australia Best Mulloway Rigs in Australia Australian Snapper Rig Guide Best Kingfish Rigs in Australia Australian Gummy Shark Rig Guide Shark Fishing Rigs Explained The species provides a starting point, but the final rig must still suit the bait, ground, current and casting method being used.

sections.heading: Diagnose Problems Instead of Guessing
sections.text: Understanding the rig makes it easier to identify the actual cause of a problem. If a bait spins, the bait shape or hook spacing may be wrong. If the rig tangles, the trace may be too long, the bait may be folding, or the layout may not suit the current. If the sinker moves, its weight or holding power may be insufficient. If the leader returns damaged, the ground may require greater abrasion resistance. The correct fix depends on what is failing. Adding more components or changing the complete setup without diagnosing the cause can create another problem elsewhere. Use Common Fishing Rig Mistakes (And How to Fix Them) for a practical fault-finding guide covering hooks, leaders, sinkers, bait shape, tangles and damaged components.

sections.heading: Built Through Real Fishing
sections.text: Wiggle ya Worm rigs began by solving fishing problems on the water. Australian beaches, estuaries and reefs quickly expose weak knots, unsuitable hook arrangements, poor spacing and leader that cannot handle the ground. Repeated use shows which details work reliably and which need to change. That same approach guides the education project. Explain what each part does, connect it to the fishing conditions and give fishos enough information to make a sensible choice. The aim is not to claim that one rig is correct for every fisho or every location. It is to explain the trade-offs clearly so the setup can be matched to the job.

sections.heading: A Fishing Knowledge Hub That Keeps Growing
sections.text: The Wiggle ya Worm Rig Education Project will continue to grow as new guides are published and existing information is improved. You do not need to read everything before going fishing. Start with the species, conditions or problem in front of you: Use Ask Wiggle for a direct question Use the Rig Finder for suitable products Use the Rig Decision Guide to compare systems Use Fishing Rigs Explained to understand a particular layout When fishos understand what the rig is designed to do, they can choose more confidently, recognise problems sooner and spend less time fighting unsuitable tackle. BAIT UP. CAST IN. HANG ON.

documents.title: Understanding Fishing Rigs: The Foundation of Successful Fishing
documents.description: A fishing rig is the working connection between the mainline, sinker, hook and bait.

sections.heading: Understanding Fishing Rigs: The Foundation of Successful Fishing
sections.text: A fishing rig is the working connection between the mainline, sinker, hook and bait. Its job is not simply to hold these parts together. The rig controls where the bait fishes, how it moves, how well the hook remains exposed and whether the complete setup can handle the cast, current, seabed and fish being targeted. When the rig suits the job, the bait reaches the intended area and fishes without creating unnecessary problems. When it does not, the bait may spin, the trace may tangle, the sinker may move or snag, and the leader may fail around structure. The goal is not to use the heaviest or most complicated rig available. It is to match each part of the setup to the fishing conditions. This guide explains what fishing rigs control, how the main rig systems work and what Australian fishos should consider before choosing one.

sections.heading: What a Fishing Rig Controls
sections.text: A well-matched rig controls five main parts of the fishing setup.

sections.heading: Bait Position and Movement
sections.text: The rig determines whether the bait sits on the seabed, moves along clean ground, remains above the bottom or drifts beneath a float. A running-sinker rig allows more movement across sand or mud. A paternoster holds the baited hooks above a bottom sinker. A float rig suspends the bait at a chosen depth. The hook must suit the bait as well as the fish. Its point and gape need to remain exposed after baiting, and longer baits may require two or more hooks positioned along their length. Hook style also affects how the setup is fished. Circle hooks need room to rotate as the line loads, while beak and J-style hooks are used when the fisho will control the strike more actively. See Fishing Hooks Explained – Types, Sizes & Materials for a closer look at hook size, shape and use. The sinker must hold or move in a way that suits the fishing area. Ball and bean sinkers allow movement on many running-sinker rigs. Star and breakaway sinkers provide more grip in surf and stronger current. On a paternoster, the sinker sits below the hooks and controls the position of the complete rig. Too little weight allows the rig to wash away from the intended area. Unnecessary weight can pin the bait down, increase tackle load and make the setup harder to manage.

sections.heading: Strength and Abrasion Resistance
sections.text: Leader strength must account for the ground as well as the fish. Clean estuary sand may allow a lighter leader than oyster-covered banks, reef, rocks or pylons. Toothy species require suitable bite protection, while sharks and other powerful predators need purpose-built leaders, wire and connections.

sections.heading: Casting or Deployment
sections.text: A short cast into an estuary channel places different demands on a rig from a powerful beach cast or a bait deployed by drone. The rig layout must keep the bait controlled during the chosen method. Long-cast systems streamline the bait beside the sinker, while deployed rigs require enough length and stability to travel cleanly beneath the drone or along a slide-bait system.

sections.heading: How the Main Fishing Rig Systems Work
sections.text: There are many fishing rig variations, but most are built around a small number of proven layouts.

sections.heading: Running-Sinker Rigs
sections.text: A running-sinker rig allows the line or leader to move through or beside the sinker. This gives the bait greater freedom to move and can reduce the initial resistance felt by a fish. Running-sinker rigs are commonly used for: Whiting, bream and flathead in estuaries Mulloway and other species over clean beach ground Fishing where natural bait movement is more useful than holding the bait above the bottom They are best suited to reasonably clean ground. If the sinker or bait repeatedly snags, another layout may provide better control. A paternoster places the sinker at the bottom of the rig and positions one or more baited hooks above it on paternoster arms. This layout is useful when the bait needs to be held above the seabed or kept under greater control in current, surf or deeper water. Paternoster rigs are used from beaches, rock platforms, jetties and boats. Hook size, leader strength, arm length and sinker choice can all be changed for the target fish and ground. See Paternoster Rigs Explained for the complete layout and the differences between mono, wire, single-hook and multi-hook versions.

sections.heading: Sliding-Snell Rigs
sections.text: A sliding-snell rig uses two hooks, with one hook able to move along the leader before being set in position. This allows the hook spacing to be adjusted for each pilchard, squid, whole fish or strip bait rather than forcing different baits onto one fixed spacing. The bait should sit straight, both hook points should remain exposed and the hooks should be positioned along the bait instead of bunched together. See Sliding Snell Rigs Explained for bait rigging and hook-spacing guidance.

sections.heading: Long-Cast Pulley Rigs
sections.text: A long-cast pulley rig holds the bait close to the sinker during the cast. This reduces loose movement and drag compared with a long bait trace flying separately behind the weight. Before casting, the hook is secured beneath the impact shield. When the rig reaches the water, the bait releases and fishes on the trace. During retrieval, the pulley action can help lift the sinker away from the seabed. These rigs suit beaches where the bait must reach a distant gutter, drop-off or feeding area without tangling during a powerful cast. Learn more in How Long Cast Pulley Rigs Really Work.

sections.heading: Wire Bite Traces and Shark Rigs
sections.text: Wire is used when teeth can cut through mono leader. The required wire strength and length depend on the species, bait, fishing method and expected contact with the fish. Tailor and other smaller toothy species may only require a short bite trace. Land-based shark fishing requires a purpose-built system with heavier wire, strong connections and enough rub leader for contact with rough skin, structure and the shoreline. See the Shark Fishing Rigs Guide for the main differences between medium and heavy shark setups.

sections.heading: Drone and Other Deployed Rigs
sections.text: A deployed rig does not need to survive a conventional cast, but it still needs to remain stable, lower cleanly and fish at the correct depth once released. Drone rigs use longer backbones and layouts matched to bottom fishing, multiple baits, float fishing or shark fishing. The complete payload—including the bait, sinker, rig and release equipment—must remain within the drone’s safe working capacity. Compare the purpose-built options in the Wiggle ya Worm Drone Fishing System.

sections.heading: How to Match a Rig to the Fishing Conditions
sections.text: Rather than memorising dozens of rig names, work through the job the rig needs to perform.

sections.heading: 1. Identify the Fishing Ground
sections.text: Clean sand, mud, reef, rocks, weed, oysters and man-made structure create different abrasion and snag risks. A rig that can move freely across an estuary sand flat may repeatedly catch when used around reef. Increase abrasion resistance and reconsider the sinker or rig layout when the ground becomes harder.

sections.heading: 2. Match the Hook Arrangement to the Bait
sections.text: Choose the hook size from the bait’s thickness and the target fish. Use a single hook for compact baits and an appropriate multi-hook arrangement for longer baits. After baiting, check that the bait sits straight and every hook point and gape remains exposed.

sections.heading: 3. Account for Current, Surf and Depth
sections.text: Stronger current and deeper water require more control. This may mean increasing sinker weight, changing to a sinker with greater grip or using a paternoster to hold the hooks above the bottom. Use enough weight to control the rig while remaining within the rod, line and deployment limits.

sections.heading: 4. Decide How Far the Bait Must Travel
sections.text: If the fish are close, a simple rig may be all that is required. When the bait must reach a distant surf gutter, use a streamlined rig built for long casting. When the bait will be deployed by drone or slide bait, choose a system built for that method.

sections.heading: 5. Allow for the Target Species
sections.text: Consider mouth size, feeding behaviour, teeth, expected fish size and how quickly the fish will try to reach structure. The same species may still require different rigs in different places. A snapper targeted from a shallow beach does not automatically need the same rig used over deep offshore reef. The Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide explains how these choices change across surf, estuary, reef, offshore and land-based shark fishing.

sections.heading: Signs That the Rig Does Not Suit the Job
sections.text: Rig problems usually leave a clue. Check what is happening before changing the complete setup. If the bait spins, straighten it and reduce loose sections. If the trace tangles, check its length, bait shape, spacing and casting tension. If the sinker moves, increase its weight or holding power. If the leader returns damaged, increase abrasion resistance and inspect the ground. If toothy fish bite through the trace, add suitable wire bite protection. If fish take the bait without hooking up, inspect the hook point, gape, size and position. If the rig repeatedly snags, reconsider the sinker arrangement and layout used over that ground. See Common Fishing Rig Mistakes (And How to Fix Them) for a complete troubleshooting guide.

sections.heading: Why Construction Details Matter
sections.text: A rig is only as reliable as its weakest connection. Knots, crimps, swivels, clips, leader and hooks must all suit the expected load and saltwater conditions. Trace length and component spacing also affect how the bait behaves and whether the rig tangles. Hand tying provides control over these details, but the words “hand tied” do not automatically make a rig suitable. The materials, construction and complete layout still need to match the job. Whether using a ready-made rig or building your own, check that every component has a clear purpose.

sections.heading: Inspecting and Reusing Fishing Rigs
sections.text: Saltwater, sand, reef, teeth and fish can damage a rig without breaking it completely. Before using a rig again, check for: Abrasion, flattened areas or cloudy sections of mono Kinks, corrosion or broken coating on wire Blunt, bent or corroded hooks Crimps that have moved or become damaged Swivels that no longer rotate freely Clips that have opened or distorted Knots showing movement or wear Rinse reusable rigs after saltwater use, allow them to dry and store them without tight bends or tangles. Replace any damaged component before the next cast.

sections.heading: Choosing a Rig Without Guesswork
sections.text: You do not need to memorise every fishing rig before choosing a useful setup. Start with the environment, target species, bait, current and required distance. Then choose a rig designed to control those conditions. Use the Rig Finder when you want recommendations matched to the job. Compare the main systems in Best Fishing Rigs in Australia, or explore the complete Fishing Rigs Explained knowledge hub. A fishing rig does not need to be complicated. It needs to put the bait where the fish can find it, keep the hook working correctly and remain reliable in the conditions being fished. Match the hook to the bait, the leader to the ground, the sinker to the current and the complete layout to the fishing method. When every part has a clear job, the rig becomes easier to cast, control, inspect and trust. BAIT UP. CAST IN. HANG ON.

documents.title: Using Colour and Contrast in Rigs to Trigger More Bites
documents.description: Most fishos focus on bait and location — but far fewer consider how colour and contrast influence how fish detect and strike a presentation. Adding or removing visual elements in your rig can mean the difference between ...

sections.heading: Using Colour and Contrast in Rigs to Trigger More Bites
sections.text: Most fishos focus on bait and location — but far fewer consider how colour and contrast influence how fish detect and strike a presentation. Adding or removing visual elements in your rig can mean the difference between a curious inspection and a confident bite. Whether you’re using attractor beads, luminous tubing, pompano candy floats or flasher hooks, colour plays an important role — especially in Australian surf conditions. If you're unsure which rig presentation suits your conditions, start with the Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide, which explains how rigs change across surf, estuary, reef and offshore environments.

sections.heading: Why Colour and Contrast Work in the Surf
sections.text: Fish rely on sight, vibration and scent to locate food. In clear or slightly coloured water, visual cues become extremely important. Colour and contrast can: • mimic natural prey like pipis, worms or crustaceans • trigger curiosity or aggression • help fish locate bait in stirred-up water • improve visibility in low-light feeding windows Even small additions like beads or luminous tubing can help fish find bait faster in moving surf. More adaptable modular trace systems now also allow fishos to quickly swap between highly visual teaser traces, natural bait presentations, and specialised colour setups as conditions change throughout a session. Understanding how presentation affects strike behaviour is part of learning how rigs actually work underwater. If you're interested in how flash, water clarity and visibility work together to influence bait presentation, read our Flasher Rigs Guide.

sections.heading: When to Use Bright vs Natural Colours
sections.text: The key to colour selection is matching water clarity and light conditions. Bright Colours (red, chartreuse, orange) Best in murky or stirred-up water where fish rely more on visual contrast than detail. Natural or Muted Colours (brown, olive, clear) More effective in clean water when fish are cautious and feeding selectively. Luminous Elements Ideal for night fishing, deep gutters and low-light feeding periods when mulloway and other predators move through the surf. Choosing the right colour often improves presentation faster than changing bait alone. See Master the Art of Selecting Fishing Rigs for how presentation fits into overall rig choice.

sections.heading: Matching Rig Colours to Target Species
sections.text: Different species respond differently to visual triggers. Whiting Small red beads often imitate pipis or worm tips in the wash zone. See the Best Whiting Rigs in Australia guide. Bream Subtle greens and natural tones work well in clear estuary and beach conditions. See the Best Bream Rigs in Australia guide. Australian Salmon and Snapper Bright attractor beads and flashers can trigger aggressive reaction strikes when fish are chasing bait schools. To learn when flashers are most effective and how to match them to different water conditions, see our Flasher Rigs Guide. For species-specific advice, see the Australian Salmon Rig Guide and Best Snapper Rigs in Australia. Mulloway Glow beads improve visibility during low-light feeding periods, especially around deeper gutters and tide changes. See the Beach Mulloway Fishing Guide. Kingfish Cleaner presentations usually work better unless water clarity drops. Larger live-bait rigs or minimal-hardware setups often perform best when targeting kingfish around structure and current edges. See the Kingfish Rig Guide for how livebait presentation changes around reef edges, pylons and bait schools Matching rig presentation to feeding behaviour improves hook-up rates noticeably. For species-based rig selection, see the Rig Decision Guide AU

sections.heading: Benefits of Using Colour in Your Rigs
sections.text: Adding colour strategically can: • improve bait visibility • increase movement through attractor components • help fish locate bait faster in surf wash • trigger reaction strikes from passing predators • adapt presentation to changing water clarity Just avoid overdoing it. In calm, clear conditions a simpler rig often produces better results. If rigs feel overly complicated or cluttered, see Common Fishing Rig Mistakes (And How to Fix Them) for practical setup adjustments.

sections.heading: When Colour Makes the Biggest Difference
sections.text: Colour and contrast become especially effective: • in stirred-up surf • during dawn and dusk feeding windows • when fishing deeper gutters • when targeting salmon and tailor in whitewater • when mulloway move through low-light zones These conditions reduce visibility and increase reliance on contrast-based strike triggers. Long-distance surf rigs often include visual attractors for exactly this reason. More adaptable modular systems now also allow fishos to quickly change between natural traces, teaser traces, and highly visual surf presentations without rebuilding complete rigs between sessions or changing conditions. Learn how these systems work in the Quick-Change Modular Long Cast System Guide → Learn how presentation changes after splashdown in How Long Cast Pulley Rigs Really Work. Using colour and contrast wisely can significantly improve bait visibility and strike response across a wide range of Australian fishing conditions. Understanding when to simplify a rig and when to add visual triggers is one of the easiest ways to improve hook-up rates without changing bait or location. Wiggle ya Worm rigs are built with species-specific colour logic to match real surf and estuary conditions — giving fishos confidence their presentation is working before the bait even hits the bottom. The Quick-Change Modular System expands on this idea further by allowing fishos to quickly swap complete trace presentations to suit changing water clarity, bait movement, surf conditions, and target species.

documents.title: Why Fishing Rigs Fail at the Worst Possible Moment
documents.description: A fishing rig normally fails at the moment of greatest pressure, but the cause may have started several casts earlier.

sections.heading: Why Fishing Rigs Fail at the Worst Possible Moment
sections.text: A fishing rig normally fails at the moment of greatest pressure, but the cause may have started several casts earlier. A leader can be weakened by reef, a hook point can become damaged, a clip can be left partly open, or a crimped connection can begin to move. The next solid fish simply exposes the problem. Before throwing the remains away or rebuilding everything heavier, inspect what came back. The end of the line often contains useful clues about which component failed and what needs to change. This guide covers knots, leaders, hooks, clips, swivels, crimps and rig setup so fishos can diagnose the actual cause rather than blaming breaking strain alone.

sections.heading: Breaking Strain Is Not Complete Rig Strength
sections.text: The breaking strain printed on line or wire describes the rated material. It does not guarantee the strength of every finished fishing rig made from it. A complete rig also contains: Knots, crimps or twisted connections Hooks, swivels, rings and clips Bends where the leader enters an eye or sleeve Sections exposed to teeth, reef, sand and repeated casting Moving parts that must slide, rotate, lock or release correctly The assembled rig is only as reliable as its weakest component in its current condition. A rod, reel drag and line stretch help manage load. Problems increase when slack line snaps tight, the drag cannot give line smoothly, the fish changes direction suddenly or the leader is pulled across structure. These forces are not represented by reading one strength number from a packet.

sections.heading: Damage Often Happens Before the Fish Is Hooked
sections.text: A rig can return apparently intact while already carrying damage. Common sources include: Dragging the leader across reef, rocks, shells or oysters Sinker and bait striking the rig during repeated casts Tooth contact from an earlier bite Mono retaining a hard kink or flattened section Wire coating being cut, cracked or displaced Hooks contacting rock or becoming blunt Saltwater remaining around swivels, clips and sleeves during storage “It held last time” only confirms that the rig survived the previous load. It does not confirm that every part remains undamaged.

sections.heading: Inspect What Came Back
sections.text: Do not start by asking how strong the complete rig was supposed to be. Start by identifying the missing or damaged part.

sections.heading: The Line Broke Beside a Knot
sections.text: A break close to a knot may point to knot damage, an unsuitable knot, poor tightening, heat or friction during tying, or repeated flexing beside the connection. Look for distortion, a short curled end, flattened mono or damage where the line entered the knot. These are clues rather than absolute proof, but they help narrow the cause. Use a knot suited to the line and component, lubricate where required, tighten it evenly and trim it correctly. Test every finished knot before casting.

sections.heading: The Leader Is Rough, Frayed or Flattened
sections.text: Roughness along the leader points toward abrasion rather than a clean overload. Check the complete length, particularly the section closest to the hook and any area that may have contacted reef, rock, shells, pylons or rough skin. The fix may be greater abrasion resistance, a heavier leader, a shorter fight near structure or a rig that holds the bait farther from the bottom. Simply tying the same damaged strength again may repeat the failure.

sections.heading: The Trace End Is Clean but the Hook Is Gone
sections.text: A clean separation near the hook may indicate tooth contact, but inspect carefully before assuming a bite-off. Sharp reef, a damaged hook eye or a failed connection can leave similar evidence. If tailor, mackerel, sharks or other toothy species are likely, use suitable wire bite protection. The wire type, length and strength must suit the species and rig rather than being added automatically to every setup.

sections.heading: A Crimped Connection Moved or Released
sections.text: If the trace pulled through a sleeve, the sleeve may have been oversized, under-compressed or formed with the wrong die. If the wire broke at the sleeve, look for over-compression, a sharp sleeve edge, damaged coating, a kink or poor alignment. The trace, sleeve material, finished diameter, crimping tool and die must work as one compatible system. See Fishing Crimps Explained for the complete crimp fault-finding guide.

sections.heading: The Hook Opened, Bent or Broke
sections.text: A straightened or distorted hook may be too light for the load, but also check the drag pressure, hook angle, snagging and whether the fish gained leverage against structure. A broken hook may have been damaged or corroded before the fish was hooked. Inspect points, eyes and bends regularly and replace anything showing distortion, cracking or significant corrosion. Hook strength must still be balanced against bait size and the target species. An unnecessarily heavy hook can make a small bait difficult to rig correctly. See Fishing Hooks Explained – Types, Sizes & Materials.

sections.heading: A Clip Opened or the Rig Detached
sections.text: Clips can fail when they are not fully closed, are too light for the job, become distorted or are loaded in a direction they were not designed to handle. Check that the clip is seated correctly after every rig change. Replace it if the wire no longer returns to its original shape or if the locking section feels loose.

sections.heading: The Swivel Stopped Turning
sections.text: A seized or damaged swivel may not separate line twist from the rest of the rig. The resulting twist can wrap traces, weaken line and interfere with how the bait fishes. Check that swivels rotate freely and that their eyes, rings and connections show no corrosion or distortion.

sections.heading: The Rig Can Fail Without Breaking
sections.text: Not every failed rig leaves a broken line. A setup has also failed to do its job when: The hook point or gape is buried in the bait The bait folds and spins during the cast Paternoster traces wrap around the backbone A running sinker cannot move freely A pulley-rig hook is not seated beneath the impact shield A sliding-snell is not adjusted to the bait The sinker repeatedly moves away from the fishing area The rig snags every time it is retrieved over that ground These problems reduce hook-ups or lose fishing time even though every component remains attached. Use Common Fishing Rig Mistakes (And How to Fix Them) to diagnose bait shape, tangles, sinker control, incorrect setup and component wear.

sections.heading: Transition Points Deserve Extra Attention
sections.text: Knots, crimps, hook eyes, sleeves and clips are common inspection points because they join materials, concentrate bends or change stiffness. That does not mean every rig fails at a connection. Line can also break through abrasion, previous damage, a wind knot, excessive load or contact with structure away from the terminal tackle. Inspect both the connection and the line leading into it. Replacing a knot will not correct damaged leader farther along the rig.

sections.heading: Why Simply Going Heavier May Not Fix It
sections.text: Heavier leader is useful when the existing leader cannot handle abrasion, structure, bait size or the expected fish. It will not correct: An incompatible crimp and sleeve A clip that is not fully closed A blunt or buried hook point An unsuitable sinker or rig layout Damage that should have caused the rig to be replaced Heavier components also add stiffness and bulk. Increase strength for a clear reason, not as a substitute for finding the failed part.

sections.heading: Pre-Cast Rig Check
sections.text: Before the first cast and after any hard contact, check: Knots are seated correctly with no visible damage Mono is free from roughness, flattening and hard kinks Wire has no broken strands or damaged coating Crimps have not moved, cracked or distorted Hooks are sharp, exposed and free from corrosion Swivels rotate and clips close securely The sinker connection is intact The bait sits straight without blocking the hook gape Every sliding, locking or release component operates correctly Run your fingers carefully along mono, then visually inspect wire and hardware. Replace questionable components before the next cast.

sections.heading: Check Again After a Fish, Snag or Heavy Cast
sections.text: A rig deserves another inspection after: Pulling free from reef, rock or weed Recovering a bait that has been bitten A cast where the bait or sinker struck the rig Finding the trace twisted around the backbone Any sudden load that felt different from normal Rinse reusable tackle after saltwater exposure, allow it to dry and store rigs without tight kinks or crushed components.

sections.heading: Match the Complete Rig to the Job
sections.text: Reliable rigs begin with suitable components, but they must also match the bait, ground, current, casting method and target fish. The Understanding Fishing Rigs guide explains how the hook, leader, sinker and layout work together as one system. Use the Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide to compare rig systems across surf, estuary, reef and offshore conditions, or use Ask Wiggle for a specific failure or setup question. When a fishing rig fails, inspect the evidence before increasing every strength rating. Identify whether the problem began at the knot, leader, hook, crimp, clip, swivel or rig setup. Then correct that specific cause and check the rest of the system for related damage. The fish may expose the weakest point, but careful inspection often finds it before the next hook-up. BAIT UP. CAST IN. HANG ON.

documents.title: Why the Right Rig Matters in Australian Fishing
documents.description: A fishing rig is not right simply because the target species appears on the packet.

sections.heading: Why the Right Rig Matters in Australian Fishing
sections.text: A fishing rig is not right simply because the target species appears on the packet. The same fish may be targeted over clean estuary sand, in surf wash, beside rock or above offshore reef. The bait, water depth, current, structure and required casting distance can all change between those locations. The right rig is the one that controls the bait, sinker, hooks and leader in the conditions being fished. A mismatch may still catch fish, but it can also create tangles, poor bait position, repeated snags, hidden hook points or a connection that cannot handle the ground. This guide explains what changes when the rig does not suit the job and why species name alone is never enough information. For a complete comparison of the main rig systems, see the Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide.

sections.heading: A Rig Controls More Than the Hook
sections.text: The rig is the working connection between the mainline, sinker, leader, hooks and bait. Its layout influences: Where the bait fishes in relation to the seabed How freely the bait moves in current Whether the sinker holds or travels How straight the bait remains during the cast Whether traces remain separated from the backbone How much protection exists against teeth and abrasion Whether the hook point and gape remain clear A hook may be the part that catches the fish, but the rest of the rig decides where that hook fishes and whether the bait reaches the water in usable condition. The Understanding Fishing Rigs guide explains how these parts operate as one complete system.

sections.heading: The Bait Fishes in the Wrong Place
sections.text: A bait intended to sit above reef may repeatedly drop into structure. A bait that should move naturally across clean ground may be pinned down by an unnecessarily fixed setup. The problem is not always the bait or fishing location. The rig may be holding it at the wrong height or giving it the wrong amount of movement.

sections.heading: The Sinker Cannot Control the Rig
sections.text: If the sinker is too light or has insufficient holding power, the complete rig may wash away from the intended area. If it is heavier or more fixed than the conditions require, it can restrict movement and make the setup harder to cast and retrieve. Sinker position matters as well as weight. A running sinker and a bottom sinker on a paternoster control the bait in different ways.

sections.heading: The Bait Spins or Folds
sections.text: Hook spacing and rig layout must suit the bait. A long bait supported at one point may fold during the cast. Loose sections can spin in current, creating drag and twisting the trace around the backbone. Adjustable sliding-snell rigs, fixed twin-hook rigs and ganged hooks provide different ways of supporting longer baits. The correct option depends on the bait shape, casting method and target fish.

sections.heading: The Rig Tangles in Current
sections.text: A bait trace that can reach the backbone, sinker or another hook may wrap around it. A folded bait can make the problem worse. Paternoster arms, trace length and hook spacing must keep the baited hooks separated without allowing excessive overlap. See Paternoster Rigs Explained.

sections.heading: The Leader Cannot Handle the Ground
sections.text: Leader strength must account for abrasion as well as fish size. A fish hooked beside oysters, rock, reef or pylons can damage light mono quickly. Toothy species may require wire bite protection even when the expected fish is not particularly large. A heavier leader is not automatically better in every situation. The aim is enough protection for the ground and fish without adding unnecessary stiffness and bulk.

sections.heading: The Same Species Can Need Different Rigs
sections.text: Species guides provide a useful starting point, but location and fishing method complete the decision. A bait fished for snapper over relatively clean inshore ground may benefit from greater movement. On deeper reef in current, a paternoster can provide more control and hold baited hooks above a bottom sinker. From the beach, casting distance and bait protection may become more important. The Australian Snapper Rig Guide compares the main options across different fishing locations. An estuary setup over clean ground may allow a large bait to move naturally. Beach fishing can add surf sweep, longer casts and the need to hold a bait in a gutter. Rock and reef edges increase abrasion risk. See Best Mulloway Rigs in Australia for bait, hook and rig options across beach, estuary and offshore conditions. Small baits and light hooks may suit whiting, but the rig still changes between calm estuary flats and moving surf water. Sinker control, trace movement and bait size must match the location. See Best Whiting Rigs in Australia for estuary and surf setups. Clean beach or bay ground may allow a different leader and sinker arrangement from rough reef or areas where other toothy sharks are likely. Bait size, casting distance and bite protection can all alter the correct setup. See the Australian Gummy Shark Rig Guide for mono, wire and rig-design considerations.

sections.heading: Running-Sinker and Fish Finder Rigs
sections.text: These layouts allow the bait and leader to move in relation to the sinker. They are useful where bait movement across relatively clean ground is desirable. See Fish Finder Rigs Explained. A paternoster uses a bottom sinker with one or more baited hooks positioned above it. It provides bait separation and control in current, surf and deeper water.

sections.heading: Sliding-Snell Rigs
sections.text: A sliding-snell adjusts the spacing between two hooks for each bait. It helps position hooks along longer fish, squid and strip baits. See Sliding Snell Rigs Explained.

sections.heading: Long-Cast Pulley Rigs
sections.text: A long-cast pulley rig holds the bait close to the sinker during flight, reducing drag and helping protect the bait during a powerful cast. Use it when reaching distant water is part of the job, not simply because the rig can cast farther. See Long Cast Pulley Rigs Explained.

sections.heading: Slide Bait and Drone Rigs
sections.text: Slide baiting and drone fishing avoid casting the complete baited rig in the normal way. They introduce additional requirements involving anchoring, deployment, payload, rig length and release systems. The rig must suit the complete method, not just the fish being targeted.

sections.heading: An All-Round Rig Always Involves Trade-Offs
sections.text: Some rigs cover a useful range of species and conditions. That does not make one layout ideal everywhere. A general-purpose rig may sacrifice: Bait movement for additional control Subtlety for abrasion resistance Simple casting for additional distance A small hook arrangement for the ability to carry larger bait These are not necessarily faults. They are trade-offs. The important question is whether the compromise suits the trip being planned.

sections.heading: What Does Not Make a Rig Right?
sections.text: A rig is not automatically correct because: It carries the target species name It uses the heaviest leader available It contains more hooks or components It worked at a different location It looks neat in the packet Another fisho uses it for a different bait or method The rig still needs to perform the required job in the water being fished.

sections.heading: Signs That the Rig Needs to Change
sections.text: Reconsider the setup when: The sinker repeatedly moves away from the fishing area The bait returns folded, twisted or missing The traces consistently wrap around the backbone The rig snags during most retrieves The leader returns abraded after each cast Toothy fish are cutting through the trace Fish take the bait without contacting an exposed hook point The required fishing area is beyond the rig's practical casting range Change the part connected to the problem rather than changing everything at once. Use Common Fishing Rig Mistakes (And How to Fix Them) for a detailed troubleshooting process.

sections.heading: Make the Choice Without Guesswork
sections.text: Use Ask Wiggle when you have a specific question about a rig, bait or fishing problem. Use the Rig Finder when you want products matched to the environment, species, bait, current and casting distance. Use Master the Art of Selecting Fishing Rigs for the seven questions to answer before tying on a rig. The right fishing rig is not selected from the species name alone. Match the layout to the ground, required bait position, sinker control, bait size, casting method and abrasion risk. When those jobs change, the correct rig may change as well. A suitable rig helps the bait reach the intended area and fish without creating unnecessary tangles, snags or weak points. That is why the right rig matters before the first cast is made. BAIT UP. CAST IN. HANG ON.

sections.heading: What Is the Best Drone Fishing Rig in Australia?
sections.text: For most Australian fishos, the best all-round drone fishing rig is a simple single-hook bottom rig. It remains stable during flight, deploys cleanly and suits common beach species including snapper, mulloway and tailor. Twin-hook rigs are better when targeting schooling fish, float rigs suspend bait above the bottom, and heavy mono-and-wire systems are required when targeting sharks. Choose your rig around the target species, bait size, fishing depth and total drone payload rather than expecting one rig to do everything. All Wiggle ya Worm Drone Fishing Rigs are compatible with Aeroo and SwellPro drone fishing systems. If you're new to drone fishing, the Standard Drone Fishing Rig is the simplest place to start. Compare every bottom, school-fish, float and shark option in the Wiggle ya Worm Drone Fishing System .

sections.heading: Everything Your Drone Manual Forgot to Tell You
sections.text: Buying a drone is easy. Learning to use it confidently, consistently and successfully for drone fishing is where the real journey begins. Your drone's manual will teach you how to fly, configure its features and return home safely. What it won't teach you is how to prepare a drone fishing rig, deploy a bait smoothly, avoid tangles, choose the right fishing location or develop the small habits experienced drone fishos rely on every time they head to the beach. Those lessons are usually learnt through real experience. This guide brings together the techniques, routines and practical knowledge we've gained through drone fishing in Australian beach conditions. It answers questions such as: • Why should you fly your biggest bait first? • Why is it worth waiting a couple of extra minutes before take-off? • Why do experienced drone fishos turn their reel clicker off? • How much payload is your drone really carrying? • What should you do if your bait doesn't release? • What small habits separate experienced drone fishos from everyone else? Some of the advice may be different from what you've seen elsewhere. That's because every recommendation is based on techniques we've personally tested and continue to use—not theory or opinions repeated around the internet. The goal is simple: To help you spend less time solving problems... ...and more time stopping them before they happen.

sections.heading: Wiggle ya Worm Tip
sections.text: Successful drone fishing isn't about flying the furthest. It's about consistently putting the right bait in the right place, then doing it again and again with confidence.

sections.heading: What Should Beginners Practise Before Drone Fishing Over Water?
sections.text: Before flying over water, become confident flying your drone over open ground. Learn where the controls are, what each button does and how the drone responds in different weather conditions before introducing any fishing gear. Once you can fly the drone by muscle memory without looking at the controls, then, and only then, start using the camera. Practice panning and tilting the camera until it becomes second nature. Later, you'll rely on these skills to accurately position your bait and confirm it has released successfully before flying home. Once you're comfortable controlling both the drone and the camera, it's time to start practising with light payloads and simple rigs. Build your confidence gradually before progressing to larger baits and more demanding fishing situations. If you're unsure which rig to start with, our Standard Drone Fishing Rig is the ideal all-round setup for beginners learning the fundamentals of drone fishing.

sections.heading: What Fish Should Drone Fishing Beginners Target First?
sections.text: If your goal is to catch sharks with a drone, make sure you already have experience targeting and safely releasing sharks from the beach. There are plenty of videos showing experienced shark fishos using drones to catch large sharks, and they make it look easy. What you don't see is the years of experience behind those flights. They already know how to land sharks, release them safely and manage the additional risks involved. If you're not already an experienced land-based shark fisho, use your drone to target bread and butter species like snapper, tailor and mulloway while you learn. If sharks are your ultimate goal, first become confident catching, landing and releasing them using normal land-based fishing techniques. Once you're comfortable doing that, you can then move on to deploying large baits and heavier tackle with a drone. Want to learn more about shark fishing? See our Land-Based Shark Fishing Guide , Shark Fishing Rigs Guide and Safe Release of Sharks Guide . The sharks... and your wallet... will thank you for it!

sections.heading: How Long Should You Wait Before Launching a Fishing Drone?
sections.text: Wait Until Your Drone Has Found as Many GPS Satellites as Possible Give your drone a couple of minutes to find as many GPS satellites as possible before launching. Although most drones will indicate they are calibrated and ready to fly much sooner, allowing the drone to acquire additional satellites improves the accuracy of features such as waypoint recording and Return to Home when you need them. Each time you drop a bait, record the drop location as a waypoint. If the bait lands in a productive area, you can return to exactly the same location for your next drop or on future fishing trips.

sections.heading: How Do You Calculate Your Real Drone Fishing Payload?
sections.text: Your drone's advertised payload is only part of the story. The total payload includes your bait, sinker, rig and any aftermarket drone release mechanism. If you're using one, also include any additional safety release clips or other accessories fitted to the system. Other factors also reduce your drone's lifting capacity. Flying into a headwind requires more power, longer flights create additional drag as more line passes through the air and eventually across the water, and drag from your reel also increases the load on the drone. In our testing, these factors could reduce the drone's effective payload by around 200 grams (7 oz). Carry a small set of fishing scales in your tackle box and weigh your complete fishing system before every flight, especially when using larger baits or heavier rigs. To make this easier, Wiggle ya Worm drone fishing rigs and compatible accessories include their individual weights on the packaging and in the product specifications. This allows you to calculate the combined weight of your rig before adding your bait and sinker, helping you better understand the total payload your drone will be lifting. Remember, your drone's advertised payload is the maximum recommended payload under optimum conditions. Always leave yourself a safety margin to allow for changing conditions and lower battery levels.

sections.heading: How Should You Prepare a Beach Launch Area for Drone Fishing?
sections.text: Before launching, position your drone so it's facing the direction you intend to fly. Starting with the drone already pointing in the right direction makes your first control inputs more natural and predictable, allowing you to concentrate on the take-off rather than correcting the drone's direction. When storing your drone rig, wind it onto the storage reel from the sinker end first so the drone attachment loop remains accessible on the outside. At the beach, connect the attachment loop to your drone while the rest of the rig is still safely wound on the reel, then walk downwind and allow the rig to unspool as you go. This prevents you having to completely unwind several metres of rig onto the beach before you can connect it to the drone, reducing the chance of tangles and keeping the rig under control in windy conditions. Lay your rig out in a straight line downwind of the drone. Every couple of meters, place a small pile of sand over the rig to stop it blowing around on the beach. This keeps the line where you want it and helps prevent it from blowing towards the drone when you take off. Once you've connected the rig to the bait release mechanism, place the rig underneath one of the drone's feet. This helps secure the rig and reduces the chance of it blowing into the propellers during take-off. When launching from sand, always use a launch mat. It doesn't need to be expensive. Even a cheap welcome mat works well. The purpose isn't to protect the drone. It's to help stop sand being blown into the motors and propellers during take-off and landing.

sections.heading: Why Should You Fly Your Heaviest Bait First When Drone Fishing?
sections.text: If you're planning several bait drops during a session, always fly your biggest bait first. The heaviest bait places the greatest demand on your drone and battery. Completing the most demanding flight while the battery is fully charged gives your drone the greatest power reserve when it needs it most. Once the largest bait has been deployed, the remaining lighter baits place less demand on the drone, allowing you to complete the rest of your drops with a greater safety margin.

sections.heading: Should You Turn Your Reel Clicker Off While Flying Out a Bait?
sections.text: If your reel has a clicker, turn it off before flying. Once the bait has been released, you can turn the clicker back on if you normally use it while fishing. Leaving the clicker on creates additional resistance as the line leaves the reel. That extra drag increases the load on the drone, reducing efficiency and causing the battery to work harder than necessary throughout the flight. The constant friction also creates unnecessary wear on the clicker mechanism itself. After enough long deployments, particularly when regularly flying several hundred metres offshore, you may find there's very little clicker left. Turning the clicker off before take-off is a simple habit that reduces drag, improves flight efficiency and helps extend the life of your reel.

sections.heading: How Should You Control the Line During a Drone Fishing Deployment?
sections.text: As the drone flies away, keep a light finger or thumb on the spool to control the speed the line leaves the reel. Wearing a glove can make this more comfortable on longer flights. Controlling the line helps prevent overruns and bird's nests. If the line locks up while the drone is still flying away, the sudden tension can be enough to pull the drone into the water. For beginners, it often helps to have two people during a flight. One person can concentrate on flying the drone while the other controls the line leaving the reel. Standing side by side also makes it much easier to communicate if something unexpected happens. Beginners should fly out at a height of around 40 to 50 metres . This keeps the line out of the water for longer, reducing drag. More importantly, if something goes wrong, the extra height gives you more time to sort it out before the drone reaches the water.

sections.heading: When Should You Check Your Fishing Drone’s Propellers?
sections.text: Each time you change your battery, check that all of your propellers are still tight and securely fitted. Propellers can gradually loosen through normal use and vibration. A quick inspection only takes a few seconds and is far better than discovering a problem once the drone is over the water.

sections.heading: How Should You Use the Camera During a Drone Fishing Bait Drop?
sections.text: Learn to fly your drone and use the camera at the same time. Before releasing your bait, adjust the camera to confirm you're dropping it in exactly the right location. After activating the bait release, don't immediately turn for home. Use the camera to confirm the rig has actually released before flying back to shore. If the bait hasn't released, you'll know immediately and can attempt to resolve the issue before returning to shore.

sections.heading: What Should You Do If Your Drone Fishing Bait Doesn’t Release?
sections.text: If your bait release mechanism doesn't activate, don't panic or start making sudden manoeuvres to try and shake the bait free. First, activate the release mechanism another one or two times. If the bait still doesn't release, assume the mechanism has jammed and stop trying. Continuing to repeatedly activate the release may place unnecessary strain on the release mechanism without solving the problem. Your priority now is getting the drone back safely. Don't simply press Return to Home. You need to remain in control of the flight in case you need to adjust your height, speed or flight path as the drone returns. A controlled manual recovery allows you to react if conditions change or another problem develops. Climb steadily to lift as much fishing line clear of the water as practical before slowly returning to shore. Fishing line creates far more drag in the water than it does in the air, so reducing the amount of line dragging through the water can significantly reduce the load on the drone. Leaving the reel's bail arm open can also help. Rather than pulling against a fixed length of line dragging through the water, the reel can continue feeding additional line as the drone returns. This reduces the load on the drone by allowing the line to extend naturally instead of dragging a large curve of line through the water against a fixed point on the beach, making the recovery safer and more efficient. Recovering extra fishing line afterwards is a far better outcome than placing unnecessary load on the drone during the flight home. Once safely back on shore, land the drone and investigate why the bait failed to release before attempting another deployment.

sections.heading: How Can You Use a Fishing Drone to Find Fish?
sections.text: Drones Can Help You Find Fish A drone can also be a valuable fish-finding tool. Before heading to the beach, spend a few minutes studying the area using Google Maps or Google Earth. Look for gutters, deeper blue holes, breaks in the reef and other likely feeding areas. This gives you a good starting point before you even arrive. Once you're on the beach, send the drone out without a bait and use the camera to relocate the features you identified earlier. This also gives you a chance to look for bait schools, sand banks, colour changes that indicate changes in water depth and other signs of fish activity. When you've found a productive area, save a waypoint. You can then fly straight back to exactly the same location on every deployment without having to search for it again. Rather than simply flying as far as possible, use your drone to locate productive water and place your bait accurately. Want to learn how to identify productive water before you deploy your bait? See our How to Read a Beach: Spotting Gutters, Banks & Breaks Like a Pro guide. The goal isn't to fly as far as possible. It's to fly to the right place.

sections.heading: How Far Below the Drone Should Your Bait Hang When Drone Fishing?
sections.text: One of the biggest causes of unstable flight is having the bait too close to the drone. If the bait is hanging too close, the sinker can begin to swing. As the drone tries to correct the movement, the swinging can become larger and faster. In extreme cases, the sinker can swing over the top of the rig and the line can enter the propellers. Through testing, we found the most stable distance between the drone and the bait was generally 6 to 12 metres . More stable flights also help preserve battery life because the drone isn't constantly using power to correct an unstable payload. This testing led to the development of the Flight Stabiliser Trace . At 8 metres long, when combined with a standard Wiggle ya Worm rig, the overall distance naturally falls within this stable range, helping to reduce bait swing, improve flight stability and reduce unnecessary battery consumption.

sections.heading: Should You Use a Safety Release Clip for Drone Fishing?
sections.text: Safety release clips are designed to protect your drone if excessive tension develops in the deployment line. This can happen if: • The rig snags during deployment. • The line jams or birds-nests on the reel. • The line doesn't feed smoothly from the spool. • In rare cases, a bird flies into the main line, creating sudden tension. As the drone continues flying away, the tension increases until the safety release clip opens, allowing the rig to drop away from the drone. The drone is then free to continue flying, helping prevent it from being dragged backwards or into the water. When they activate, safety release clips generally do exactly what they're designed to do. Once the rig has been deployed, the safety release clip remains attached to the rig. During retrieval, the clip is dragged across the seabed where it can catch on rocks, reef or other underwater structure. If that happens, the clip may release from the rig and remain on the bottom. Because the clip itself is often lost during retrieval after a release, it becomes a consumable item that needs replacing before the next deployment. Some drone fishos attach small floats or even foam ear plugs to the clips to help keep them off the bottom during retrieval. While this may reduce the chance of losing a clip, it doesn't eliminate the problem completely. Safety release clips solve a genuine problem and, when activated, generally do exactly what they're designed to do. After weighing up the advantages and disadvantages, we've chosen not to incorporate safety release clips into our Drone Fishing System. However, all of our drone fishing rigs remain fully compatible with safety release clips should you choose to use one. In our experience, the ongoing replacement of lost clips outweighs the relatively low likelihood of needing one during a normal deployment.

sections.heading: Should You Use a Safety Release Clip for Drone Fishing?
sections.text: Instead, we focus on ensuring the line feeds smoothly from the reel and monitoring it throughout every deployment. All Wiggle ya Worm Drone Fishing Rigs are fully compatible with safety release clips. If you choose to use one, simply attach it to the drone attachment loop before deployment. Other drone fishos may reach a different conclusion, and that's perfectly fine. Understanding both the advantages and limitations of safety release clips will help you decide whether they're the right choice for the way you fish.

sections.heading: When Should You Attach the Rig to a Fishing Drone?
sections.text: Before connecting your rig, check that the bait release mechanism is working correctly by opening and closing it a couple of times. Once you're satisfied it's operating properly, connect your rig while the drone is stationary and the motors are not running. Never hover the drone at shoulder height while someone attaches the rig. The line can blow into the propellers, the drone can move unexpectedly or the controls can be knocked. Once the rig is connected, secure it underneath one of the drone's feet until take-off.

sections.heading: Why Should You Wind In the Slack Immediately After a Drone Bait Drop?
sections.text: As soon as your bait has been released, wind in the slack until the main line comes under light tension. Leaving slack in the water allows the current to push your main line around. As it drifts, it can come into contact with reef, rocks and other underwater obstacles, increasing the risk of abrasion or the line being cut during retrieval. Keeping light tension on the line helps maintain a straighter path between you and your rig, reducing the amount of line lying across the seabed and minimising contact with underwater structure. It's a simple habit that can reduce lost rigs, prevent unnecessary line damage and make retrieving your rig much easier. Drone fishing is only one part of successful fishing. Understanding where fish feed, choosing the right rig and using equipment that's been designed for Australian conditions can all help improve your results. Continue your drone fishing journey by exploring our Drone Fishing System to compare every rig in the range, browse our Drone Fishing Shop , explore Rigs Explained for practical fishing rig tutorials, or visit the Wiggle ya Worm Blog for more Australian fishing tips and techniques.

sections.heading: Help Improve This Guide
sections.text: Drone fishing is evolving all the time, and so is this guide. If you've discovered a practical tip, technique or lesson through your own experience, I'd love to hear it. The best ideas may be tested and included in future updates, helping make this one of Australia's most practical drone fishing resources. Whether it's a simple tip, a lesson learned the hard way, or a technique that's consistently worked for you, your experience could help other Australian drone fishos avoid common mistakes and catch more fish. Together, we can continue building one of Australia's most practical drone fishing guides. Have a tip worth sharing? Contact us through the website or send us a message on Facebook.

sections.heading: Drone Fishing System
sections.text: Drone fishing has revolutionised the way many Australian fishos reach productive water, allowing baits to be deployed hundreds of metres offshore with remarkable accuracy. But flying the bait is only part of the system. The fishing rig hanging beneath the drone plays an equally important role. It needs to remain stable during flight, deploy cleanly, fish naturally once it reaches the water and have the strength to handle Australian conditions. That's why we developed the Wiggle ya Worm Drone Fishing System. Rather than offering a collection of unrelated rigs, we've designed a complete range where every rig has a specific purpose. Whether you're fishing the surf for snapper, suspending baits beneath a balloon or targeting large sharks, each rig has been developed to solve a particular fishing problem while following the same simple design philosophy. Every rig is individually hand tied in Queensland and built around practical experience gained fishing Australian beaches and coastlines. No unnecessary complexity. Just purpose-built drone fishing rigs designed for Australian conditions. All Wiggle ya Worm Drone Fishing Rigs are compatible with Aeroo and SwellPro drone fishing systems.

sections.heading: Why We Built Our Own Drone Fishing System
sections.text: When we first started drone fishing, we did what most fishos do. We bought drone fishing rigs online. Some worked reasonably well, but it didn't take long to realise that many were little more than standard fishing rigs being sold as drone rigs. They hadn't really been designed around the additional demands of drone fishing. Many were quite short, making them less stable when suspended beneath the drone during flight, while some used lighter-duty components than those required for the harsh surf conditions and powerful fish commonly encountered around Australia's coastline. Drone fishing introduces challenges that conventional fishing rigs were never designed to deal with. A rig needs to remain stable while suspended beneath the drone, carry the intended payload safely, deploy cleanly, fish naturally once it reaches the water and still have the strength to handle powerful Australian fish. We quickly found ourselves modifying existing rigs, changing components and experimenting with different designs in an attempt to improve their performance. Eventually we stopped modifying other people's rigs and started building our own. We didn't set out to build a range of drone fishing rigs. We set out to solve the problems we experienced while drone fishing. That eventually became the Wiggle ya Worm Drone Fishing System.

sections.heading: What Makes a Drone Fishing Rig Different from a Conventional Fishing Rig?
sections.text: Every rig in the Wiggle ya Worm Drone Fishing System has been designed around one simple idea. Drone fishing places different demands on a fishing rig than conventional fishing. It's not simply a matter of attaching an ordinary rig beneath a drone and hoping for the best. Every rig in the range has been developed to remain stable during flight, deploy cleanly, fish naturally once it reaches the water and withstand the demanding conditions often encountered around Australia's coastline. Just as importantly, every design has been kept as simple as possible. Rather than adding unnecessary hardware or features, we've focused on using only the components that genuinely improve performance, reliability and ease of use. If a component doesn't serve a clear purpose, it doesn't belong on the rig. That's the design philosophy behind every Wiggle ya Worm Drone Fishing System product.

sections.heading: Which Drone Fishing Rig Should You Choose?
sections.text: No single drone fishing rig is perfect for every species, bait or fishing situation. That's why the Wiggle ya Worm Drone Fishing System has been developed as a complete range of purpose-built rigs, with each one designed to solve a specific fishing problem. Some rigs are designed for everyday bottom fishing. Others are built for suspending baits beneath a balloon, targeting school-sized fish, or handling the heavy tackle required for Australia's largest sharks. Rather than expecting one rig to do everything, we've developed a system where you can choose the right tool for the job while knowing every rig has been built around the same design philosophy of simplicity, reliability and practical Australian experience. Whether you're just getting started with drone fishing or already have years of experience, there's a Drone Fishing System rig designed to suit the way you fish.
