sections.heading: Gummy Shark Rigs Guide
sections.text: Gummy sharks are one of Australia’s most popular target species. They’re also one of the most misunderstood. They don’t have razor-sharp teeth like other sharks, but they’re powerful, persistent feeders that often move into shallow water as conditions change. Choosing the right rig for gummies isn’t about going heavier — it’s about matching the setup to where you’re fishing and how the fish are feeding. This guide explains how castable, paternoster and sliding snell gummy shark rigs work, where mono and wire each make sense, and when each design suits different fishing conditions. Looking for a quick rig recommendation? See our Best Gummy Shark Rigs in Australia page. Releasing sharks safely is part of responsible land-based fishing. See the shark release guide here →

sections.heading: How Does Gummy Shark Feeding Behaviour Affect Rig Choice?
sections.text: Gummy sharks don’t feed the same way as many other sharks. They often move slowly, pick up baits carefully, and swim off rather than smashing a bait at speed. Because of this, the wrong rig can lead to missed hook-ups, dropped baits, or fish swallowing the bait too deeply before you even realise they’re there. Factors like water temperature, depth, current, and fishing pressure all affect how gummies feed — and the rig you use needs to suit those conditions. Experienced gummy fishos don’t rely on a single “do-everything” setup. They adjust their rigs based on where they’re fishing and how the fish are behaving on the day.

sections.heading: Where Should You Use Wire and Mono in a Gummy Shark Rig?
sections.text: Gummy sharks don’t have the razor-sharp teeth of many other shark species, which is why mono leaders are often talked about as a good option for them. But in real-world fishing, the decision isn’t that simple. Conditions, bait size, fish size, and the chance of encountering other shark species all play a role. That’s why experienced gummy fishos don’t think in terms of wire or mono — they think about where wire is needed, and where mono makes sense . Wire comes into play when targeting bigger gummies, fishing rough ground, running large or tough baits, or when there’s a real chance of mixed shark species. In these situations, wire protects against bite-offs and abrasion and gives you confidence to fish properly without babying your gear. Mono still has an important role. It offers flexibility, natural bait movement, and controlled stretch — which is why it’s often used strategically rather than everywhere. In some rigs, mono is used in sections where strength is needed without over-building the entire setup. This is also why hybrid gummy rigs exist. By combining mono and wire in specific sections, you get bite protection where it matters most, while still keeping the rig balanced, practical, and forgiving in real fishing conditions. There’s no single “best” leader material for gummies. The right choice depends on the size of the fish you’re targeting, the ground you’re fishing, and what else might turn up on the end of your line.

sections.heading: Castable Gummy Shark Rigs (Beach & Surf)
sections.text: When fishing for gummies from the beach, the rig needs to do two things well — cast cleanly and present the bait properly once it hits the bottom. Castable gummy shark rigs are designed to streamline the bait during the cast and allow it to sit naturally once the sinker settles. A sliding sinker setup lets the fish pick up the bait and move off without immediately feeling resistance. These rigs are well suited to targeting gummies feeding beyond the breakers, fishing in current, or running larger slab or whole baits. Heavier wire versions come into their own when chasing bigger gummies or when there’s a chance of mixed shark species moving through the same water.

sections.heading: Gummy Shark Paternoster Rigs (Boat & Deeper Water)
sections.text: In deeper water or when fishing from a boat, keeping baits organised and reducing snags becomes more important than casting distance. Gummy shark paternoster rigs are designed to hold baits slightly off the bottom while maintaining strength where it matters most. By separating the bite section from the sinker line, these rigs help manage tangles and make it easier to fish rough ground or structure. A key advantage of this style of rig is control. If a sinker becomes snagged, the lower section can break away without costing you the fish or the entire rig — a practical feature when fishing areas where gummies are known to hold close to the bottom.

sections.heading: Sliding Snell Rigs for Variable Baits
sections.text: Sliding snell rigs are useful when bait size varies or when gummies are feeding cautiously. With one fixed hook and one sliding hook, the rig can be adjusted to suit different baits while improving hook placement. This style of rig works well when gummies mouth a bait before committing, allowing the hooks to sit where they’re most effective without over-complicating the setup. It’s a practical option for fishos who want flexibility without constantly re-rigging.

sections.heading: How Do Seasonal Conditions Change Where Gummy Sharks Are Fou
sections.text: Yes — gummy sharks can be caught throughout the year in many parts of Australia. Their location and feeding patterns change with water temperature and conditions, but they don’t disappear. In cooler months they often hold in deeper water, while in warmer conditions they’re more likely to move into shallower ground, beaches, and bays. That’s why the rigs on this page cover different fishing styles. Some are better suited to beach and surf fishing, others to boat fishing or deeper water — but all are proven setups for targeting gummies when they’re present. If you’re fishing for gummies now, the key isn’t the time of year — it’s matching the rig to where you’re fishing and how the fish are feeding . This guide is designed to help you do exactly that.

sections.heading: Australian Snapper Rig Guide: How Different Rigs Work
sections.text: Snapper are one of Australia’s most targeted fish. They’re not always the hardest fighters, but they are highly sensitive to how a bait is rigged. Small changes in hook layout, leader strength and bait movement can make the difference between consistent sessions and quiet ones. The challenge is that snapper are caught across surf beaches, rocks, reefs and offshore grounds. A rig that works in calm, clear water may be too light around reef, while a heavy offshore setup can reduce bites in cleaner, shallower water. Casting distance, sinker resistance, abrasion risk, current and bait size all influence how a rig needs to work. Rather than treating one setup as the best choice for every situation, this guide explains how twin-hook sliding snell, long cast, running sinker, flasher and paternoster rigs work, what problem each design solves and the conditions each one suits. Looking for a quick rig recommendation? See our Best Snapper Rigs in Australia page. If you’re new to fishing rigs, start with our complete fishing rig guide .

sections.heading: What Determines How a Snapper Rig Behaves?
sections.text: A good snapper rig is not one particular design. It is a rig whose leader strength, hook layout and sinker arrangement suit the bait, ground, structure and water movement being fished. Four parts of the rig have the greatest influence: • Leader strength — The leader needs enough strength and abrasion resistance for rocks, reef and rough ground without being unnecessarily heavy in calm or clear water. • Hook layout — Hook spacing should match the size and shape of the bait. This helps the bait sit naturally while keeping the hooks positioned where a snapper is most likely to take it. • Sinker arrangement — A running sinker reduces resistance when a fish picks up the bait, a paternoster holds bait above the bottom, and a pulley-style rig helps streamline the bait during a long cast. • Fishing environment — Beach fishing may require casting distance, rocks and reef require additional abrasion resistance, and deeper offshore water requires greater bait control in current. The goal is enough strength to land the fish while still allowing the bait to behave naturally. That balance is why no single snapper rig performs equally well in every environment.

sections.heading: How Does the Fishing Environment Change a Snapper Rig?
sections.text: The same Snapper rig can behave very differently depending on water movement, casting distance and the ground being fished. Choosing the rig should begin with the environment rather than the species alone. Snapper often hold in deeper gutters or beyond the breakers. When fish are holding wide, a pulley-style long cast rig helps streamline the bait during the cast and reduces tumbling in the air. In calmer gutters or clear water where distance is less important, a running sinker rig allows the fish to pick up the bait with less immediate resistance. Rocks and Headlands Rocks, oysters and reef edges create a greater risk of abrasion. Leader strength, connection quality and resistance to damage become more important than maximum casting distance. The rig still needs to allow natural bait movement, but it must also provide enough strength to handle contact with rough ground and structure. Depth, current and reef structure create different demands. Paternoster rigs keep baits organised, hold them above the bottom and help reduce tangles as the rig descends or moves in current. Flasher rigs can add movement and visibility in deeper water, low light or when Snapper are feeding aggressively around reef and bait schools. No single rig layout suits all three environments. The correct setup is the one that provides the casting distance, bait control and abrasion resistance needed for the ground being fished.

sections.heading: How Different Snapper Rig Designs Work
sections.text: Each rig design changes how the bait is cast, positioned and taken by the fish. The following sections explain the mechanics of the five main snapper rig styles covered in this Guide, the problem each one solves and the conditions in which its design is most useful.

sections.heading: How Does a Twin-Hook Sliding Snell Rig Work?
sections.text: A twin-hook sliding snell rig uses one fixed hook and one adjustable hook. Moving the sliding hook changes the distance between them, allowing the rig to match the length and shape of the bait being used. With the spacing adjusted correctly, the hooks can be positioned at different points along a pilchard, squid or strip bait without forcing the bait to bunch or fold. This helps the bait sit naturally while providing hook coverage along more of its length. The design is versatile because the same rig can be adjusted when bait size changes. That makes it useful across beach, rock and offshore Snapper fishing without requiring a separate fixed hook spacing for every bait. Best for: All-round Snapper fishing and changing bait sizes Mechanical advantage: Adjustable hook spacing and coverage along longer baits For a deeper explanation of adjustable hook spacing, bait placement and how the rig behaves when a fish takes the bait, see Sliding Snell Rigs Explained .

sections.heading: How Does a Long Cast Snapper Rig Control the Bait During Casting?
sections.text: Long baits can create significant wind resistance and may tumble during a cast. This reduces casting efficiency and increases the chance of the bait becoming damaged or the rig tangling before it reaches the water. A pulley-style long cast rig holds the bait and sinker inline during the cast. This creates a more aerodynamic shape, reduces wind resistance and helps the rig travel further than a bait and sinker moving separately through the air. Keeping everything aligned also reduces bait movement and tumbling during the cast. Once the rig reaches the water, it deploys and allows the bait to fish normally. This design becomes useful when Snapper are holding outside the closer gutters or when additional casting distance is genuinely required. Its main advantage is reaching that water while keeping the bait and rig controlled throughout the cast. For a detailed explanation of pulley-rig mechanics, bait control and long-cast setup, see Long Casting Pulley Rigs . Best for: Beach Snapper holding beyond the breakers Mechanical advantage: Bait and sinker held inline for reduced wind resistance, improved casting distance and clean deployment

sections.heading: How Does a Running Sinker Rig Reduce Resistance?
sections.text: A running sinker rig allows the sinker to move independently along the main line rather than fixing its full weight directly to the baited leader. When a Snapper picks up the bait and moves away, line can pass through the running sinker before the fish feels the sinker’s full resistance. This can encourage a more confident take, particularly in calm, clear water or areas where fish are feeding cautiously. The sliding arrangement also allows the bait to move more naturally with gentle water movement. However, as current or surf movement increases, the rig can become harder to control and a paternoster or other fixed-sinker layout may become more suitable. Running sinker rigs are simple, but their low-resistance design is why they remain widely used by experienced fishos. Best for: Calm water, clear conditions and cautious Snapper Mechanical advantage: Reduced initial sinker resistance and natural bait movement For a deeper explanation of sliding sinkers, reduced resistance and the different running-sinker layouts, see Fish Finder Rigs Explained .

sections.heading: How Flasher Rigs Work for Snapper
sections.text: A flasher rig uses reflective material tied close to the hook. As the material moves in the water and catches the available light, it creates a visual cue immediately beside the bait. This can help Snapper locate the bait in deeper water or low-light conditions. The movement and changing reflection can also trigger reaction bites when fish are feeding aggressively around reef or bait schools. The amount of flash should suit the conditions. More flash is not automatically better, and water clarity, available light and the way fish are feeding all influence how visible the rig needs to be. For a detailed explanation of water clarity, contrast, flash quantity and when flasher rigs work best, see our Flasher Rigs Guide . Best for: Offshore Snapper, deeper water and low-light conditions Mechanical advantage: Movement and reflected light positioned directly beside the bait

sections.heading: How Paternoster Rigs Work for Offshore Snapper
sections.text: A paternoster rig places the sinker at the bottom of the rig with the baited hooks positioned on paternoster arms above it. The sinker carries the rig down while the arms keep the baits separated from the sinker and slightly above the seabed. This vertical layout helps keep the rig organised during the descent and reduces tangles when fishing in current. It also provides better control over where the baits sit in relation to reef and bottom structure. For a detailed explanation of paternoster layouts, leader materials and when different versions are used, see Paternoster Rigs Explained . Best for: Boat fishing, deeper water and reef Snapper Mechanical advantage: Controlled bait position above the sinker and seabed

sections.heading: Circle Hooks vs J Hooks for Snapper
sections.text: Circle hooks are designed to move towards the corner of the mouth as the fish takes the bait and the line comes under tension. Rather than striking hard, allow the line to tighten so the hook can rotate and take hold. This makes circle hooks well suited to larger baits and situations where the rod is left to load up as the Snapper moves away. Beak and J-style hooks rely more on the fisho setting the hook. They remain useful when actively fishing, but the timing of the strike becomes more important. The choice depends on how you are fishing: • Circle hooks — allow the line to tighten rather than striking hard • Beak or J-style hooks — better suited to an actively worked bait and a timed strike If you’re unsure which style suits the way you fish, circle hooks remain the simplest starting point. For a detailed explanation of hook styles, hook-setting behaviour and matching hooks to bait, see Choosing the Right Fishing Hook .

sections.heading: Choosing Snapper Leader Strength for Different Ground
sections.text: Leader strength should be chosen around abrasion risk, water clarity and what else may take the bait—not the Snapper alone. Many experienced fishos use leaders in the 40–60 lb range, adjusting within or beyond that range to suit the ground being fished. • Clean surf and estuaries — Lighter leaders allow better bait movement and are often more effective in calm or clear water. • Rocks and reef — Additional leader strength and abrasion resistance may be needed where the line can contact oysters, reef edges or rough ground. • Mixed shark waters — A heavier setup may be required when other species are likely to take the bait. Increasing leader strength also increases leader diameter and stiffness. Stepping up unnecessarily can reduce bait movement, so use the additional strength only when the ground or likely bycatch justifies it. For more detailed guidance on leader strength, sinker weight and fishing around coral and reef structure, see Best Reef Fishing Rigs in Australia . The goal is enough strength and abrasion resistance for the ground without making the rig heavier than the conditions require.

sections.heading: Why Hand-Tied Snapper Rigs Suit Specific Conditions
sections.text: Mass-produced rigs can work, but they are generally designed as one setup intended to cover a broad range of fishing situations. A purpose-built hand-tied rig can be matched more closely to how and where it will be used. Practical differences can include: • Hook spacing selected to suit the intended bait size • Leader strength matched to clean water, surf, rocks or reef • Rig layout chosen around casting distance and water movement • Components selected for the expected load and fishing conditions These details become more important in heavy surf, rough ground and when targeting larger Snapper. The advantage of a purpose-built hand-tied rig is not how it looks. It is the ability to build the hook layout, leader and components around a specific fishing purpose rather than a generic set of conditions.

sections.heading: Common Snapper Rig Mistakes and Why They Cause Problems
sections.text: Using the Same Rig Everywhere A running sinker may suit calm water but become difficult to control in stronger current. A light leader may work in clean surf but provide insufficient abrasion resistance around rocks and reef. Match the rig to the ground and water movement rather than using one setup everywhere. Overbuilding the Rig Heavier leaders provide additional strength and abrasion resistance, but unnecessary diameter and stiffness can reduce bait movement and make the leader more noticeable to line-shy fish, particularly in calm or clear water. Using Hook Spacing That Does Not Match the Bait If the hooks are too close together or too far apart for the bait, the bait may bunch, fold or leave the hooks poorly positioned. Adjust hook spacing to the bait rather than forcing every bait onto the same layout. Using the Wrong Sinker Arrangement A running sinker reduces resistance in calm conditions, while a paternoster provides greater bait control in current and deeper water. Choosing the wrong arrangement can leave the bait drifting, tangling or sitting in the wrong position. Rigging the Bait Poorly A bait that is not secured straight can spin or tumble during casting, descent or water movement. Correct bait position begins with matching the rig and hook layout to the bait being used. For a broader breakdown of setup problems and how to correct them, see Common Fishing Rig Mistakes . Correcting these issues can improve how the bait behaves without changing bait type or fishing location.

sections.heading: Snapper Rig Designs and the Problem Each One Solves
sections.text: Each rig belongs in a Snapper kit for a different reason: • Changing bait sizes — A twin-hook sliding snell rig allows the hook spacing to be adjusted to suit the bait. • Fish holding beyond the breakers — A long cast pulley rig holds the bait and sinker inline to reduce wind resistance and improve casting distance. • Cautious fish in calm or clear water — A running sinker rig reduces the initial resistance felt when the fish takes the bait. • Deeper water or low-light conditions — A flasher rig places movement and reflected light beside the bait. • Current, reef and offshore fishing — A paternoster rig controls the bait above the sinker and seabed. If you regularly move between beach, rock and offshore fishing, carrying several of these designs gives you options as conditions change. If you mostly fish one environment, build your rig selection around the specific problems you encounter there.

sections.heading: Bringing It All Together
sections.text: A Snapper rig works when the hook layout suits the bait, the leader suits the ground, the sinker arrangement suits the current and depth, and the overall design suits the required casting distance and visibility. When conditions change, adjust the part of the rig that solves the new problem. That may mean changing hook spacing for a different bait, using a streamlined rig to cast further, reducing sinker resistance in calm water, adding visibility in deeper water or using a paternoster to gain more bait control in current. Looking for the quick recommendation rather than the mechanics? See Best Snapper Rigs in Australia . For a broader breakdown covering other Australian species and fishing environments, start with the complete fishing rig guide . Fishing mixed shark waters or targeting Gummies? See the Gummy Shark Rigs Guide . Prefer a ready-to-fish setup? Browse our hand-tied Snapper rigs in the online shop.

sections.heading: Best Australian Salmon Rigs for Beach and Surf Fishing
sections.text: For most Australian Salmon bait fishing from the beach, a 40 lb twisted paternoster rig with two heavy-duty 2/0 hooks is the best all-round starting setup. The sinker sits below the baited paternoster arms, helping keep the baits separated, slightly above the shifting sand and visible in the moving wash where Salmon commonly feed. Unlike Tailor, Australian Salmon do not generally require ganged hooks or wire leader purely for bite protection. A strong single hook on each paternoster arm provides a simpler setup for pilchards, whitebait clusters, squid and fish strips. The most important factors are keeping the bait in the active whitewater or gutter, using enough sinker weight to control the rig and matching the hook size to the bait. This guide explains where Australian Salmon feed from the beach, why twisted paternoster rigs suit moving surf, which baits and hooks to use, and when a popper teaser can provide an additional visual target. Need a direct recommendation matched to your fishing conditions? Use the Rig Finder. Want to compare rig styles and understand why each one suits different conditions? Start with the Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide.

sections.heading: Where Australian Salmon Feed in the Surf
sections.text: Australian Salmon patrol moving water where waves and current concentrate baitfish. Productive areas can include: • Whitewater running along sandbanks • Shallow surf gutters • Edges of deeper channels • Shore breaks during moving tides • River mouths where bait is being pushed into the surf • Areas where birds or visible bait schools indicate feeding activity The productive zone can change as the tide moves. Watch where waves break, where whitewater travels along the bank and where calmer gutter water meets the moving wash. A paternoster rig helps keep the baits slightly above shifting sand and weed while holding them in the moving water where Salmon can locate them. If you’re unsure how to recognise gutters, sandbanks, channel edges and productive whitewater, see the Beach Fishing Structure Guide →

sections.heading: How a Twisted Paternoster Rig Works for Australian Salmon
sections.text: A twisted paternoster rig positions the sinker at the bottom with the baited hooks held on paternoster arms above it. Twisting the arms makes them firmer and helps them stand away from the main leader. This keeps the two baits separated and reduces the chance of the hooks wrapping around the leader in moving surf. For Australian Salmon, this layout: • Holds the baits slightly above shifting sand and weed • Keeps the hooks and baits separated from the sinker • Places two baits at different positions in the moving wash • Provides better control than a freely moving bait when surf sweep increases The sinker still needs to suit the conditions. It should provide enough hold to control the rig without using more weight than the surf requires. For a detailed explanation of paternoster layouts and how different versions work, see Paternoster Rigs Explained →

sections.heading: Single Hooks vs Ganged Hooks for Australian Salmon
sections.text: For a standard Australian Salmon paternoster rig, one strong single hook on each paternoster arm is usually sufficient when the hook size is matched to the bait. Single hooks suit: • Pilchard halves • Whitebait clusters • Squid strips • Mullet and other fish strips Ganged hooks become useful when fishing longer whole baits such as whole pilchards because the hooks can be positioned at different points along the bait. They may also be preferred when Tailor are feeding in the same water. Ganged hooks are therefore an option for particular baits and mixed-species conditions—not a requirement for every Australian Salmon rig. If you’re specifically targeting Tailor, see the Tailor Rig Guide →

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Hook Size for Australian Salmon
sections.text: Hook sizes are not standardised across manufacturers. A 2/0 hook from one supplier can be physically similar to a 3/0 or 4/0 pattern from another, so the number alone should not determine your choice. For pilchard halves, whitebait clusters, squid strips and fish strips, choose a strong single hook with enough gape to remain clear after the bait has been fitted. Match the physical hook size to the bait: • The bait should sit naturally without bunching around the hook • The hook point and gape should remain exposed • The hook should be strong enough for Salmon and likely surf bycatch • The hook should not be so large that it overwhelms the bait For more information about differences between hook patterns, sizing and strength, see Choosing the Right Fishing Hook →

sections.heading: How Paternoster Rig Height Controls the Baits in Moving Surf
sections.text: A paternoster positions the baited hooks on arms above the sinker rather than allowing the baits to sit directly beside it on the bottom. In moving surf, this helps: • Keep the baits slightly above shifting sand and loose weed • Hold the baits within moving whitewater • Place the baits at different positions along the rig • Reduce the chance of both baits being buried or fouled at the same time The aim is not to suspend the baits at one exact feeding depth. It is to keep them controlled and accessible as the wash moves through the gutter or along the edge of a sandbank. A running sinker rig can still work in calmer conditions, but a paternoster generally provides better bait control when surf sweep and sand movement increase.

sections.heading: What Is a Popper and Ganged-Hook Paternoster Rig?
sections.text: The Wiggle ya Worm Popper and Ganged-Hook Paternoster is a two-arm surf rig developed to combine a highly visible teaser with a natural bait. The upper twisted paternoster arm carries a coloured 2nd Generation Popper with realistic 3D eyes and its own matching 4/0 teaser hook. The lower arm carries a 4/0 ganged-hook bait section designed to hold longer baits such as: • Whole pilchards • Squid strips • Garfish This allows the rig to fish two different targets at the same time. The popper provides colour, movement and an additional hook above the main bait, while the ganged hooks keep the longer bait straight below it. Fish may strike the natural bait or attack the popper during aggressive feeding. A small piece of bait can also be added to the popper hook to introduce scent around the visual teaser. This configuration is particularly useful when: • Salmon or Tailor are feeding aggressively in schools • Birds are working over visible baitfish • Whitewater or stirred-up water reduces visibility • Whole pilchards or other longer baits are being used • Fish are actively chasing moving bait through the surf It is a specialised alternative for active feeding conditions rather than a replacement for the standard single-hook Australian Salmon paternoster. See the Wiggle ya Worm Popper and Ganged-Hook Paternoster Rig →

sections.heading: Best Baits for Australian Salmon from the Beach
sections.text: Reliable Australian Salmon baits include: • Whole pilchards • Pilchard halves • Whitebait clusters • Squid strips • Mullet and other fish strips • Garfish Match the bait to the hook layout. Whole pilchards and garfish suit ganged hooks because the hooks can be positioned along the length of the bait. Pilchard halves, whitebait clusters, squid and fish strips can be matched to the strong single hooks used on the standard Salmon paternoster. Rig the bait so it remains secure and reasonably straight in moving surf. Keep the hook point and gape exposed rather than burying them inside the bait. Bait choice matters, but the rig still needs to hold it in the active whitewater or gutter where Salmon are feeding.

sections.heading: What Other Species Can an Australian Salmon Rig Catch?
sections.text: A 40 lb twisted paternoster with strong single hooks may also catch: • Tailor • Mulloway • Trevally • Kingfish • Flathead • Other surf predators These are possible crossover catches, but the same rig is not automatically the best deliberate setup for every species. Tailor can damage mono leader, particularly when larger fish are feeding aggressively. Kingfish encountered near rocks, reef or other structure may require a stronger purpose-built rig to control the first run. Targeting Mulloway specifically? See the Mulloway Rig Guide. Targeting Kingfish around structure or bait schools? See the Kingfish Rig Guide. If several species are moving through the same gutter and you’re unsure which rig best suits the conditions, use the Rig Finder.

sections.heading: Recommended Australian Salmon Paternoster Setup
sections.text: The standard Wiggle ya Worm Australian Salmon rig uses: • Approximately 900 mm overall length • 40 lb monofilament leader • Twisted double-paternoster configuration • 2 × heavy-duty chemically sharpened 2/0 hooks • Twisted paternoster arms • 108 lb rolling swivel The approximately 900 mm leader provides separation between the two baits, while the twisted paternoster arms help hold the hooks away from the main leader and reduce tangles in moving surf. Although the hooks are described as heavy-duty 2/0, hook sizing is not standardised between manufacturers. This particular hook pattern is physically larger than many standard 2/0 hooks, with an overall size and gape closer to the 3/0–4/0 patterns sold by many other manufacturers. This makes the hooks suitable for pilchard halves, whitebait, squid strips, fish strips and other meaty bait pieces without requiring a different rig for common surf bycatch. The rig is available individually and in 4 Pack and 10 Pack options. View the Australian Salmon Twisted Paternoster Rig →

sections.heading: When to Fish for Australian Salmon from the Beach
sections.text: Australian Salmon can feed throughout the day when baitfish are concentrated in active surf water. Useful signs include: • A rising tide pushing water and bait into shallow gutters • A falling tide draining water from sandbanks and channels • Active whitewater moving along the edge of a bank • Shore breaks exposing or concentrating bait • Birds working over visible bait schools • Salmon or baitfish visibly moving through the surf Neither a rising nor falling tide is automatically best on every beach. The useful stage is the one that moves bait through the gutter, channel or whitewater being fished. Salmon often feed confidently during daylight, so visible surf structure, bait movement and bird activity can be more useful than relying on low-light periods alone.

sections.heading: Bringing It All Together
sections.text: For most Australian Salmon bait fishing from the beach, start with a 40 lb twisted paternoster rig using two strong single hooks. Match the sinker weight to the surf so the rig remains controlled, position the baits in active whitewater or a productive gutter, and choose a hook size that leaves the point and gape exposed after baiting. Use the standard single-hook paternoster for pilchard halves, whitebait clusters, squid and fish strips. When Salmon or Tailor are feeding aggressively around visible bait schools, the Popper and Ganged-Hook Paternoster provides an alternative that combines a visual teaser with a longer whole bait. The rig does not need to be complicated. It needs to hold the chosen bait securely, resist tangles and keep fishing in the water where the Salmon are feeding.

sections.heading: Keep the Bait Moving Naturally Around Structure
sections.text: Bream are found throughout Australian estuaries, rivers, coastal lakes and surf beaches. They commonly feed around rock walls, bridge pylons, oyster racks, channel edges and other areas where current carries food past structure. A suitable bream rig needs to keep the bait moving naturally while using only enough sinker weight to reach and remain near the feeding zone. Running-sinker rigs are a reliable choice in estuaries because they allow the line to move through the sinker when a bream takes the bait. Light paternoster rigs become useful where stronger current, deeper water or surf wash makes the bait difficult to control. This guide explains how to choose between these setups and match the hook, sinker and bait to the water being fished. If you’re unsure which rig suits your location, start with the Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide →

sections.heading: Why Fishing Too Heavy Costs Bream Bites
sections.text: One of the most common bream rigging mistakes is using more sinker weight than the conditions require. Bream often mouth or pick at a bait before moving away. Excessive weight restricts bait movement and can make these lighter bites harder to detect. For most estuary fishing, a running-sinker rig is a reliable starting point. The line passes through the sinker as the fish moves with the bait, while the sinker keeps the rig close to the bottom. This setup works particularly well around: • Bridge pylons • Oyster racks • Mangrove edges • Pontoons and boat hulls • Rock walls with tidal flow • Channel edges beside shallow flats Use only enough sinker weight to control the bait and keep it near the feeding zone. The aim is not to pin it firmly in place when the current could be moving it naturally past the structure.

sections.heading: Example: A Complete Running-Sinker Rig for Bream
sections.text: The Wiggle ya Worm Bream Running Sinker Rig is approximately 600mm long and supplied complete with: • 20lb monofilament leader • 1/0 hook • Built-in 15g sliding bean sinker • Red luminous knot-protecting bead • 95lb rolling swivel The bean sinker slides along the monofilament leader, allowing the bait and line to move while keeping the rig near the bottom. Because the sinker is already fitted, the rig is ready to attach to the mainline, bait up and fish without any additional assembly. The rigs are hand tied in Queensland and available in ready-to-fish multipacks. See the 4 Pack Bream Running Sinker Rigs →

sections.heading: When a Paternoster Rig Is Better
sections.text: A running-sinker rig becomes harder to control when stronger current or surf wash continually carries the bait away from the feeding area. A paternoster rig places the sinker at the bottom of the rig, with the baited hooks held above it on paternoster arms. This provides greater control while keeping the baits clear of sand, shell grit and uneven ground. Consider changing to a paternoster rig when: • Fishing deeper channels beside shallow flats • Current repeatedly carries the bait away from structure • Surf wash makes a running sinker difficult to control • Fishing rock edges or broken ground • The bait needs to remain slightly above the bottom The Bream Twisted Paternoster Rig provides two baited hooks on twisted paternoster arms for these conditions. Learn more in Paternoster Rigs Explained →

sections.heading: How to Fish Bream Around Structure
sections.text: Bream often feed beside structure where shade, current breaks and flowing water concentrate prawns, baitfish and other food. Productive areas include: • The downstream side of bridge pylons • Shade lines beneath pontoons and boats • Current edges along rock walls • Oyster rack drop-offs • Mangrove drains on a falling tide • Channel edges beside shallow flats Avoid casting directly into heavy structure where the rig is likely to snag. Cast slightly upstream or alongside it and allow the bait to move towards the edge with the current. Maintain enough line tension to detect a bite without continually dragging the sinker and bait away from the feeding area. Recast when the bait has travelled beyond the structure or leaves the current line being fished.

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Hook Size for Bream
sections.text: Hook size should match the bait being used rather than the expected size of the fish alone. Reliable starting options include: • Size 1 long-shank hooks for worms and slimmer baits • Size 1/0 beak hooks for prawns, yabbies and fish strips The bait should sit naturally on the hook without covering the point or filling the hook gape. Keep the hook point clearly exposed to improve hook-ups when a bream mouths or moves away with the bait. The Wiggle ya Worm Complete Bream Running Sinker Rig uses a 1/0 hook, providing enough room for common estuary baits without requiring an oversized bait.

sections.heading: Choosing a Sinker for Bream Fishing
sections.text: The sinker needs to keep the bait near the feeding zone without preventing it from moving naturally with the current. Common choices include: • Small ball or bean sinkers for shallow estuary flats • A 15g sliding bean sinker for general estuary channels and structure • A paternoster sinker where deeper water or stronger current requires greater control • A small star sinker where surf wash makes a rounded sinker move too quickly The Wiggle ya Worm Complete Bream Running Sinker Rig has a built-in 15g bean sinker intended as a practical all-round estuary setup. If the rig is moving away from the feeding area too quickly, change the casting angle or position before changing the complete setup. Where substantially more control is required, move to a paternoster rig suited to the conditions.

sections.heading: Fishing Bream Through the Tide
sections.text: Bream change position as the tide moves food between shallow flats, drains, channels and structure. On a run-out tide, concentrate on: • Yabby banks draining into channels • Mangrove and creek outflows • Rock-wall drop-offs beside flats • Sand edges beside weed beds • The downstream side of drains and current seams Cast slightly upstream and allow the bait to move through the flow just outside the draining water. On a run-in tide, concentrate on: • Bridge pylons • Oyster racks • Rock walls • Jetty and pontoon edges • Newly covered flats beside deeper water Fish the first push of water along these edges as bream move back towards structure and newly flooded feeding ground. On either tide, the most productive position is usually where moving water meets slower water beside structure—not directly in the strongest current.

sections.heading: Fishing for Bream Along Surf Beaches
sections.text: Bream feeding along surf beaches commonly move through shallow gutters and whitewater where worms, pipis and other food have been disturbed from the sand. • Shallow inside gutters • Whitewater running beside sandbanks • Coffee-rock edges • Wash zones beside headlands • Darker holes and channels close to shore A light paternoster rig is often the better choice in these conditions because it keeps the bait above the shifting sand and gives greater control in the surf wash. Use enough sinker weight to keep the rig fishing inside the gutter without being swept rapidly along the beach. For help identifying gutters, banks and breaks, see: How to Read a Beach: Spotting Gutters, Banks & Breaks Like a Pro →

sections.heading: Adjusting the Rig as Conditions Change
sections.text: In clear, calm water, begin with the lightest running-sinker setup that will keep the bait near the feeding area. This allows the bait to move naturally and reduces the resistance felt when a bream picks it up. As current increases: • Cast slightly upstream to give the bait time to reach the structure • Use enough sinker weight to control the drift • Recast when the rig moves beyond the feeding area • Change to a paternoster rig if the bait cannot be controlled near the bottom In dirty water or low light, fresh bait and accurate placement beside structure become especially important. Fish the current edges, shaded areas and drains where bream can locate food moving past them. Adjust the rig to the conditions on the day rather than relying on one setup for every location.

sections.heading: A Simple Bream Setup That Works in Most Locations
sections.text: For estuaries, rivers and structure fishing, begin with: • A running-sinker rig • A size 1 or 1/0 hook matched to the bait • Prawn, yabby, worm or fish-strip bait • Just enough sinker weight to control the bait near the bottom Cast slightly upstream or alongside the structure and allow the bait to move through the feeding area. If stronger current, deeper water or surf wash prevents the running-sinker rig from staying in the strike zone, change to a light paternoster rig. Between these two rig styles, fishos can cover most Australian bream fishing conditions without making the setup unnecessarily complicated.

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Bream Rig
sections.text: For lighter estuary fishing around rock walls, pontoons, pylons and drains, start with a running-sinker rig that allows the bait to move naturally near the bottom. For stronger current, deeper channels or surf wash, use a light paternoster rig to hold the bait above the bottom with greater control. sections.heading: Best Flathead Rigs in Australia (Beach, Estuary & Channel)
sections.text: Flathead are commonly targeted from Australian estuaries, tidal channels and surf beaches, and a running sinker—also known as a fish finder rig—is one of the best all-round setups for bait fishing. The sliding sinker reduces the initial resistance felt by the fish and allows the bait to move naturally with the current along channel edges, drains, sandbank drop-offs and surf gutters. An adjustable twin-hook version is particularly useful when fishing longer baits such as pilchard tails, whitebait, strip baits or poddy mullet. The hook spacing can be adjusted to match the length of the bait while keeping both hook points properly positioned and exposed. Flathead regularly hold near changes in depth where moving water carries bait past them. Working these edges methodically is usually more productive than simply casting into the deepest water and leaving the bait in one place. This guide explains how to choose and fish a Flathead rig across beach, estuary and channel conditions. Need a direct rig recommendation? Use the Rig Finder Tool → Want to understand and compare the available options? Start with the Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide →

sections.heading: Choosing Between 20lb and 40lb Flathead Rigs
sections.text: The Wiggle ya Worm Flathead Fish Finder Rig is available with either a 20lb or 40lb monofilament leader. Both versions use the same adjustable twin-hook fish finder layout, but each is intended for different conditions. 20lb Estuary Flathead Fish Finder Rig The 20lb version is designed for lighter estuary fishing over clean sand and mud. It suits drains, tidal channels, sandflat drop-offs and other areas where severe abrasion is unlikely. Its lighter leader suits smaller natural baits, lighter estuary tackle and fishos wanting a less heavily built rig for Flathead. See the 4 Pack 20lb Estuary Flathead Fish Finder Rigs here 40lb Flathead Fish Finder Rig The 40lb version provides additional abrasion resistance for surf gutters, shell grit, coffee rock edges, larger baits and locations where heavier bycatch may be encountered. It is the better choice when additional leader durability matters more than using the lighter estuary setup. See the 4 Pack 40lb Flathead Fish Finder Rigs here Both versions include: • Approx. 600mm clear monofilament leader • Fixed bottom 1/0 chemically sharpened beak hook • Adjustable sliding-snelled top 1/0 chemically sharpened beak hook • Soft green luminous bait-attractor bead • Sliding sinker clip supplied loose • Red knot-protecting bead supplied loose • 108lb black barrel swivel • Hand tied in Queensland, Australia Fit the sliding sinker clip to your mainline first, followed by the red bead, before attaching the mainline to the rig’s swivel. The sinker is not included, allowing its weight and style to be matched to the water movement and ground being fished. Choose the 20lb rig for cleaner estuary ground and the 40lb rig when additional abrasion resistance is needed.

sections.heading: A Running Sinker Rig for Longer Flathead Baits
sections.text: Longer baits such as pilchard tails, whitebait, strip baits and poddy mullet benefit from a running sinker rig with two adjustable hooks. Our 40lb Mono Flathead Fish Finder Rig uses this layout. The spacing between the two 1/0 hooks can be adjusted to match the length of the bait, helping it remain straight while keeping both hook points properly positioned and exposed. At approximately 600mm long, the rig provides useful separation between the sinker and bait while remaining manageable for casting and drifting through estuary channels, sandbank edges and surf gutters. The sliding sinker clip and red knot-protector bead are supplied loose. Thread the clip onto your main line first, followed by the red bead, before attaching the main line to the rig’s swivel. The bead sits between the sliding clip and the knot, helping protect the knot as the clip moves along the main line. A suitable sinker can then be attached to the clip. The sinker is not included, allowing its size and style to be matched to the water movement and ground being fished. Each rig includes: • 40lb monofilament leader • Approx. 600mm overall rig length • 2 × adjustable, chemically sharpened 1/0 hooks • Loose sliding sinker clip for fitting to the main line • Red bead to help protect the main-line knot from the sliding clip • Soft green luminous bait-attractor bead • 108lb black barrel swivel • Hand tied in Queensland, Australia See the 4 Pack 40lb Mono Flathead Fish Finder Rigs here →

sections.heading: Why Adjustable Twin Hooks Suit Longer Baits
sections.text: Adjustable twin hooks are particularly useful when fishing longer baits for Flathead. One hook remains fixed while the position of the sliding hook can be adjusted to match the length of the bait. This allows the hooks to be placed across the bait rather than being crowded together at one end. • Keep longer baits straight during casting and drifting • Reduce bait spin when the bait is rigged correctly • Position the hook points across more of the bait • Match the hook spacing to different bait lengths • Keep both hook points clear and properly exposed This setup works well with pilchard tails, whitebait, strip baits and live poddy mullet. Avoid burying either hook deeply inside the bait. Match the hook spacing to the bait being used and leave both hook points exposed to improve the chance of a clean hook-up. See How Sliding Snell Rigs Work →

sections.heading: Where to Look for Flathead
sections.text: Flathead often hold on or beside changes in depth where moving water carries prawns, baitfish and other food between shallow and deeper water. Productive areas include: • Channel edges • Sandbar drop-offs • Creek mouths • Feeder drains • River bends • Edges of weed beds • Transitions between shallow flats and deeper water The edge of a drop-off or drain is usually a good place to begin because the change in depth creates a natural route for moving bait. Flathead can also spread across shallow flats as the tide rises or move with concentrations of bait. Work the edge first, then cover the nearby shallow and deeper water rather than assuming every fish will be sitting in one exact position.

sections.heading: How to Drift a Flathead Rig Along an Edge
sections.text: A Flathead bait should move gradually through likely holding areas while remaining close to the bottom. Cast across or slightly up-current from a channel edge, drain or sandbank drop-off. Allow the sinker to settle, then let the current move the bait along the contour rather than washing it quickly across open water. If there is very little current, move the rig yourself using short, slow retrieves followed by pauses. This allows the bait to cover new ground without being pulled rapidly away from the bottom. A controlled drift can involve: • Casting slightly up-current and allowing the bait to move along a drop-off • Working the bait across channel lips and sandbank edges • Using short retrieves and pauses when current is limited • Casting at different angles to cover the edge methodically • Moving position after several casts if the area produces no interest If the rig moves too quickly, increase the sinker weight. If it remains pinned in one place, try a lighter sinker or move it in short stages. The aim is to maintain contact with the bottom while steadily working the bait through the areas where Flathead are likely to be holding.

sections.heading: Fishing Drains on a Falling Tide
sections.text: A falling tide can create productive Flathead fishing around drains because prawns, baitfish and other food are carried from shallow flats into deeper channels. • Yabby banks draining into channels • Small feeder creeks entering rivers • Sandflat run-off points • Narrow gutters between banks • Visible current lines where draining water meets the main channel Flathead often hold near the deeper edge of the outflow where they can intercept food being carried from the flats. Cast beyond or across the drain exit and allow the bait to move through the outflow and along the adjacent channel edge. Avoid repeatedly casting into the shallowest part of the drain if the moving water is carrying your rig away from the likely holding area. The strongest flow is not necessarily the best position. Work the slower water beside the main current as well, particularly where the bottom drops into the channel.

sections.heading: Surf Flathead vs Estuary Flathead Behaviour
sections.text: Surf flathead and estuary flathead hold in similar structure but respond differently to water movement. Estuary flathead prefer: • channel edges • drains • river bends • sandflat drop-offs Surf flathead prefer: • inside gutters • sandbank lips • shallow troughs • coffee rock edges In both environments, flathead sit facing into current waiting for bait to drift past rather than chasing it across open ground. If you're unsure how to identify productive gutters and sandbank edges, see How to Read a Beach: Spotting Gutters, Banks & Breaks Like a Pro →

sections.heading: How Flathead Take the Bait
sections.text: A Flathead bite can register as a firm strike, several smaller taps, the line beginning to move or weight gradually building through the rod. Maintain enough contact to detect the bite without continually dragging the sinker and bait away from the strike zone. Avoid striking at the first small tap. When the taps develop into steady pressure or the rod begins to load, strike firmly to set the beak hooks without giving the fish unnecessary time to swallow the bait. When using longer baits, adjust the sliding top hook to match the bait length and make sure both hook points remain clearly exposed.

sections.heading: Best Baits for Flathead
sections.text: Flathead will take a wide range of natural baits, including: • Pilchard tails • Whitebait • Prawns • Poddy mullet • Small herring • Fish or squid strips Longer baits are particularly well suited to an adjustable twin-hook rig. Move the sliding top hook to match the bait length, keeping the bait straight and both hook points clearly exposed. If the bait bunches up or spins in the current, reposition the sliding hook or use a small amount of bait elastic to hold it securely without covering the hook points.

sections.heading: A Simple Flathead Setup to Start With
sections.text: For fishing over clean estuary sand or mud, start with the 20lb Estuary Flathead Fish Finder Rig. Fit the supplied sliding sinker clip to your mainline, followed by the red knot-protecting bead, then tie the mainline to the rig’s swivel. Attach the lightest sinker that will maintain contact with the bottom in the current being fished. Adjust the sliding top hook to match your bait length, keeping the bait straight and both hook points exposed. Cast across a drain, channel edge or sandbar drop-off and allow the bait to move gradually along the bottom with the current. Move to the 40lb version when fishing surf gutters, shell grit, coffee rock or other areas where additional abrasion resistance is needed. For more information about locating and targeting Flathead, see Flathead Fishing: Tips and Tricks for Landing the Lizard →

sections.heading: Best Gummy Shark Rigs in Australia
sections.text: Gummy sharks are one of Australia’s most popular target species — and one of the easiest to get wrong with the wrong rig. They don’t have razor-sharp teeth like some sharks, but they’re powerful, persistent feeders that often move into shallow water when conditions line up. Choosing the right gummy rig isn’t about going heavier — it’s about matching the setup to where you’re fishing and how the fish are feeding. This page breaks down the gummy shark rigs that actually work — and when to use each one. If you’re new to fishing rigs, start with our complete fishing rig guide. Releasing sharks safely is part of responsible land-based fishing. See the shark release guide here →

sections.heading: Which Gummy Shark Rig Should You Choose?
sections.text: If you’re unsure where to start: • Beach and surf fishing → Castable gummy shark rig • Mixed shark waters → Hybrid gummy shark rig • Boat and deeper-water fishing → Gummy shark paternoster rig • Variable bait sizes → Sliding snell gummy shark rig View our full range of Gummy Shark Rigs Use the rig that suits the conditions, not the heaviest one you own. Want to understand why each design suits different fishing conditions? Read our Gummy Shark Rigs Guide for the detailed explanation.

sections.heading: Why Gummy Sharks Need the Right Rig
sections.text: Gummies don’t smash baits like many other sharks. They often pick up a bait slowly and move off. That feeding style means the wrong rig can lead to: Missed hook-ups Dropped baits Deep-hooked fish Water temp, depth, current, and fishing pressure all change how gummies feed — and your rig needs to match those conditions. Most experienced gummy fishos don’t rely on a single “do-everything” rig. They adjust based on where they’re fishing and what else might turn up.

sections.heading: Wire vs Mono for Gummy Sharks
sections.text: Gummy sharks do not always require a full wire leader, but wire becomes important around rough ground, with larger baits, when targeting bigger gummies or wherever other shark species may be encountered. Gummies don’t have razor teeth, which is why mono leaders get talked about a lot. But real gummy fishing isn’t that simple. Wire becomes important when: Fishing rough ground Running bigger baits Targeting larger gummies Fishing where other sharks are around Mono still plays a role. It gives better stretch and more natural bait movement, which can help in calmer conditions. That’s why many modern gummy rigs use a hybrid approach — mono where flexibility helps, and wire where bite protection matters. There’s no single “best” leader material for gummies — it depends where you’re fishing.

sections.heading: Which Gummy Shark Rig Should You Use for Beach and Surf Fishing?
sections.text: When targeting gummies from the beach, the rig needs to do two things well: Cast cleanly and present the bait naturally. Castable gummy rigs are built to streamline the bait during the cast and fish cleanly once the sinker settles. A sliding sinker or weight clip allows the fish to pick up the bait and move off without instant resistance — which suits how gummies feed. These rigs are ideal for: Surf fishing Rock ledges Riverbanks Mixed shark waters If you’re fishing from land, this is the most common gummy setup.

sections.heading: When Should You Use a Hybrid Gummy Shark Rig?
sections.text: Hybrid rigs combine mono and wire in specific sections, giving you natural bait movement with bite protection where it matters most. This style is extremely popular in Australian waters where gummies and sharks overlap. Better bait presentation than full wire Bite protection where needed A more forgiving, all-round setup For many fishos, hybrids are the everyday gummy sweet spot.

sections.heading: Which Gummy Shark Rig Should You Use from a Boat or in Deeper Water?
sections.text: When fishing deeper water or from a boat, control becomes more important than casting distance. Paternoster-style gummy rigs keep baits slightly off the bottom and help reduce tangles in current. Most modern versions use a hybrid layout: Mono backbone for control Wire bite section for protection Lighter sinker dropper to reduce full rig loss They’re a proven option for: Boat fishing Deep channels Rough bottom areas If you’re targeting gummies offshore, this is the most reliable rig design.

sections.heading: When Should You Use a Sliding Snell Rig for Gummy Sharks?
sections.text: Sliding snell rigs are useful when bait size changes or gummies are feeding cautiously. With one fixed hook and one sliding hook, you can adjust hook spacing to suit: Squid Fish fillets Whole baits This helps keep hook placement consistent without constantly re-rigging. They’re a great option when: Bait sizes vary Gummies are tentative You want flexibility without complexity

sections.heading: Can You Catch Gummies Year-Round?
sections.text: Yes — gummy sharks can be caught year-round across much of Australia. They don’t disappear, but they do move. In cooler months they often hold deeper. In warmer conditions they push into: Bays Beaches Shallow inshore ground That’s why different gummy rigs exist — conditions change, and the rig needs to match. Match the rig to the location and you’ll stay in the game.

sections.heading: Hand-Tied vs Store-Bought Gummy Rigs
sections.text: Mass-produced rigs can work, but many are built for generic conditions rather than real Australian fishing. Hand-tied rigs are usually built with: Stronger connections Better hook spacing Components chosen for durability You notice the difference most in rough surf, heavy structure, or long soak sessions. That’s why many experienced fishos move toward hand-tied rigs over time — not for looks, but for reliability.

sections.text: If you’re fishing new water, targeting multiple species, or just want a shortcut, our Rig Finder can help narrow it down. Where you’re fishing How you’re fishing What you’re targeting Then points you toward rigs that match those conditions. Use the Rig Finder to remove the guesswork.

sections.heading: Match the Rig to the Bait and Structure
sections.text: Kingfish are powerful fish commonly targeted around reefs, wrecks, headlands, rock ledges, pylons and bait schools. There is no single kingfish rig that suits every situation. The right setup depends on: • Whether you are using livebait, whole dead bait or strip bait • The size and shape of the bait • How close the fish are to reef, pylons or other structure • Whether you are fishing from shore or a boat • Which toothy species may also take the bait Sliding snelled rigs allow the hook spacing to be adjusted for longer baits. Paternoster rigs provide greater control when fishing baits vertically or close to the bottom, while wire bait rigs provide additional bite protection where mackerel, tailor or other toothy fish are present. This guide explains how these different kingfish rigs work and how to choose a setup suited to the bait, fishing method and ground being fished. Not sure which rig style suits your conditions? Start with the Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide →

sections.heading: Where Kingfish Are Commonly Caught
sections.text: Kingfish are commonly found wherever current and structure concentrate bait. Productive areas include: • Reef edges and drop-offs • Offshore pinnacles and wrecks • Headlands and rock ledges • Harbour markers, wharves and bridge pylons • Bays and channels holding schools of baitfish • Mid-water bait schools over deeper ground Kingfish can feed at different depths, so the rig needs to place the bait where the fish are moving rather than automatically keeping it on the bottom. Around reef, rocks and pylons, leader strength and abrasion resistance become especially important because a hooked fish can reach structure quickly. In more open water, bait size, hook arrangement and keeping the bait at the feeding depth may be more important than using the heaviest possible leader.

sections.heading: Best Leader Strength for Kingfish
sections.text: For most Australian kingfish bait fishing, 60lb monofilament leader is a practical starting point . • 40–60lb mono for smaller kingfish in open water or over clean ground • 60–80lb mono for general reef edges, headlands, deeper water and boat fishing • 80–100lb mono around pylons, wrecks, heavy reef and other structure where fish must be turned quickly • 100lb or heavier mono when deliberately targeting large kingfish with heavy tackle and large baits around demanding structure The closer the bait is to reef, rocks or pylons, the less room there is to use lighter leader. A 60lb leader suits many general kingfish situations, while 80lb provides a better starting point around heavier structure or when larger fish are expected .

sections.heading: Sliding Snelled Rigs for Kingfish Baits
sections.text: A sliding snelled rig uses two hooks on the same bait trace: • The bottom hook is fixed • The top hook can be moved along the leader • Hook spacing is adjusted to match the length of the bait This makes the rig particularly useful for: • Yakka • Slimy mackerel • Garfish • Whole squid • Bonito strips • Other long fish baits Move the top hook until both hooks sit naturally along the bait without stretching, bending or bunching it. Keep both hook points and gapes exposed. The adjustable spacing provides hook coverage across more of the bait, which is useful when kingfish grab the head, middle or tail rather than taking the complete bait cleanly. The sliding hook requires pressure to move and normally remains where it has been positioned. Because each rig is hand tied, the amount of pressure required can vary slightly. When using whole dead baits, squid or long strips, bait elastic can be wrapped around the bait and leader to keep the bait straight and help hold both hooks in their chosen positions. View the 80lb Sliding Snelled Double Hook Rig with Twin 8/0 Circle Hooks → For a detailed explanation of adjustable hook spacing, see: Sliding Snell Rigs Explained →

sections.heading: When to Use a Flasher Paternoster Rig for Kingfish
sections.text: A flasher paternoster rig is a practical kingfish option when fishing vertically from a boat around reef edges, pinnacles, wrecks and schools of bait. The sinker is attached at the bottom of the rig, while the baited hooks are held above it on twisted paternoster arms. This allows the complete rig to be lowered to the required depth and kept under control in current. Use a flasher paternoster rig when: • Livebait is unavailable or difficult to keep • Fishing pilchard pieces, squid or fish strips • Kingfish are holding above reef or around bait schools • Fishing vertically from an anchored or drifting boat • Snapper, trevally and other reef species are being targeted at the same time • Current makes an unweighted bait difficult to control Flasher material adds colour and movement around each hook, while the bait provides scent and a natural food source. The Wiggle ya Worm Kingfish & Snapper Twisted Flasher Paternoster Rig uses a 60lb mono leader and twin 6/0 recurve circle hooks, providing a practical setup for kingfish and mixed reef fishing. View the Kingfish & Snapper Twisted Flasher Paternoster Rig →

sections.heading: When to Use a Kingfish & Tailor Stinger Rig
sections.text: The Wiggle ya Worm Kingfish & Tailor Stinger Rig uses an 80lb coated-wire trace with a main hook and an adjustable sliding treble hook. Move the treble along the wire to place it farther along the bait while keeping the main hook and treble exposed. This differs from a mono sliding-snell rig in two important ways: • The sliding treble provides additional hook coverage farther along the bait • The 80lb coated wire provides bite protection in mixed schools containing tailor, mackerel and other toothy predators Use this rig when toothy fish are likely to take the same bait being fished for kingfish, particularly around headlands, reef edges and mixed predator schools. View the Kingfish & Tailor Stinger Rig with Sliding Treble Hook →

sections.heading: Slide Bait Rigs for Land-Based Kingfish
sections.text: Slide baiting allows a large live or whole bait to be sent beyond normal casting range from a beach, headland or rock ledge. The breakaway sinker is cast first and anchored firmly. Once the mainline is held under tension, the baited slide trace is attached to the line using the one-way trolley and worked down towards the stopper near the sinker. Because only the sinker is cast, the bait is not damaged or restricted by the casting process. This makes slide baiting particularly useful when targeting kingfish with larger baits that would be difficult to cast effectively. For the system to work correctly: • The breakaway sinker must remain firmly anchored • The mainline must stay under tension • The trolley must travel fully down to the stopper • The hook trace, leader and hook must be matched to the expected kingfish and surrounding structure Slide baiting is most useful where kingfish patrol current lines, reef edges and deeper water beyond normal casting range.
