sections.heading: Best Mulloway Rigs in Australia
sections.text: Mulloway are one of Australia’s most iconic target fish, but the rig needs to suit where they are holding, the bait being used and the water movement. A setup suited to calm estuary water may be difficult to control in open surf, while a light beach rig may not provide enough abrasion resistance around rocks, pylons or other structure. For most fishos, a twin-hook sliding snell rig is the most versatile all-round Mulloway setup because the hook spacing can be adjusted to suit squid, whole fish and large fillets. Use a long cast pulley rig when Mulloway are holding beyond the breakers, a running sinker rig on calmer beaches or in estuaries, a stronger twin-hook rig around rocks, pylons or other abrasive structure, and a paternoster in deeper offshore water. This guide explains how these Mulloway rig designs work and when to use each one across Australian beaches, rock ledges, estuaries and offshore water. If you’re new to fishing rigs, start with our complete fishing rig guide.

sections.heading: How Mulloway Feeding Behaviour Affects Rig Choice
sections.text: Mulloway don’t always smash a bait. A lot of bites start as: Slow pickups Soft taps Weight loading up That feeding style means the wrong rig can cause: Missed hook-ups Dropped baits Pulled hooks mid-fight Water movement, structure, and bait size all influence how mulloway feed — and your rig needs to match those conditions. Most experienced mulloway fishos rotate between a few proven setups rather than relying on one rig. When Mulloway pick up a bait cautiously, a running sinker rig can reduce the initial resistance they feel. With longer baits such as squid, whole fish or large fillets, an adjustable twin-hook rig allows the hook spacing to be matched to the bait. As current, surf movement or snag risk increases, bait control, leader strength and abrasion resistance become more important. If you also target snapper, see our snapper rigs guide .

sections.heading: Where Mulloway Are Caught (And Why It Changes the Rig)
sections.text: Mulloway live in a wide range of environments across Australia, and each one demands a slightly different rig style.

sections.heading: Beach & Surf Mulloway
sections.text: Surf mulloway often sit in gutters, holes, or just beyond the breakers. If you're specifically targeting mulloway from the sand, see our Beach Mulloway – How to Land the Silver Ghost from the Sand guide for timing, bait choice, and gutter selection tips → • A streamlined bait-and-sinker layout when additional casting distance is required • Hook spacing matched to the length of the bait • Enough sinker control to hold the chosen gutter without adding unnecessary resistance Long cast pulley rigs suit Mulloway holding beyond the breakers because they keep the bait and sinker inline during the cast, reducing wind resistance and helping the rig travel further. Twin-hook sliding snell rigs allow the hook spacing to be adjusted for squid, whole fish and large fillets. In rivers and estuaries, Mulloway can be cautious — especially in clear water. Here, finesse matters more than brute strength. A running sinker rig suits these conditions because the line can move through the sinker as the Mulloway takes the bait, reducing the initial resistance felt by the fish. Lighter leaders and simple rigs often outfish heavy setups.

sections.heading: Rock & Breakwall Mulloway
sections.text: Land-based Mulloway fishing around structure is brutal on gear. Oysters, pylons and rock edges demand: • Strong leaders • Solid hook connections • Reliable components Stronger twin-hook rigs suit these conditions because the hook spacing can be matched to squid, whole fish and large fillets while maintaining two correctly positioned hooks in the bait. Offshore Mulloway are usually found around reefs, deep holes or wrecks. In these conditions, control and durability matter more than casting distance. A paternoster rig positions the sinker below the baited paternoster arms. This carries the rig down while keeping the baits separated from the sinker and slightly above the bottom, helping reduce tangles in current.

sections.heading: Mulloway Rig Designs and When to Use Them
sections.text: There are dozens of Mulloway rig variations, but only a handful suit the different conditions encountered across Australian beaches, estuaries, rock ledges and offshore waters.

sections.heading: Twin-Hook Sliding Snell Rigs for Mulloway
sections.text: Twin-hook sliding snell rigs are the most versatile all-round Mulloway setup. The adjustable hook spacing allows the rig to be matched to: • Squid • Whole fish • Large fillets Matching the hook spacing to the bait helps keep longer baits straight and positions the hooks along the bait rather than forcing every bait onto one fixed layout. This same adjustable layout is widely used when livebaiting for Kingfish around reef edges, pylons and pressure points where longer baits require correctly positioned hooks. See the Kingfish Rig Guide → If you’re only carrying one Mulloway rig style, a twin-hook sliding snell is usually the most versatile place to start.

sections.heading: Long Cast Pulley Rigs for Surf Mulloway
sections.text: When Mulloway are holding beyond the breakers or in deeper outer gutters, additional casting distance becomes important. Before the cast, the hook is held by the impact shield and the bait is drawn tight against the sinker. This keeps the bait and sinker inline, creating a more compact and aerodynamic shape with less wind resistance. Holding everything together also prevents the bait from flapping, tumbling or twisting around the leader during flight, helping the rig cast further with fewer mid-air tangles. When the sinker hits the water, the impact shield triggers the release so the hook and leader can separate from the sinker and the rig can fish normally. For a detailed explanation of the casting and release system, see Long Casting Pulley Rigs Explained →

sections.heading: Running Sinker Rigs for Estuary and Calm-Water Mulloway
sections.text: A running sinker rig allows the sinker to move independently along the main line rather than fixing its full weight directly to the baited leader. When a Mulloway picks up the bait and moves away, the line can pass through the sinker before the fish feels its full resistance. This suits the slower pickups and gradually increasing weight often associated with Mulloway bites. Running sinker rigs are best suited to: • Estuaries • Calm beaches • Clear water • Cautiously feeding fish As current or surf movement increases, the rig can become harder to control and a fixed-sinker layout may become more suitable. For a detailed explanation of running sinker layouts and reduced resistance, see Fish Finder Rigs Explained Simple does not mean ineffective—many large Mulloway are caught using running sinker rigs.

sections.heading: Paternoster Rigs for Offshore Mulloway
sections.text: In deeper water, controlling the bait during the descent and once it reaches the bottom becomes more important than casting distance. A paternoster rig positions the sinker at the bottom of the rig with the baited hooks on paternoster arms above it. This layout helps: • Keep the baits separated from the sinker • Reduce tangles during descent and in current • Hold the baits slightly above the seabed • Maintain better control around reef, deep holes and wrecks Paternoster rigs are commonly used from boats and deep ledges where current, depth and bottom structure make a running sinker rig harder to control. For a detailed explanation of paternoster layouts and how different versions work, see Paternoster Rigs Explained →

sections.heading: Circle Hooks vs J and Beak Hooks for Mulloway
sections.text: Hook choice affects how the rig needs to be fished and when the hook takes hold. Circle hooks are designed to move towards the corner of the mouth as the Mulloway takes the bait and the line comes under tension. Rather than striking hard, allow the line to tighten so the hook can rotate and take hold. Circle hooks are well suited to: • Slower Mulloway pickups • Larger baits and livebaits • Fishing with the rod left to load up • Fishos who do not want to time an immediate strike J and beak hooks rely more on the fisho setting the hook. They remain useful when: • Actively fishing the bait • Using strip baits • Timing and setting the hook manually Both styles can be effective. The correct choice depends on the bait being used and whether you intend to let the line tighten or actively strike. For a broader explanation of hook styles, sizes and how different hooks take hold, see Choosing the Right Fishing Hook →

sections.heading: Choosing Mulloway Leader Strength for Different Ground
sections.text: Leader strength should be chosen around abrasion risk, water clarity, bait size and likely bycatch—not the Mulloway alone. Many experienced fishos use: • 40–60 lb leader for general Mulloway fishing • Heavier leader where rocks, pylons, oysters or other abrasive structure create additional risk Increasing leader strength also increases its diameter and stiffness. Going heavier than the conditions require can restrict bait movement and make the leader more noticeable to line-shy fish, particularly in calm or clear water. Extra strength may also be justified where powerful bycatch such as Kingfish are likely around the same structure. The goal is enough strength and abrasion resistance for the ground without making the rig heavier than the conditions require.

sections.heading: Why Purpose-Built Hand-Tied Mulloway Rigs Suit Specific Conditions
sections.text: Mass-produced rigs can work, but they are generally designed as one setup intended to cover a broad range of fishing situations. A purpose-built hand-tied Mulloway rig can be matched more closely to the bait, location and conditions in which it will be used. Practical differences can include: • Hook spacing selected for squid, whole fish or large fillets • Leader strength matched to beaches, estuaries, rocks or offshore ground • Rig layout chosen around casting distance, current and water depth • Connections and components selected for the expected load These details become more important when fishing around structure, running larger baits or targeting larger Mulloway. The advantage of a purpose-built hand-tied rig is the ability to build the hook layout, leader and components around a specific fishing purpose rather than a broad set of conditions.

sections.heading: Common Mulloway Rig Mistakes and Why They Cause Problems
sections.text: Using the Same Rig Everywhere A running sinker rig may suit calm estuary water but become difficult to control in stronger surf or current. A light leader may work over clean sand but provide insufficient abrasion resistance around rocks, pylons and oysters. Match the rig to the location and water movement rather than using one setup everywhere. Building the Rig Too Heavy Heavier leaders provide additional strength and abrasion resistance, but unnecessary diameter and stiffness can restrict bait movement and make the leader more noticeable to line-shy Mulloway in calm or clear water. Using Hook Spacing That Does Not Match the Bait If the hooks are too close together or too far apart for the bait, squid, whole fish and large fillets may bunch, fold or leave the hooks poorly positioned. Adjust the hook spacing to the bait rather than forcing every bait onto the same layout. Using the Wrong Sinker Arrangement A running sinker reduces initial resistance in calm water, while a long cast pulley rig controls the bait during a distance cast and a paternoster provides greater control in deeper water or current. Choosing the wrong arrangement can leave the bait drifting, tangling or failing to reach the intended feeding area. Rigging the Bait Poorly Match the hook size to the bait and rig the bait so it remains straight without burying the hook. The hook point and gap need to remain well exposed so the hook can take hold when a Mulloway picks up the bait. A bait that is not secured straight can also spin or tumble during casting, descent or water movement. Correct bait position begins with matching the hook size, rig layout and hook spacing to the bait being used. For a broader breakdown of setup problems and how to correct them, see Common Fishing Rig Mistakes Correcting these issues can improve how the bait behaves without changing bait type or fishing location.

sections.heading: Choosing a Mulloway Rig for Different Locations
sections.text: Use the fishing location, water movement, casting distance and bait size to narrow down the rig: • Most versatile all-round setup — Twin-hook sliding snell rig • Beach fishing when Mulloway are holding wide — Long cast pulley rig • Calm beaches and estuaries — Running sinker rig • Rocks, breakwalls, pylons and abrasive structure — Stronger twin-hook rig with leader strength matched to the ground • Offshore, deeper water and stronger current — Paternoster rig Use the rig that solves the problems created by the conditions—not the heaviest rig you own.

sections.heading: Can Mulloway Be Caught Year-Round?
sections.text: Yes—Mulloway can be caught throughout the year, but their availability and most productive locations vary between regions. Their movements and feeding activity can be influenced by: • Water temperature • Bait movement • River flow • Current and water conditions • Seasonal breeding and movement patterns There is no single Australia-wide seasonal rule that applies to every beach, estuary or offshore area. Rather than selecting a rig by the calendar alone, match it to where the fish are holding, the water movement, the required casting distance and the bait being used. Mulloway are commonly targeted after dark. For practical advice on choosing a beach, managing lighting and fishing safely at night, see Night Fishing from the Beach →

sections.heading: Still Not Sure Which Mulloway Rig to Use?
sections.text: If you’re fishing unfamiliar water or deciding between several suitable setups, use the Rig Finder to match a rig to your target species, fishing environment, bait, current and required casting distance. Planning a dedicated surf session? The Beach Mulloway Guide covers tide timing, bait selection and gutter choice in more detail. sections.heading: Match the Rig to the Reef, Current and Bait
sections.text: Reef fishing rigs must get the bait to the required depth, keep it under control in current and provide enough strength and abrasion resistance for the ground being fished. The right setup depends on: • Water depth and current strength • Whether the boat is anchored or drifting • Coral, rock, rubble or cleaner ground • Bait size and shape • Target species and likely bycatch • How close the bait needs to fish to the bottom Paternoster rigs hold baited hooks above the sinker and provide greater control in current. Running-sinker rigs allow more bait movement near the bottom, while adjustable twin-hook and ganged-hook arrangements help keep longer baits straight. Wire provides additional bite protection where mackerel, sharks or other toothy species are likely to be encountered. Leader strength, sinker weight and hook arrangement must then be matched to the conditions. A sinker that is too light may leave the bait drifting above the required depth, while insufficient leader strength or abrasion resistance can quickly become a problem around coral and reef edges. This guide explains how to choose suitable rigs for Australian reef fishing—from broken inshore reef to heavy coral ground such as the Swains. Not sure which rig style suits your conditions? Start with the Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide →

sections.heading: What Makes Reef Fishing Different
sections.text: Reef fishing combines water depth, current and abrasive ground. The rig must pass through the water without tangling, reach the required depth and remain manageable as the boat moves. The sinker does more than carry the bait down. Its weight and position determine how quickly the rig descends and how well the baited hooks remain under control near the reef. Different conditions create different requirements: • Strong current requires enough sinker weight to reach and maintain the required depth • Coral, rock and shell demand suitable leader strength and abrasion resistance • Drifting boats require rigs that remain organised as they descend and move over the ground • Small fish can strip exposed or loosely secured baits before they reach larger reef species • Mixed-species fishing requires hooks and leader capable of handling the strongest likely catch Leader strength should therefore be chosen for the ground and fishing conditions—not only the expected size of the fish. A light rig may suit cleaner ground and moderate current, while heavy coral, strong tidal flow or larger reef species may require considerably stronger leader, hooks and connections.

sections.heading: Choosing Reef Rigs for Coral Trout and Red Emperor
sections.text: Coral trout and red emperor are both commonly targeted around reef, but the most suitable rig depends on how the bait needs to be fished. A compact single-arm paternoster is useful when fishing close to reef ledges, drop-offs and isolated structure. With the sinker below the baited arm, the fisho can lower the rig to the bottom and work the bait close to the reef without managing a second baited hook. The Wiggle ya Worm Trout Crusher™ uses this layout with an artificial crab positioned close to the sinker. It can be fished with the crab alone or baited with a small piece of squid or flesh bait for added scent. Slow lifts allow the crab and bait to move close to reef edges where coral trout are being targeted. A twin-arm paternoster provides a different option for red emperor and general reef fishing. It allows two baits to be fished at once while the sinker remains at the bottom of the rig, keeping the baited hooks separated and above the reef. Whichever layout is used, the sinker must be heavy enough for the depth and current. If the rig cannot reach or remain close to the required depth, changing hook arrangements will not solve the problem. Explore the Swains Slayer Series™ →

sections.heading: Twisted Paternoster Rigs for Reef Fishing
sections.text: A twisted paternoster is one of the most practical rigs for fishing vertically over reef. The sinker is attached at the bottom of the backbone, with one or two baited paternoster arms positioned above it. This allows the sinker to carry the complete rig down while keeping the hooks separated from the weight and seabed. Twisting the paternoster arms makes them stiffer than simple loop droppers and helps hold the baited hooks away from the backbone as the rig descends and moves in current. Use a single-arm paternoster when: • One bait needs to be worked close to a specific ledge or reef edge • A compact rig provides better control • A second baited hook would add unnecessary movement or tangling Use a twin-arm paternoster when: • Fishing two baits • Targeting mixed reef species • Covering slightly different heights above the sinker • Fishing vertically from an anchored or drifting boat The sinker weight can then be changed to suit the depth and current without changing the basic rig layout. For a complete explanation of the different layouts, see: Paternoster Rigs Explained →

sections.heading: When to Use a Running-Sinker Reef Rig
sections.text: A running-sinker rig allows the mainline to move through the sinker rather than fixing the full sinker weight directly to the baited leader. This layout suits: • Anchored fishing over cleaner reef or rubble • Slow drifts where the rig can remain under control • Shallower reef where a heavy fixed-sinker paternoster is unnecessary • Fishing one bait close to the bottom • Conditions where less immediate sinker resistance is preferred The sinker should still be heavy enough to maintain the required depth. If current or boat movement causes the rig to drift uncontrolled, changing to a fixed-sinker paternoster provides greater control. Running-sinker rigs become less suitable where the sinker repeatedly rolls into coral, the line angle becomes difficult to manage or two baited hooks need to be held separately above the bottom. For a detailed explanation of running-sinker layouts, see: Fish Finder Rigs Explained →

sections.heading: When to Use a Flasher Paternoster Rig
sections.text: A flasher rig is normally a paternoster with reflective or coloured material tied close to each hook. The sinker and paternoster arms perform the same mechanical job as a standard paternoster. The flasher material adds movement, colour and reflected light beside the bait. Flasher paternosters are useful when: • Fishing deeper water with reduced available light • Baitfish are holding around reef structure • Targeting mixed reef species with baited hooks • Adding a visible target immediately beside the bait • Fishing dawn, dusk or overcast conditions The hooks can be baited with squid, fish strips, pilchard pieces or other suitable reef baits. Keep the bait clear of the flasher material and leave the hook points and gapes exposed. For more on choosing colours and reflective materials, see: Using Colour and Contrast in Rigs to Trigger More Bites →

sections.heading: Matching Leader Length to the Boat
sections.text: Leader length affects how a fish can be controlled beside the boat. If the leader is too short, the fisho may reach the end of the mono while the fish is still below the boat, leaving loaded braid as the only line available to hold during landing. Braid is difficult and unsafe to handle under tension. A leader that is too long can create the opposite problem. If it terminates in a swivel, the swivel may reach the top rod guide before the fish is close enough to land. Choose the leader length around: • The height of the boat’s deck above the water • Rod length • The method used to land the fish • Whether the leader connects through a swivel or directly to the mainline Some longer Wiggle ya Worm reef rigs allow the top swivel to be removed so the mono leader can be connected directly to the mainline when additional leader length is required. Do not wind a swivel into the rod guides. Set the leader length and connection before fishing so the fish can be brought within safe landing distance without handling loaded braid.

sections.heading: Choosing Mono or Wire for Reef Rigs
sections.text: Monofilament is the usual starting point for general reef fishing. It remains flexible, allows natural bait movement and can be selected in different strengths to suit the ground and expected fish. As a practical starting point: • 60lb mono suits general reef fishing over cleaner or moderately broken ground • 80lb mono provides additional strength and abrasion resistance around reef edges, rubble and mixed structure • 100lb mono suits heavy coral, larger reef species and situations where fish need to be turned quickly These are starting points rather than fixed rules. Leader strength should increase as the reef becomes sharper, the fish become larger or the available room to stop them decreases. Wire serves a different purpose. Its main advantage is protection from species capable of cutting monofilament, including mackerel, sharks and other toothy fish commonly encountered around reef. • Toothy bycatch is unlikely • Bait movement and flexibility are priorities • Leader strength can be matched to the reef and expected fish • Knotted connections or adjustable hook arrangements are required • Mackerel, sharks or other toothy species are likely • Repeated bite-offs are occurring • The rig is specifically designed around a coated-wire trace • Additional protection is required immediately ahead of the hook Wire is not automatically the best choice simply because the ground is reef. Leader material should be chosen for the expected contact point—mono for general reef abrasion and wire where teeth create the greater risk.

sections.heading: Choosing Sinker Weight for Reef Fishing
sections.text: The sinker must carry the rig to the required depth and provide enough control to keep the bait fishing where the fish are holding. The required weight depends on: • Water depth • Current strength • Boat drift speed • Mainline diameter • Bait size and water resistance • Whether the rig needs to remain close to the bottom Use the lightest sinker that still allows the rig to reach and maintain the required depth. Increase the sinker weight when: • The line is scoping too far behind the boat • The rig is taking too long to reach the bottom • The bait is being carried above the intended depth • A larger bait is catching more current and moving the rig Reduce the weight when the sinker repeatedly lodges in broken ground or when less weight will still provide adequate control.

sections.heading: Matching the Hook Arrangement to the Bait
sections.text: Hook arrangement should be chosen around the bait’s length and shape rather than the target species alone. Use a single hook for compact baits that can be secured without folding or covering the hook point. Use a twin-hook arrangement for longer slab baits, whole squid or fish baits that need support at two points. The hooks may be fixed at a set distance or use a sliding top hook that can be adjusted to match different bait lengths. Ganged hooks suit long, narrow fish baits where several hooks help keep the bait straight and provide hook coverage along its body. Whichever arrangement is used: • Keep the bait straight rather than stretched or bunched • Leave every hook point and gape exposed • Match the distance between hooks to the actual bait • Use bait elastic where needed to prevent soft or long baits twisting during the descent • Choose hook size around the bait thickness as well as the expected fish A well-matched hook arrangement keeps the bait secure as it travels through the water and prevents the hooks being hidden inside a folded or poorly fitted bait. For adjustable twin-hook rigs, see: Sliding Snell Rigs Explained →

sections.heading: Choosing a Rig for Anchored or Drift Fishing
sections.text: Anchoring and drifting move the bait across reef in different ways, so the rig and sinker need to be selected accordingly. When anchored, the boat remains in one position while the current controls the line angle and bait movement. A paternoster provides direct depth control and keeps the baited hooks above the sinker. A running-sinker rig can also be used where the bait needs more freedom to move near the bottom. When drifting, the boat carries the rig across the ground. The sinker must maintain the required depth without continually catching in coral, rock or broken reef. When drift fishing: • Use enough sinker weight to keep the rig at the required depth • Reduce the weight if the sinker repeatedly digs into broken ground • Keep long baits straight so they do not spin as the rig moves • Monitor the depth as the boat crosses reef edges and drop-offs • Wind up before the rig is dragged into ground that is too rough to fish safely A long mono leader with a ganged or twin-hook trace suits whole fish and slab baits moving across reef, while a compact paternoster provides greater control when the rig needs to remain more vertical. The Swains Slayer Series™ includes rigs developed for both anchored and drifting reef fishing.

sections.heading: How Heavy Coral Changes the Rig
sections.text: Heavy coral, bommies and sharp ledges can contact several parts of the rig—not only the short section immediately ahead of the hook. A heavy-coral setup should be treated as a complete system. Increasing the hook trace strength will not help if the backbone, paternoster arms, swivel or connections remain weaker. • Use 80lb or 100lb mono where additional abrasion resistance is required • Match the hook strength, swivels and connections to the leader • Keep the layout compact enough to control close to the reef • Use a single-arm paternoster when one bait needs to be worked close to a specific ledge • Use enough sinker weight to reach the reef without allowing the rig to drift uncontrolled above it • Check the complete rig after every fish or contact with the bottom Damage may appear anywhere along the leader. Run the mono between your fingers and inspect the paternoster arms, knots, crimps and hook connection before dropping again. For the lessons that shaped Wiggle ya Worm’s heavy-reef rigs, read: Field Notes from Swains—What the Reef Taught Us →

sections.heading: Matching Rigs to Other Reef Species
sections.text: The target species does not determine the complete rig by itself, but it provides a useful starting point when combined with the bait, depth, current and ground. Sliding-snelled rigs suit whole fish, squid and longer strip baits because the hook spacing can be adjusted. Paternoster and flasher rigs provide greater control when fishing vertically over deeper reef. See the Best Snapper Rigs in Australia Guide → Cod, sweetlip, tuskfish and mixed reef species A twin-arm twisted paternoster is a practical starting point because two baited hooks can be fished above the sinker while the rig remains under control near the bottom. Mackerel and other toothy reef predators Use a coated-wire bite trace where teeth create a genuine bite-off risk. Ganged hooks help hold whole fish and other long baits straight while drifting or fishing around reef edges. These are starting points rather than fixed combinations. Increase the leader, hook and connection strength where the reef is heavier or the fish must be stopped before reaching structure.

sections.heading: Explore Reef Rigs and Setup Guides
sections.text: The right reef rig is the one that reaches the required depth, remains under control and provides enough strength and abrasion resistance for the ground being fished. sections.heading: Why Tailor Rigs Need Ganged Hooks and Bite Protection
sections.text: Tailor are fast, aggressive surf predators with sharp teeth and a habit of striking long baits from the side. A suitable beach rig needs to keep the bait straight in moving water, position hooks along its length and provide protection where the fish is most likely to bite through the leader. Ganged hooks suit whole pilchards, garfish and longer strip baits because they support the bait and provide hook coverage beyond a single fixed point. A short coated-wire bite trace also helps prevent tailor cutting through the rig during a strike. This guide explains how to match the gang arrangement, bite trace, sinker style and rig length to the bait and surf conditions being fished. If you’re unsure which surf rig suits your local conditions, start with the Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide →

sections.heading: Where Tailor Feed in the Surf
sections.text: Tailor patrol active surf water where waves and current concentrate baitfish. Productive areas include: • Whitewater washing across sandbanks • The edges and entrances of deeper gutters • Channels running between sandbanks • Rips carrying bait away from the beach • River mouths and creek entrances • Gutter edges near rocks, headlands or other structure The deepest part of a gutter is not always the best place to cast. Tailor often travel along the edges where baitfish are being pushed between shallow whitewater and deeper water. Working birds, scattering baitfish and sudden surface activity are strong signs that a tailor school is moving through. Bites may come in short bursts, so rebaiting and returning the rig to the same feeding lane quickly can matter. For help identifying gutters, banks, channels and rips, see How to Read a Beach: Spotting Gutters, Banks & Breaks Like a Pro →

sections.heading: Why Ganged Hooks Suit Tailor Baits
sections.text: Ganged hooks are particularly effective for tailor because they place hook points along the length of a long bait rather than relying on one fixed hook position. This is useful when tailor strike the head, middle or tail of the bait instead of swallowing it cleanly. Ganged hooks also help: • Keep whole pilchards and garfish straight • Support longer strip baits during casting • Reduce bait spinning in surf wash • Provide hook coverage along the bait • Keep multiple hook points exposed Single hooks can still work with smaller or compact baits. For longer fish baits, correctly spaced gangs provide better support and cover more of the areas where tailor commonly strike.

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Gang Size for Your Bait
sections.text: The gang should match both the length and thickness of the bait. The complete gang needs to support the bait without bunching it up or leaving a long section unsupported.

sections.heading: 3 × 3/0 Ganged Hooks
sections.text: • Longer pilchards • Garfish • Slim strip baits • Whitebait clusters The third hook extends the gang along longer, slimmer baits and provides hook coverage closer to the tail.

sections.heading: 2 × 4/0 Ganged Hooks
sections.text: • Shorter or chunkier pilchards • Slab mullet • Squid strips • Thicker bait sections The larger hook gape suits thicker baits, while the shorter two-hook gang avoids forcing too much hook length into a compact bait. Whichever arrangement is used, keep the bait straight and leave the hook points clearly exposed. If the gang is too long, the bait will bunch up. If it is too short, the unsupported tail can fold or spin in the surf.

sections.heading: Why Tailor Rigs Use a Coated Wire Bite Trace
sections.text: Tailor can cut monofilament with their teeth when they strike across the bait or bite ahead of the hooks. The Wiggle ya Worm tailor rigs use a monofilament leader connected to a coated-wire bite trace and ganged hooks. This places bite protection around the bait while retaining monofilament through the main section of the rig. This combination provides: • Protection against teeth around the bait • Fewer bite-offs during fast sideways strikes • Monofilament through the main length of the rig • Enough flexibility for the bait to move naturally in the surf • Better durability when tailor are feeding in schools

sections.heading: Why Sliding Ball Sinkers Suit Tailor Fishing
sections.text: A sliding ball sinker allows the bait to move with the sweep instead of holding it in one fixed position. As waves and current move across the gutter, the rounded sinker can roll or shift along the bottom and carry the bait through areas being patrolled by tailor. The sliding design also allows a fish to move away with the bait without immediately pulling against the full weight of the sinker. • Move the bait naturally through the wash • Cover more of the gutter or channel edge • Keep the bait travelling with the current • Reduce resistance when a fish takes the bait • Place the bait in front of moving tailor schools Wiggle ya Worm purpose-built Tailor & Surf Fishing Rigs include a genuine Australian-made size 7 sliding ball sinker. The sinker is already fitted to the rig, so no additional assembly or separate sinker is required before fishing.

sections.heading: When a Popper and Ganged-Hook Paternoster Rig Suits Tailor
sections.text: A Popper and Ganged-Hook Paternoster Rig is a specialised surf rig developed for aggressive feeding conditions. The upper paternoster arm carries a highly visible popper with its own 4/0 teaser hook. The lower arm carries a 4/0 ganged-hook section for a whole pilchard, garfish, squid strip or another longer bait. This gives tailor two separate targets at different heights in the whitewater. The rig is particularly useful when: • Tailor are actively chasing baitfish • Birds are working over the surf • Bait schools are moving through a gutter • Whitewater or stirred-up sand reduces visibility • Tailor, Australian salmon and kingfish are feeding together Fish may strike the natural bait or the popper itself. A small piece of bait can also be added to the popper hook to provide scent around the visual attractor. See the Popper & Ganged Hook Twisted Paternoster Rig →

sections.heading: Timing Tailor Sessions on K’gari and Other Surf Beaches
sections.text: K’gari is a good example of how tailor movement is influenced by tide, light, bait activity and the direction of the surf sweep. Dawn and dusk are productive periods, particularly when moving water is carrying bait through an established gutter. The later part of the run-in tide and the beginning of the run-out can both produce fish, but the structure and movement of the water matter more than following the tide alone. Watch which way the sweep is travelling and cast slightly up-current of the feeding area. This allows the sliding-sinker rig and bait to move naturally along the gutter edge instead of immediately drifting away from the fish. Because the Wiggle ya Worm purpose-built tailor rig has a built-in size 7 sinker, control where the bait travels by changing your casting angle, casting distance or position along the beach. Recast as needed to keep the bait moving through the active feeding lane.

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Tailor Rig Length
sections.text: Rig length affects casting control, bait movement and how easily the setup can be managed from the beach. A longer rig provides more separation between the sinker and bait, allowing the bait to move naturally through deeper gutters and open surf. A shorter rig can be easier to control when fishing: • Tight gutters close to shore • River mouths • Strong side winds • Rock platforms with limited casting room • Shallow wash zones Wiggle ya Worm purpose-built tailor rigs are approximately 1.5 metres long. The separation between the built-in sinker and bait allows the bait to move naturally in the current, mimicking a wounded baitfish.

sections.heading: Best Baits for Tailor from the Beach
sections.text: Tailor respond well to long fish baits that move naturally through the surf. Reliable options include: • Whole pilchards • Garfish • Mullet strips • Squid strips • Whitebait clusters Whole pilchards and garfish suit ganged hooks because the hooks support the bait along its length. Mullet and squid strips are tougher options when softer baits are being damaged by casting or surf wash. Keep the bait straight along the gang and leave the hook points clearly exposed. Use a small amount of bait elastic where needed to prevent the bait folding, spinning or tearing away during the cast and keep the hooks exposed.

sections.heading: Night Fishing for Tailor
sections.text: Tailor commonly feed after dark, particularly around gutter entrances, channel edges, river mouths and whitewater near structure. Productive night conditions usually still have moving water carrying bait through the surf. Darkness alone will not create a feeding area, so identify the gutter and cast position before the light disappears where possible. Luminous beads or tubing can provide a visible attractor close to the bait, while a strong fish bait supplies the scent and movement. Prepare spare rigs and bait before the session so damaged traces and bitten baits can be replaced quickly without tying complicated setups on a dark beach. For more practical low-light advice, see the Night Fishing from the Beach Guide →

sections.heading: A Proven Ready-to-Fish Tailor Setup
sections.text: Wiggle ya Worm purpose-built Tailor & Surf Fishing Rigs include: • 60lb monofilament leader • 40lb black coated-wire bite trace • Genuine Australian-made size 7 sliding ball sinker • Ganged hooks matched to the bait size • Two 95lb rolling swivels • Green luminous knot protectors • Approximately 1.5 metres overall length Choose 3 × 3/0 ganged hooks for longer, slimmer baits or 2 × 4/0 ganged hooks for shorter, thicker baits. The sinker is built into the rig, so the complete setup is ready to bait and fish straight from the packet. Browse the complete Tailor Rig Range →

sections.heading: Other Species Caught on Tailor Rigs
sections.text: The same long baits, ganged hooks and moving surf water that attract tailor can also produce: • Australian salmon • Trevally • Mulloway • Kingfish around headlands and bait schools • Other aggressive surf predators Australian salmon commonly feed in the same gutters and whitewater as tailor, while mulloway may pick up a larger bait moving along the bottom. Trevally and kingfish can also enter the surf when bait schools move close to shore. Learn more in the: Australian Salmon Rig Guide → Mulloway Rig Guide → Kingfish Rig Guide →

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Tailor Rig
sections.text: For most beach sessions, start with a sliding-sinker rig using ganged hooks and a coated-wire bite trace. Match the hook arrangement to the bait: • 3 × 3/0 gangs for longer, slimmer baits • 2 × 4/0 gangs for shorter, thicker baits • Popper and ganged-hook paternoster rigs when tailor are feeding aggressively in whitewater The Wiggle ya Worm sliding-sinker setup has been one of our go-to tailor rigs on K’gari and has accounted for hundreds of tailor over the years. If you’re fishing unfamiliar water, use the Rig Finder to match the rig to your target species and location. For a broader comparison of Australian fishing rigs, visit the Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide → BAIT UP. CAST IN. HANG ON.

sections.heading: Best Whiting Rigs in Australia (Surf & Estuary Guide)
sections.text: Whiting are one of the easiest fish to catch in Australia — but they’re also one of the easiest to miss if your rig doesn’t match the conditions in front of you. Most lost bites happen because the bait is dragging sideways, sitting too deep in the sand, or fishing the wrong part of the gutter altogether. Changing rigs at the right time usually improves results faster than changing bait. On calm beaches and estuary flats a simple running sinker rig works perfectly. Add sweep, weed, distance or shallow whitewater movement and a light paternoster rig quickly becomes the better option. This guide explains which whiting rigs actually work around Australia — and when to change your setup as conditions shift. If you’re unsure what suits your beach or estuary, start with the Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide → If you’re completely new to fishing, the Beginner Fisho Rig Kit is the easiest way to get started with proven rigs for whiting, bream and flathead while learning how different setups behave in real conditions.

sections.heading: What Are the Two Best Whiting Rigs for Australian Surf and Estuaries?
sections.text: You don’t need a complicated setup to catch whiting. Nearly every consistent whiting rig used around Australia falls into one of two styles: Running sinker rigs Best for estuaries, shallow gutters and calm beaches Light paternoster rigs Best when sweep, weed or casting distance become factors Knowing when to switch between them matters more than bait choice. To understand why paternoster rigs perform so well in moving surf, see Paternoster Rigs Explained →

sections.heading: When Should You Use a Running Sinker Rig for Whiting?
sections.text: Running sinker rigs allow whiting to pick up bait naturally without feeling sinker resistance. They work best when: • there’s little sideways sweep • fish are feeding close to shore • gutters are shallow and clean • the water is clear • worms or yabbies are moving naturally in the wash This is why running sinker rigs dominate estuary whiting fishing across Australia. They are also the easiest place for beginners to start. On many beaches, especially after a few calm days, whiting will feed right along the inside edge of the first sandbank where worms are being washed out of the sand. In these situations a simple running sinker rig often outfishes heavier surf setups.

sections.heading: When Should You Switch from a Running Sinker Rig to a Whiting Paternoster?
sections.text: Many fishos stay with a running sinker rig too long. Switch earlier and catches improve immediately. Move to a light whiting paternoster rig when: • surf sweep drags your bait sideways • weed starts collecting on your trace • pickers strip bait before whiting reach it • fish are feeding slightly above the bottom • casting past the inner gutter becomes necessary These conditions are common on open surf beaches, which is why dedicated surf whiting rigs nearly always use paternoster layouts.

sections.heading: What Hook Size Should You Use for Whiting in Australia?
sections.text: Most Australian surf and estuary whiting are best targeted using: • size 4 long shank hooks (red) • size 6 long shank hooks (red) Long shank hooks present worms naturally and make hook removal easier. Large hooks rarely improve fish size. Instead, they often miss bites completely because whiting mouth bait sideways before committing.

sections.heading: When Should You Change the Leader Length on a Whiting Rig?
sections.text: Leader length makes a bigger difference than most fishos expect. Use longer traces when: • fishing calm estuary flats • targeting cautious fish • using worms or yabbies Use slightly shorter traces when: • sweep increases • surf becomes messy • casting distance matters The goal is to reduce the potential for tangles while keeping the bait stable but natural.

sections.heading: What Sinker Should You Use for Whiting Fishing?
sections.text: Sinker size should always match conditions. Start as light as possible and increase only when needed. • estuaries — small ball sinkers • calm surf gutters — light ball or bean sinkers • moderate sweep — slightly heavier ball/bean sinkers • stronger sideways movement — star sinkers if required If bait drifts sideways, increase weight or switch rigs rather than recasting repeatedly.

sections.heading: What Are the Best Baits for Whiting in Australia?
sections.text: Consistent performers include: • beach worms • bloodworms • yabbies • pipis • squid strips Fresh worms almost always outfish frozen bait in shallow gutters, especially when fish are feeding along the inside bank close to shore.

sections.heading: Where Do Whiting Feed in the Surf?
sections.text: Whiting rarely sit in deep holes like mulloway. Instead they patrol: • shallow gutters behind the first sandbank • edges of sandbanks • areas where waves flatten before breaking • clean water beside whitewater • moving sand patches where worms are exposed On many beaches the best bite zone is only ankle-to-knee-deep water along the inside gutter edge. Flathead often sit along the deeper edges of these same gutters waiting for bait to move past — see our flathead rig guide here → Finding the right gutter often matters more than changing rigs. If you’re unsure how to identify productive gutters and sandbanks, see How to Read a Beach: Spotting Gutters, Banks & Breaks Like a Pro →

sections.heading: What Is the Best Tide for Whiting Fishing?
sections.text: Tide movement has a major impact on whiting activity. Reliable bite periods include: • the last half of the run-out tide along sandbanks • the first push of incoming tide into shallow gutters • rising water over exposed flats in estuaries As water covers fresh feeding ground, worms and small shellfish become exposed and whiting move in quickly.

sections.heading: What Is the Best Time of Day to Catch Whiting?
sections.text: Whiting feed throughout the day but are most consistent during: • early morning • late afternoon • periods of light onshore wind • gentle surf movement across sandbanks Low light combined with moving water usually produces the most reliable bites.

sections.heading: How Does Whiting Behaviour Change with the Seasons in Australia?
sections.text: Through spring and summer, warming water pushes whiting into shallow surf gutters where they actively hunt worms and pipis along the sandbanks. During cooler months they are often found further inside estuaries or holding in slightly deeper channels. Adjusting rig weight and trace length between seasons helps maintain natural bait presentation.

sections.heading: What Is a Simple Whiting Setup That Works Across Australia?
sections.text: Use a running sinker rig with a red size 4 or 6 long shank hook and fresh worm bait. If sweep increases or casting distance becomes necessary, switch to a light whiting paternoster rig. That combination covers most Australian whiting fishing situations.

sections.heading: Not Sure Which Surf Rig to Start With?
sections.text: If you fish beaches regularly and conditions change between gutters, tides and target species during the same session, the Ultimate Surf Rig Collection provides a practical spread of proven surf rigs — including dedicated whiting paternoster rigs and light running sinker options matched to real Australian conditions.

sections.heading: Fishing a New Beach or Estuary?
sections.text: Conditions change between locations. If you're unsure which rig suits your area, start with the Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide → or use the Rig Finder Tool to match rigs to your species and fishing location If you're travelling interstate, State-Based Fishing Rig Packs provide proven combinations matched to local surf and estuary conditions across Australia

sections.heading: Fish Finder Rigs Explained
sections.text: A Fish Finder Rig is a running sinker setup in which the sinker—or a sinker clip—is positioned on the mainline above a knot-protecting bead, swivel and hook leader. Unlike a fixed-sinker rig, the mainline can move through the sliding component when a fish takes the bait. This reduces the immediate resistance created by the sinker while still allowing its weight and style to be matched to the current and ground being fished. That does not make the rig resistance-free. Sinker weight and shape, water movement, line angle and tension through the rod all affect how easily the mainline moves through the sliding connection. A Fish Finder Rig commonly includes: • A sliding sinker or sinker clip fitted to the mainline • A bead positioned between the sliding component and the knot • A swivel connecting the mainline to the leader • A monofilament or wire leader selected for the target species and ground • A single hook or adjustable twin-hook arrangement matched to the bait Fish Finder Rigs can be used across estuaries, beaches and surf gutters. Lighter mono versions suit clean estuary ground, heavier mono provides additional strength and abrasion resistance, and wire versions provide bite protection when toothy species are likely to be encountered. This guide explains how the rig works, how its components fit together and how to choose a suitable leader, hook arrangement and sinker for the conditions.

sections.heading: How Does a Fish Finder Rig Work?
sections.text: After casting, the sinker settles on the bottom while the leader and bait extend beyond the swivel. When a fish takes the bait and moves away, the mainline can pass through the sliding sinker or sinker clip. If the sinker maintains its position, the fish can move the leader without immediately having to move the full sinker weight. The bite is still transmitted directly through the mainline to the rod. The sliding connection reduces the sinker’s immediate resistance; it does not prevent the fisho from feeling the bite. Fish Finder Rigs work particularly well when: • Fishing over clean sand or mud • Fishing estuary channels, drains and sandflat edges • Fishing beach and surf gutters • Using natural baits close to the bottom • Using longer baits that benefit from an adjustable twin-hook layout • A less restrictive running-sinker setup is preferred The sinker should provide enough weight to maintain the required contact with the bottom without unnecessarily restricting the bait’s movement. When strong current, heavy weed or rough ground makes the rig difficult to control, a fixed-sinker layout such as a paternoster rig may be more suitable. See Paternoster Rigs Explained →

sections.heading: Which Fish Finder Rig Should You Choose?
sections.text: Standard Fish Finder Rigs vary in three important areas: how the sinker is attached, the hook arrangement and the leader used. Direct-Sliding Sinker or Sinker Clip A ball or bean sinker can be threaded directly onto the mainline. This creates a simple running-sinker setup, but changing the sinker normally requires the mainline to be untied. A sliding sinker clip allows the sinker weight and style to be changed without rebuilding the rig. The clip is fitted to the mainline first, followed by a bead to protect the knot before the mainline is attached to the rig’s swivel. Single-Hook or Adjustable Twin-Hook Rig Single-hook Fish Finder Rigs suit smaller baits and situations where a simple hook trace is all that is required. Adjustable twin-hook versions suit longer baits such as pilchard tails, whole baitfish and strip baits. One hook remains fixed while the sliding-snelled hook is moved to match the bait length, keeping the bait straight and both hook points exposed. Monofilament or Wire Leader Monofilament is suitable when bite protection is not required. Leader strength should be selected according to the ground, bait size, tackle being used and likely bycatch. As a practical guide: • A 20lb mono version suits lighter estuary fishing over clean sand and mud • A 40lb mono version provides additional abrasion resistance in surf gutters, around shell grit and along coffee rock edges • A wire leader or bite section becomes appropriate when targeting toothy species or when bite-offs from likely bycatch are a genuine risk Stronger current may require a heavier or differently shaped sinker, but it does not automatically mean the entire leader must be made heavier. Sinker choice and leader strength solve different fishing problems.

sections.heading: When Should You Use a Peg Float Fish Finder Rig?
sections.text: A Peg Float Fish Finder Rig adds an adjustable float to the hook leader, helping lift the baited end of the rig slightly above the seabed. The float does not lift the sinker. It adds buoyancy near the hook, helping raise the baited end of the leader slightly above the seabed. This variation is particularly useful when: • Small crabs are repeatedly reaching baits sitting on the bottom • Weed or silt is fouling the bait and hook • Light wash is burying the bait in sand • Fish are feeding slightly above the seabed • Additional bait visibility is useful in stirred-up water The float is supplied at a practical starting distance from the hook. To change its position, loosen or remove the black peg, slide the float along the leader and then refit the peg to lock it in place. The actual bait height will depend on the float position, bait weight, current and the angle of the leader. The float can help lift the bait, but it does not hold every bait at one exact depth. 40lb Mono Peg Float Fish Finder Rig The mono version uses an approximately 700mm 40lb monofilament leader and a chemically sharpened 4/0 circle hook. It suits surf and inshore fishing where wire bite protection is not required. 40lb Wire Peg Float Fish Finder Rig The wire version uses an approximately 700mm 40lb black coated wire leader and a chemically sharpened 5/0 circle hook. It provides additional bite protection when Tailor or other toothy species are likely to be encountered. Both versions include a sliding sinker clip, red knot-protecting bead and 108lb rolling swivel. The sinker is not included, allowing its style and weight to be selected for the conditions. Browse the Fish Finder and Peg Float Rig Range →

sections.heading: What Sinker Should You Use with a Fish Finder Rig?
sections.text: The correct sinker depends on whether you want the rig to move gradually across the bottom or remain in one position. For estuary fishing over clean sand or mud, a ball or bean sinker threaded directly onto the mainline can allow controlled movement with the current. A sliding sinker clip provides more flexibility because different sinker styles and weights can be attached without rebuilding the complete rig. Common choices include: • Ball or bean sinkers when gradual movement is wanted • Pyramid or star sinkers when additional grip is needed in sand • Grapnel sinkers when stronger surf or sideways sweep requires firmer holding power Use the lightest sinker that produces the intended result. If the rig is rolling uncontrollably, increase the sinker weight or change to a shape that grips the bottom more effectively. If the rig is holding too firmly when gradual movement is wanted, reduce the weight or use a less aggressive sinker shape. Sinkers are not supplied with Wiggle ya Worm Fish Finder Rigs because the required weight and style depend on the current, surf movement, ground and fishing method.

sections.heading: Common Fish Finder Rig Mistakes
sections.text: Using the Same Sinker in Every Condition A sinker that allows controlled movement in an estuary may roll uncontrollably in stronger surf. Match the sinker’s weight and shape to whether you want the rig to move gradually or remain in one position. Fitting the Sliding Clip and Bead in the Wrong Order Fit the sliding sinker clip to the mainline first, followed by the red knot-protecting bead. The mainline is then tied to the swivel on the rig. Choosing Leader Strength by Fish Size Alone Leader choice also depends on the ground and likely bycatch. Use lighter mono over clean estuary sand and mud, heavier mono where additional abrasion resistance is required, and wire when toothy species create a genuine bite-off risk. Not Matching the Hooks to the Bait Adjustable twin-hook rigs work best when the sliding hook is positioned to suit the bait length. Keep longer baits straight and make sure the hook points remain clearly exposed. Using a Standard Fish Finder Rig When the Bait Needs to Be Lifted When small crabs, weed, silt or light wash are repeatedly affecting a bait sitting on the seabed, changing to a Peg Float Fish Finder Rig may be more effective than repeatedly replacing the same bait.

sections.heading: Is a Fish Finder Rig the Same as a Running Sinker Rig?
sections.text: A Fish Finder Rig is a type of running sinker rig. The terms are sometimes used interchangeably, but the layouts can differ. On a basic running sinker rig, a ball or bean sinker is normally threaded directly onto the mainline above the hook or swivel. A Fish Finder Rig commonly uses a dedicated sliding sinker clip, followed by a knot-protecting bead, swivel and separate hook leader. The clip allows the sinker style or weight to be changed without untying and rebuilding the complete rig. Both layouts allow the mainline to move through the sinker connection, reducing the immediate resistance created by a fixed sinker. The main reason for choosing a clip-based setup is the ability to change sinker weight or style more easily. Leader length, hook arrangement and bait size are separate choices that do not depend on whether a sliding sinker clip is used. Neither layout is automatically better. The appropriate choice depends on how the sinker will be attached and whether it may need to be changed as the conditions vary.

sections.heading: Australian Land-Based Shark Fishing Guide
sections.text: Land-based shark fishing in Australia isn’t the same as what you’ll see in overseas videos or tackle catalogues. Surf conditions, reef edges and the size of fish we regularly hook from the beach all change how rigs need to be built and how sharks should be handled once they’re landed. From leader choice through to hook removal and release, each step affects how safely sharks can be landed from the beach. Not sure which rig suits your conditions? See the Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guid e → Or use the Rig Finder to narrow down the best shark rig for your location and target species →

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Shark Rig
sections.text: Most problems in land-based shark fishing start with the wrong leader setup. As fish size increases or structure gets rougher, longer abrasion leaders and proper bite traces become more important than casting distance alone. Many of the same abrasion and leader-length lessons apply offshore — see Field Notes from Swains for examples from heavy reef conditions → See the Shark Rig Guide → Browse our Shark Fishing Rigs or explore the Drone Fishing System if you're deploying large baits by drone. Heavy coated wire traces around 2–3 metres long are commonly used when deploying large baits by kayak or drone, and can still be cast when needed where a full long-leader landing rope system isn’t required. Our Standard Shark Drone Fishing Rig follows this proven approach, combining a heavy mono leader backbone with a 200 lb coated wire bite trace for fishos targeting medium to large sharks by drone.

sections.heading: Casting vs Drone Deployment
sections.text: Casting still accounts for most land-based shark captures around Australia, especially along surf beaches and estuary entrances where moving between gutters matters. When sharks are holding wider or conditions allow it, longer deployment systems let you fish heavier leaders without sacrificing bait placement. For fishos targeting medium to large sharks, the Standard Shark Drone Fishing Rig provides a simpler deployment system. If you're targeting Australia's biggest sharks with oversized baits and maximum abrasion protection, the Apex Pro Shark Rig is our ultimate long mono deployment system.

sections.heading: Targeting Gummy Sharks from the Beach
sections.text: For many fishos, gummy sharks are where land-based shark fishing starts, especially along southern surf beaches and estuary entrances. They don’t usually need extreme deployment gear, but they do reward clean bait presentation and the right balance between casting distance and bite-trace protection. See the Gummy Shark Rig Guide →

sections.heading: Slide Baiting Large Sharks
sections.text: Slide baiting comes into its own when bigger sharks are moving along deeper gutters, reef edges or headlands that sit just beyond normal casting range, particularly where sharks are holding just outside casting distance. Dedicated slide bait shark rigs allow large baits to be positioned beyond casting range while keeping the main leader controlled in the surf zone without moving to full long-leader landing rope systems. See the Slide Bait Rig Guide →

sections.heading: Safe Hook Removal and Release
sections.text: Landing a shark is only half the job. Planning how you’re going to remove the hook and release the fish safely should happen before the bait even goes out. See the Shark Release Guide → Planning to target sharks with a drone? Our Australian Drone Fishing Guide covers payload management, bait deployment and practical tips for getting the most from your drone fishing system.

sections.heading: Reducing Fight Time Improves Release Success
sections.text: Using leader systems that match the fish you’re targeting shortens the fight and gives sharks a better chance of swimming away strongly after release, especially on open surf beaches.

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Dehooking Equipment
sections.text: Large hooks and long leaders change how sharks can be handled at the water’s edge. Long-reach dehookers make hook removal safer and quicker without putting you too close to the mouth See the Shark Dehooker Guide →

sections.heading: Common Land-Based Shark Fishing Mistakes
sections.text: A lot of release problems come from fighting sharks too long on light gear, dragging them too far onto dry sand, or trying to remove hooks without the right tools ready before landing. Successful land-based shark fishing in Australia starts with the right rig, the right landing approach and a release plan sorted before the bait even hits the water — not after the shark is on the beach. Drone fishing has made it possible to deploy larger baits further offshore than ever before, but it doesn't change the fundamentals of successful shark fishing. The right rig, proper preparation and safe release practices remain just as important, whether your bait reaches the water with a cast, a slide bait or a drone.

sections.heading: Maximum Distance. Clean Flight. Reliable Release.
sections.text: Long cast pulley rigs are designed to hold the bait and sinker closely in line during the cast, creating a compact, aerodynamic setup with less wind resistance than a bait and rig hanging separately. This allows more of the casting energy to carry the bait forward instead of being lost through drag, movement and the bait rotating through the air. When the rig hits the water, the impact shield uses a mechanically forced release to eject the hook and unlock the pulley loop. The bait trace can then drop away from the sinker so the rig fishes normally. This guide explains how each stage works, why the release mechanism is important and how pulley rigs can also help reduce sinker snags when fishing rocks, reef, weed and other rough ground.

sections.heading: What a Long Cast Pulley Rig Is Designed to Do
sections.text: A Long Cast Pulley Rig must perform two separate jobs: remain compact and controlled during the cast, then release and deploy correctly after entering the water. During the cast, the rig is designed to: Hold the hook securely beneath the impact shield’s trigger arm Keep the bait close to and in line with the sinker Prevent the bait trace from flapping, twisting or rotating through the air Reduce wind resistance and improve the transfer of casting energy When the rig hits the water, it is designed to: Trigger a deliberate, mechanically forced hook release Unlock the tensioned pulley loop Allow the bait trace to separate from the sinker Let the bait settle and move normally once the rig reaches the bottom Both stages need to work properly. A rig that flies cleanly but fails to release has not completed its job, while a rig that releases easily but cannot hold the bait securely during the cast will lose distance and control.

sections.heading: How a Long Cast Pulley Rig Works
sections.text: The release system is created by the combined movement of the pulley bead, tensioned leader loop, fixed crimp, sliding bead and impact shield. The process happens in three stages.

sections.heading: Stage 1: Locked for the Cast
sections.text: The hook is seated securely beneath the impact shield’s trigger arm The hook sits in front of the leader that passes through the impact shield The sliding bead sits firmly against the fixed crimp above the impact shield The sinker pulls downward while the mainline pulls upward through the pulley bead This opposing tension draws the rig tight and creates the tensioned pulley loop. With the hook correctly seated: The bait is held close to and in line with the sinker The bait trace is restrained during the cast The rig remains compact and aerodynamic Uncontrolled movement and rotation are reduced Correct hook seating, leader position and tension are what allow the bait and sinker to fly together as one streamlined unit.

sections.heading: Stage 2: Release Triggered on Splashdown
sections.text: When the sinker and impact shield enter the water: The sinker decelerates sharply Water pressure drives the impact shield upward towards the fixed crimp The sliding bead is held against the crimp The bead rides down the impact shield’s angled trigger arm as the shield moves upward The angled trigger arm converts the impact shield’s upward movement into the controlled sideways movement needed to begin releasing the hook. The system does not rely on the leader becoming slack or the hook accidentally falling free. Splashdown provides the mechanical movement that triggers the release process.

sections.heading: Stage 3: Hook Released and Pulley Loop Unlocked
sections.text: As the sliding bead rides down the angled trigger arm: The leader passing behind the hook is forced sideways The sideways-moving leader pushes against the hook The hook is forced clear of the trigger arm The tensioned pulley loop unlocks Once the loop is unlocked: The pulley bead can move freely The bait trace drops away from the sinker The bait and hook settle into their normal fishing position Because the hook sits in front of the leader, the sideways movement of the leader physically pushes it off the trigger arm. The hook is mechanically forced to release—it does not simply fall free.

sections.heading: When a Candy Float Is Used
sections.text: Some long cast pulley rigs include a small candy float positioned above the hook. The candy float has no role in locking or releasing the rig during the cast. Its purpose begins after the hook has released and the bait trace has dropped away from the sinker. The float helps hold the bait slightly above the bottom, where it may be easier for fish to locate. It can also help keep the bait clear of light weed, uneven ground and small crabs. Candy floats are not fitted to every long cast rig because added lift is not suitable for every bait or fishing situation. Whether one is used depends on the bait size, bottom type and where the bait needs to sit after the rig has deployed. Candy floats are included on some long cast rigs and are also available in our accessory tackle packs for fishos who want to adjust how their bait fishes above the bottom.

sections.heading: Why the Locked Cast and Forced Release Work Together
sections.text: The locked casting arrangement and forced-release mechanism perform two separate jobs. During the cast, the tensioned pulley loop keeps the bait close to the sinker and prevents the bait trace from flapping or rotating freely. This reduces wind resistance and helps more of the casting energy carry the rig forward. When the sinker enters the water, the impact shield and sliding bead force the hook to release so the bait trace can separate from the sinker and fish normally. Working together, these two stages provide: A more compact and aerodynamic cast Less bait movement and rotation during flight Fewer mid-air tangles More consistent casting performance Reliable hook release and rig deployment The rig remains securely locked when it needs to be and is mechanically released when it reaches the water.

sections.heading: How Long Cast Pulley Rigs Vary
sections.text: Every long cast pulley rig uses the same basic casting and release system, but the hook arrangement, leader strength and bait trace can be changed to suit different baits, species and fishing conditions. Common variations include: Single-hook rigs for smaller or more streamlined baits Adjustable twin-hook rigs for longer baits and variable hook spacing Ganged-hook rigs for whole pilchards and other long fish baits Mono bait traces for general surf fishing Wire bait traces where additional protection from toothy fish is required Different backbone and bait-trace strengths to suit the expected fish, bait and ground Candy-float versions where the bait needs to sit slightly above the bottom after release The component layout may vary, but the casting principle remains the same: the bait is held close to the sinker during flight, then mechanically released when the rig enters the water.

sections.heading: How Pulley Action Helps Over Rough Ground
sections.text: The pulley system also provides a practical advantage when retrieving a fish over rocks, weed, kelp or broken ground. When pressure comes onto a hooked fish, the pulley arrangement uses the weight of the fish and the fisho’s retrieve to lift the sinker. This brings the fish, sinker and mainline into line, keeping the sinker raised away from potential snags as the fish is retrieved. Lifting the sinker away from the bottom helps reduce the chance of it catching in: Cracks and crevices Rocks and reef Heavy weed Kelp Other uneven ground This is particularly useful when the fish must be brought up and away from rough ground quickly. The pulley action cannot remove every snag risk, but it helps keep the sinker away from the bottom during the retrieve instead of leaving it trailing through rough ground.

sections.heading: When to Use a Long Cast Pulley Rig
sections.text: A long cast pulley rig is useful whenever the bait needs to remain controlled and streamlined during the cast. Common situations include: Reaching gutters, channels or sandbanks beyond the breakers Casting into a headwind or crosswind Casting whole pilchards, fish fillets or other baits that can flap or rotate in flight Reducing bait movement and tangles during longer casts Fishing from rocks, reef edges or ground where the sinker could snag during retrieval Reaching feeding zones that are beyond the range of a conventional rig The pulley system is not only about achieving the longest possible cast. It also helps fishos cast baits more cleanly and consistently while ensuring the hook releases and the bait trace fishes normally after landing.

sections.heading: Species Commonly Targeted with Long Cast Pulley Rigs
sections.text: The species a long cast pulley rig can target depends on its hook arrangement, bait trace material, leader strength and the bait being used. Long cast pulley rigs are commonly used for: Mulloway (Jewfish) Tailor Australian salmon Whiting Bream Trevally Kingfish Gummy sharks Other Australian surf species Choose the rig strength, hook arrangement and bait trace material for the species being targeted and any likely by-catch.
