sections.heading: Paternoster Rigs Explained
sections.text: A paternoster rig has a sinker attached at the bottom of a main backbone, with one or more hook-bearing paternoster arms positioned above it. This layout separates the baited hooks from the sinker and holds them above the seabed. The sinker provides the weight needed to lower, cast or control the rig while the paternoster arms keep the hooks fishing away from the backbone. Paternoster rigs can be built with a single hook or multiple hooks. The backbone, paternoster arms, hook arrangement and leader material can then be adjusted for estuary, beach, surf, reef, offshore or species-specific fishing. Unlike a running sinker rig, the sinker is fixed at the lower end of the paternoster. This provides greater control in current and deeper water, although the fish encounters the fixed-sinker layout when it takes the bait. The basic design is simple, but mono, wire, hybrid, twisted-arm, single-hook and multi-hook versions all solve different fishing problems. This guide explains how paternoster rigs work, when to use them and how to choose a suitable layout for the species, ground and water movement being fished.

sections.heading: When Should You Use a Paternoster Rig?
sections.text: A paternoster rig is particularly useful when controlling the bait’s position above the bottom is more important than allowing a fish to move away with minimal sinker resistance. Consider using one when: • Current or surf movement makes a running rig difficult to control • Fishing deeper water from a boat, rocks or another structure • Fish are feeding above rather than directly on the seabed • Weed, silt, shell grit or rubble is repeatedly fouling bottom baits • More than one bait needs to be fished at different heights, where local regulations allow • You want the sinker positioned below the hooks Because the sinker is fixed at the bottom of the backbone, the fisho maintains direct control over the complete rig. Changing the sinker weight or shape allows that control to be adjusted for the depth, current and ground. The trade-off is that a fish may encounter the resistance of the fixed sinker sooner than it would with a running-sinker layout. When reduced initial sinker resistance is more important than holding the hooks above the bottom, a Fish Finder Rig may be the better choice. See Fish Finder Rigs Explained →

sections.heading: Mono Paternoster Rigs: Light to Heavy
sections.text: A mono paternoster rig uses monofilament for its backbone and paternoster arms. The same basic layout can be built in different leader strengths, so light and heavy mono paternosters are variations of the same rig rather than completely different designs. Lighter Mono Paternosters Lighter mono versions are commonly used for: • Estuary fishing over clean ground • Calm beaches and shallow surf gutters • Smaller hooks and baits • Whiting, Bream and other common estuary or surf species Their lighter construction suits smaller tackle and baits where heavy abrasion or toothy bycatch is unlikely. See Best Whiting Rigs in Australia → Heavier Mono Paternosters Heavier mono versions are better suited to: • Stronger surf and deeper water • Larger hooks and baits • Reef, rubble or other abrasive ground • Larger target species or heavier likely bycatch • Sinkers and casting loads that require a stronger backbone Thicker mono generally provides additional strength and abrasion resistance, but it is also stiffer and more visible. Use enough leader strength for the fish, ground and casting load without making the rig unnecessarily heavy. Mono provides abrasion resistance according to its material and diameter, but it does not provide reliable bite protection against sharp teeth. A twisted mono paternoster is also a proven layout for presenting baits to Australian Salmon in active surf. See the Australian Salmon Rig Guide →

sections.heading: When Should You Use Wire on a Paternoster Rig?
sections.text: Wire is used on a paternoster rig when protection against sharp teeth is required around the hooks. It should not be added simply because the water is deeper or the current is stronger. Heavier mono can provide additional strength and abrasion resistance, while wire solves the separate problem of bite-offs from toothy fish. Wire can be incorporated into the hook traces or paternoster arms while retaining a monofilament backbone. This combination of different leader materials creates a hybrid paternoster rig. Wiggle ya Worm Hybrid Gummy Shark Paternoster Rig The Wiggle ya Worm hybrid version is a specialised Gummy Shark paternoster consisting of: • A monofilament backbone • Wire paternoster arms for bite protection near the hooks • A deliberately weaker mono section below the backbone for attaching the sinker If the sinker becomes firmly snagged, the weaker bottom section is designed to break before the stronger fish-carrying sections of the rig. This can reduce the likelihood of losing the complete rig when fishing rough bottom. This is a heavier, species-specific setup intended for Gummy Shark and mixed-shark fishing. It is not recommended as a general Mulloway, estuary or light reef paternoster. For a complete explanation of when this design is appropriate, see the Australian Gummy Shark Rig Guide →

sections.heading: Single-Hook vs Multi-Hook Paternoster Rigs
sections.text: A paternoster rig can carry one hook or multiple hooks. The appropriate layout depends on the target species, bait size, current, how the rig will be handled and the fishing regulations that apply. Multi-Hook Paternoster Rigs A multi-hook rig allows two or more baits to be fished from paternoster arms positioned along the backbone. This can be useful when: • Fishing for schooling species • Trying different baits during the same drop • Fish may be feeding at slightly different heights • Local regulations allow multiple baits or hooks per line Additional hooks also create more drag and more possible tangle points. As current, bait size or hook size increases, a simpler layout may become easier to control. Single-Hook Paternoster Rigs A single-hook version uses one paternoster arm and one bait. This layout may be preferred when: • Local regulations permit only one bait or lure per line • Fishing one larger bait • Strong current makes multiple arms difficult to manage • A simpler rig is wanted for rough ground or deeper water The number of hooks does not determine the required leader strength. Hook count, leader strength and sinker choice should each be selected for their own purpose. Western Australian Demersal Fishing Rules Western Australian rules currently allow a maximum of one bait or lure on each line when fishing for demersal scalefish in the West Coast Bioregion. Separate regional closures, species rules and other restrictions may also apply. Fishos should confirm the current rules for their location and target species before fishing. View the Current Western Australian Recreational Fishing Rules → For fishos requiring a single-arm layout, see our WA-Compliant Single-Arm Twisted Paternoster Rig Blanks →

sections.heading: How Do You Choose the Right Paternoster Rig?
sections.text: Choosing a paternoster rig involves more than selecting a leader strength. The complete layout needs to suit the target species, bait, ground, water movement and fishing regulations. Work through these questions before choosing: What Are You Targeting? The likely fish and bycatch determine the hook size, leader strength and whether wire bite protection is required. Where Are You Fishing? Clean estuary sand and calm beaches may suit lighter mono, while surf, reef, rubble and deeper offshore ground can require stronger leaders and a more robust layout. What Bait Are You Using? Hook size and paternoster arm spacing should suit the bait. Larger baits create more drag and require enough separation to prevent them tangling with the backbone or other hooks. How Strong Is the Water Movement? Current and depth affect the sinker weight and shape required to control the rig. Larger baits and multiple paternoster arms also create additional drag, so a simpler layout may be easier to manage in stronger flow. Is Bite Protection Required? Heavier mono provides additional strength and abrasion resistance. Wire should be used near the hooks when toothy target species or likely bycatch create a genuine bite-off risk. How Many Baits Are Permitted? Check the current fishing rules for your location and target species before choosing a single-hook or multi-hook layout. As a practical starting point: • Light estuary and calm beach fishing → Lighter mono paternoster • Active surf and larger baits → Stronger twisted mono paternoster • Reef, rubble and deeper water → Heavier mono paternoster • Gummy Shark or mixed-shark fishing → Purpose-built hybrid paternoster • One-bait fishing regulations → Single-arm paternoster If you’re learning how different rigs work or want to practise assembling your own, the Beginner Fisho Rig Kit provides ready-to-fish examples, blank paternosters and knot-tying information.

sections.heading: Common Paternoster Rig Mistakes
sections.text: Choosing Leader Strength by Current Alone Stronger current normally requires a heavier or more suitable sinker, but it does not automatically require a heavier leader. Leader strength should be selected for the target species, likely bycatch, ground, bait and casting load. Confusing Abrasion Resistance with Bite Protection Heavier mono can provide additional resistance against reef, rubble and shell grit, but it does not provide reliable protection against sharp teeth. Use wire near the hooks when bite-offs are a genuine risk. Using Too Many Hooks for the Conditions Additional hooks and baits create more drag and more possible tangle points. In strong current or when using large baits, a single-hook or simpler layout may be easier to control. Using the Wrong Sinker A sinker that is too light may allow the rig to move uncontrollably, while using more weight than necessary increases the load during casting and retrieval. Match the sinker’s weight and shape to the depth, current and ground. Poor Paternoster Arm Length or Spacing Paternoster arms positioned too close together can allow the hooks and baits to cross. Larger baits require enough separation to fish without tangling with another arm, the backbone or the sinker. Rigging the Bait Poorly Match the hook size to the bait, keep the bait secure and make sure the hook point remains clearly exposed. A well-built paternoster cannot compensate for a hook buried inside the bait. Ignoring Local Fishing Regulations Hook and bait limits vary between fisheries, species and locations. Check the current rules before using a multi-hook paternoster, particularly when targeting regulated demersal species.

sections.heading: When Should You Use Candy Floats or Flasher Hooks?
sections.text: Candy floats and flasher materials can both be added near a paternoster hook, but they serve different purposes. A small candy float adds buoyancy near the hook, helping lift the bait slightly above the seabed. • Weed, silt or shell grit is repeatedly fouling the bait • The bait is being buried by light sand movement • Small crabs are repeatedly reaching baits on the bottom • Fish are feeding slightly above the seabed The amount of lift depends on the float size, bait weight, current and its position near the hook. A candy float helps raise the bait, but it does not hold every bait at one exact height. Candy floats are included on selected Wiggle ya Worm paternoster and long cast rigs where additional lift serves a practical purpose. Flasher material adds movement and changing reflection around the hook. It is intended to make the bait or hook easier for fish to locate in deeper water, low light, whitewater or reduced visibility. Unlike a candy float, flasher material does not provide meaningful buoyancy or lift the bait away from the bottom. Neither feature is required on every paternoster rig. Use a candy float when bait height is the problem and a flasher hook when additional visibility is the objective. For more information, see the Flasher Rigs Guide →

sections.heading: When Should You Use a Paternoster Rig for Gummy Sharks?
sections.text: A paternoster rig can be useful when targeting Gummy Sharks from a boat, in deeper channels or over rough bottom where controlling the bait and sinker is more important than casting distance. Gummy Sharks do not have the razor-sharp teeth associated with many other shark species, so wire is not automatically required for every Gummy Shark rig. The decision depends on: • The size of the Gummies being targeted • The ground being fished • Bait size • The likelihood of other shark species taking the bait • Whether the sinker is likely to become snagged For these conditions, the Wiggle ya Worm Hybrid Gummy Shark Paternoster Rig uses a mono backbone, wire paternoster arms and a deliberately weaker mono sinker section. The wire arms provide protection near the hooks when mixed shark species may be encountered. If the sinker becomes firmly lodged, the weaker bottom section is designed to break before the stronger fish-carrying sections of the rig. This is a specialised setup for heavier Gummy Shark and mixed-shark fishing. It is not necessary for every Gummy Shark location or a substitute for lighter castable and sliding-sinker rigs when those layouts better suit the conditions. See the Australian Gummy Shark Rig Guide for a complete comparison of castable, sliding-snell and paternoster options

sections.heading: Still Not Sure Which Paternoster Rig to Use?
sections.text: If you know the species and location but aren’t sure which rig suits the water movement, ground and bait being used, try the Rig Finder Tool for a quick recommendation. sections.heading: What Rig Should I Use for My Fishing Conditions?
sections.text: The best fishing rig changes depending on where you are fishing. Surf rigs prioritise casting distance and stability in moving water. Estuary rigs focus on natural bait presentation. Reef rigs are built for strength near structure. Offshore rigs must handle depth and larger fish. Matching your rig to conditions improves hook-up rates more than changing bait alone.

sections.heading: Surf Fishing Rigs (Australian Conditions)
sections.text: Surf fishing conditions change quickly between shallow gutters, deep holes, current, and casting distance. The best rig depends on how the bait needs to sit in the water and how far it must travel from shore. If you're unsure how to identify productive gutters and banks before choosing a rig, see our guide on How to Read a Beach: Spotting Gutters, Banks & Breaks Like a Pro → Subtle presentation changes like bead colour, flash and contrast can also affect how easily fish locate bait in moving surf. See Using Colour and Contrast in Rigs to Trigger More Bites → The rigs below reflect what works consistently on Australian beaches when targeting common surf species. Fishos wanting a more adaptable surf setup for changing beach conditions can also explore the Quick Change Long Cast System , designed around reusable backbone rigs and interchangeable trace packs for faster rig changes on the beach. In some regions such as Western Australia, demersal fishing regulations restrict the number of hooks or baits per line. In these situations, single-hook paternoster rigs provide a compliant alternative while still maintaining strong bait control in current and deeper water. Surf structure and species behaviour vary between Australian states. See Best Beach Fishing Locations by State (Australia) →

sections.heading: Whiting (Australian Conditions)
sections.text: Best rig Double Paternoster Rig – No.4 Worm Hooks – Lumo Beads This rig presents natural baits like beach worms, pipis, and peeled prawns close to the sand where whiting feed along shallow gutters and shoreline edges. Two hooks allow coverage of active feeding lanes, and luminous beads improve bait visibility in stirred surf water and broken light conditions. When to switch rigs If the surf is calm and fish are feeding cautiously in shallow gutters, a running sinker rig allows lighter, more natural bait movement. Alternative option Running Sinker Rig – 20lb Mono – 1/0 Hook – 15g Sinker Light paternoster rigs and running sinker setups both work well depending on sweep and gutter depth. See the full guide here → Best whiting rigs in Australia See how paternoster rigs work here →

sections.heading: Bream (Australian Conditions)
sections.text: Best rig Running Sinker Rig – 20–40lb Mono – Size 1 to 1/0 Hook Bream feed along rock walls, bridge pylons, surf edges, and estuary drop-offs where natural bait movement matters more than weight-holding ability. Hook size and wire gauge affect how naturally bait moves in current. See Choosing the Right Fishing Hook (Why Most Fishos Get It Wrong) → See the full guide here → Best bream rigs in Australia

sections.heading: Mulloway (Australian Conditions)
sections.text: Mulloway are typically targeted using larger baits presented along deep gutters, channel edges, and structure where fish intercept bait moving with tide and current. The most effective rig depends on bait size, casting distance, and whether fish are holding beyond normal casting range. Recommended rig Sliding Snelled Double Hook Rig – 60lb Mono – 2 × 6/0 Circle Hooks This rig presents whole pilchards, slab baits, and whole squid naturally along gutter edges where mulloway patrol for larger prey. If you are fishing in calmer estuaries we recommend our lighter 40lb Mulloway Estuary rig If casting distance is required Fishos regularly changing between bait sizes, surf conditions, or trace styles may also benefit from interchangeable long cast systems that allow quick trace changes without rebuilding complete rigs. Long Cast Pulley Rig – Twin Hook Configuration This setup protects larger baits during casting and allows presentations to reach deeper water beyond the inside gutters. If fish are feeding along structure edges or channel drop-offs Surf & Estuary Fish Finder Rig – Single 6/0 Circle Hook Allowing bait to move naturally with current improves presentation when mulloway are holding along bridge pylons, rock bars, or deeper channel edges. If deploying large live or whole baits beyond casting range Slide Bait Rig System This approach allows large baits to be positioned accurately after anchoring the sinker in deep gutters and current edges where larger mulloway patrol. Whole pilchard → Sliding snelled rig Whole squid → Sliding snelled rig Large slab bait → Pulley rig Live bait → Slide bait rig See our Beach Mulloway guide here → See our Sliding Snell Guide here → See available sliding snelled mulloway rigs here → Mulloway often feed more confidently after dark along gutter edges and channel structure. See Night Beach Fishing Tips →

sections.heading: Tailor (Australian Conditions)
sections.text: Tailor respond strongly to bait size, movement in the wash, and strike speed. The most effective rig depends on whether you are fishing whole pilchards, smaller bait profiles, or casting beyond the inside gutters where larger fish often hold. Sliding Ball Sinker Rig – 3 × 3/0 Ganged Hooks (Mono/Wire Hybrid) This rig presents whole pilchards naturally in the surf while reducing bite-offs from sharp teeth. It remains the most reliable starting point when targeting tailor along beaches, headlands, and active gutter systems. If using smaller pilchards or targeting chopper tailor Sliding Ball Sinker Rig – 2 × 4/0 Ganged Hooks Lighter gangs improve hook exposure with smaller bait profiles and increase hook-up rates on fast-moving fish. If fish are feeding beyond the inside gutters Long Cast Pulley Rig with Ganged Hooks on Wire. Interchangeable long cast systems can also help tailor fishos quickly swap between gang hook sizes, wire traces, and bait presentations as conditions change throughout a session. This setup protects softer pilchards during the cast and allows larger bait presentations to reach deeper water where bigger tailor often hold. If bite-offs are frequent or mixed species are present Switch to wire-trace ganged hook rigs Wire reduces lost fish when tailor are striking aggressively or when species like mackerel move through the same gutters. If fishing estuary mouths or channel entrances The same ganged hook sliding sinker rigs remain effective wherever pilchards drift naturally with tide movement. Whole pilchard → 3 × 3/0 gangs Half pilchard → 2 × 4/0 gangs Large slab bait → pulley rig with gangs See the Australian Tailor Rig Guide → See available tailor surf rigs here →

sections.heading: Australian Salmon (Australian Conditions)
sections.text: Australian salmon respond strongly to moving bait in foam lines and deeper gutters. See the Australian Salmon Rig Guide → The most effective rig depends on bait size, feeding depth, and whether fish are working close to shore or beyond the inside gutters. Recommended rig Twisted Paternoster Rig – 40lb Mono – 2 × Heavy Duty 2/0 Hooks This rig keeps strip baits and pilchard pieces slightly elevated above the sand where salmon intercept bait moving through wash and gutter edges. If salmon are feeding deeper along the bottom This allows strip baits to drift naturally through deeper gutters and slower water where salmon hold below the main wash zone. If schools are feeding beyond normal casting range Long Cast Rig with Snelled Hooks for Half Pilchards Some fishos also prefer interchangeable long cast systems when switching between strip baits, pilchards, and different surf conditions during mobile salmon sessions. This setup improves casting distance while protecting softer bait during the cast, allowing presentations to reach fish working outside the inside gutters. If using larger strip baits or whole pilchards Fish Finder Rig – Single 6/0 Circle Hook Larger baits sit more naturally on a single-hook presentation when allowed to move with current through deeper channels. If fishing estuary mouths or tide flow zones The same paternoster and fish finder rigs remain effective wherever bait is pushed through current lines at river entrances and channel edges. Pilchard pieces → Twisted paternoster rig Half pilchard → Long cast snelled rig Strip bait → Fish finder rig See available salmon paternoster rigs here → See the full Australian Salmon Rig Guide here →

sections.heading: Flathead (Australian Conditions)
sections.text: Flathead feed along sandy bottoms, drop-offs, and channel edges where bait moves naturally with current. The most effective rig depends on whether bait needs to stay on the bottom, remain slightly elevated, or drift along structure zones. Want a step-by-step guide to targeting flathead in estuaries, drop-offs and surf gutters? Read the Flathead Fishing Tips here → See our FULL Flathead rig guide here → Recommended rig Flathead Fish Finder Rig – 40lb Mono – 2 × 1/0 Hooks – Sliding Weight Clip & Bead s This rig allows strip baits and whole baitfish to move naturally along the bottom where flathead ambush prey in gutters, channel edges, and sandy flats. If current increases or bait needs to stay slightly elevated “Everyday” Hand Twisted Paternoster Rig – 2 × 1/0 Hooks – Luminous Beads Keeping bait just above the sand improves visibility in stirred water and reduces snagging when fishing uneven bottom. If using larger strip baits or targeting bigger fish Sliding Snelled Double Hook Rig – 40lb Mono – 2 × 3/0 Circle Hooks – Lumo Bead Twin hooks improve hook-up rates when presenting longer strip baits or whole baitfish. If fishing estuary drop-offs, weed edges, or channel structure The same fish finder rig remains effective wherever bait moves naturally with tidal flow along ambush zones. Strip bait → Fish finder rig Whole baitfish → Sliding snelled rig Pilchard pieces → Twisted paternoster rig See available flathead surf rigs here → If you're fishing a new beach or unsure what species are present, starting with a flexible paternoster or sliding snelled rig allows you to cover multiple bait sizes and feeding depths until fish behaviour becomes clearer.

sections.heading: Mixed Surf Species (Australian Conditions)
sections.text: When fishing new beaches or changing conditions, targeting multiple species at once is often the most effective approach. A flexible rig allows different bait sizes to be presented naturally while covering both smaller feeding fish and larger opportunistic predators moving through the same gutters. Modular long cast systems can also reduce downtime in mixed-species surf sessions by allowing quick changes between bait presentations, wire traces, and hook configurations without rebuilding complete rigs. Recommended rig Pompano Paternoster Float Rig – 2 × 1/0 Hooks This rig keeps bait visible slightly above the sand and works well when targeting species like whiting, bream, dart, and smaller tailor feeding along active gutter edges. Floats and beads improve bait visibility in moving water and stirred surf conditions. See How colour and Contrast trigger reaction strikes in mixed-species surf fishing If larger predators are moving through the gutter All Species Beach Fishing Rig – 40lb Black Coated Wire – 5/0 Fixed Bead Hook + 1/0 Stinger Hook This setup handles mixed-species situations where tailor or mulloway may strike the same bait being presented for smaller fish. If conditions are calm and fish are feeding cautiously Sliding Snelled Double Circle Hook Rig – 20lb Mono – 2 × Circle Hooks – Luminous Bead A lighter presentation improves hook-up rates when fish are line-shy or feeding slowly in shallow gutters. The same paternoster and sliding snelled rigs remain effective wherever bait is pushed naturally through current lines at channel entrances. Beach worms or pipis → Pompano paternoster rig Pilchard strips → Sliding snelled rig Whole pilchard or slab bait → Wire trace mixed-species rig See available mixed-species surf rigs here → If targeting larger sharks from surf beaches, dedicated shark rigs or purpose-built drone shark rigs become the better option once bait size exceeds standard casting presentations.

sections.heading: Deploying Large Live or Whole Baits (Slide Bait System)
sections.text: When target species are holding beyond normal casting distance, slide bait rigs allow large live or whole dead baits to be positioned after the sinker is anchored. This makes it possible to present bigger baits in deeper water where larger predators patrol outside the inside gutters. Slide bait systems are one of the most reliable ways to position large baits beyond casting distance on Australian beaches where deeper gutters sit outside the inside bank. Recommended setup Slide Bait Rig System See how slide bait rigs are deployed from Australian beaches in the Slide Bait Rig Guide → This method allows large baits such as live baitfish, whole squid, or slab baits to be delivered accurately into deep gutters and current edges without damaging bait during casting. If targeting larger mulloway beyond casting range Slide bait rigs allow whole pilchards, squid, and live bait to remain stable in position along deep gutter edges where larger fish intercept bait moving with tide flow. Where local regulations allow, drone fishing provides another effective method of deploying large live or whole baits beyond casting distance. Explore our Drone Fishing System to compare purpose-built drone fishing rigs for Australian conditions. If targeting mackerel kingfish or other pelagic predators from headlands See the Kingfish Rig Guide → A slide bait rig keeps larger live baits positioned in current lanes where fast-moving fish patrol close to structure. If targeting sharks from beaches or ledges Slide bait rigs provide controlled placement of large bait beyond the surf zone while maintaining strong hook exposure and stable presentation. Live baitfish → Slide bait rig Whole squid → Slide bait rig Large slab bait → Slide bait rig Learn how slide bait rigs work here → See available slide bait rigs here →

sections.heading: Shark Fishing Rigs (Beach, Rocks & Offshore)
sections.text: Shark fishing from Australian beaches, rock platforms and reef edges requires heavier leaders, longer abrasion protection, stronger hooks and safer release planning from the start. Many imported “shark rigs” are simply too short or too light for surf zones, reef edges, or large land-based fish. For a full breakdown of land-based shark setups, deployment methods and release planning, see the Land-Based Shark Fishing Guide → The right rig depends on how you are deploying your bait and what species you expect to encounter. Where sharks are holding beyond casting distance, slide bait rigs allow large baits to be positioned safely outside the surf zone without increasing casting load. Many larger sharks are most active after dark along deep gutters and current edges. See Night Beach Fishing Tips for timing and positioning strategies that improve results when targeting sharks from the shore. Shark rigs scale quickly with fish size. Castable coated-wire rigs suit gummies and smaller bronzies, while long mono deployment systems are used when targeting larger sharks from beaches and ledges.

sections.heading: Best rigs for shark fishing
sections.text: Land-based shark fishing (casting or drone deployment) Use long heavy mono leaders combined with coated wire bite traces and large circle hooks. These rigs protect against tail strikes, reef contact and long fights in the surf. Start here: Shark Fishing Rig Guide Drone deployment (medium to large sharks) → Standard Shark Drone Fishing Rig Drone deployment (Australia's largest sharks) → Apex Pro Shark Rig Compare both systems → Drone Fishing System Medium sharks from beaches and estuaries (gummy sharks, small bronzies) Castable coated-wire shark rigs with sliding sinker clips allow distance casting while keeping bait presentation natural. Gummy shark-specific setups: Gummy Shark Rig Guide Offshore shark fishing Offshore shark fishing typically uses shorter heavy wire bite traces connected to strong swivels or paternoster-style leaders, allowing controlled vertical presentation near reef edges where sharks patrol structure and current lines.

sections.heading: Choosing the right shark rig
sections.text: Use this quick guide: Casting from the beach → castable coated-wire shark rig Drone or kayak deployment → long heavy mono shark system Targeting gummies specifically → lighter coated-wire hybrid rigs Fishing reef edges offshore → short heavy wire traces Each setup balances casting distance, abrasion resistance and safe hook-up mechanics differently.

sections.heading: Circle hooks matter for shark fishing
sections.text: Circle hooks improve hook placement and make release safer and are now widely preferred for land-based shark fishing in Australia for this reason. They also reduce deep-hooking compared with traditional J-hooks when used correctly. Most Australian land-based shark rigs are designed around heavy-gauge circle hooks for this reason.

sections.heading: Safe shark handling and release
sections.text: If you are targeting sharks intentionally, plan your release before you cast. Large sharks cannot be handled safely without proper tools. See the safe handling & release guide here: Safe Shark Release Guide This explains positioning, hook removal options and when cutting the leader is the safest choice.

sections.heading: Why shark rigs are different in Australia
sections.text: Australian surf zones, reef edges and current strength mean shark rigs need: longer leaders stronger abrasion resistance heavier swivels and connections proper bite-trace wire release planning built into the setup This extra length also allows safer landing control from the shoreline, especially when fish must be guided through shallow surf before release. These design differences are why dedicated Australian land-based shark rigs are typically longer and heavier than overseas equivalents built for calmer beaches and smaller species. These aren’t “nice extras” — they’re what stops you getting smoked, busted off, or dealing with a situation you can’t control on the beach. New to shark fishing from the beach? Start with the Land-Based Shark Fishing Guide →

sections.heading: Rock Fishing (Australian Conditions)
sections.text: Rock fishing platforms allow access to deeper water close to shore, where fish feed along wash zones, current edges, and structure lines. Rig choice depends on whether bait is being presented on the bottom, suspended in wash, or positioned for passing pelagic species. Recommended rig for wash feeders Paternoster Rig – 2 × 1/0 Hooks – Luminous Beads This rig keeps bait slightly above the bottom where species such as bream, tarwhine, and drummer feed along rocky ledges and wash zones. Luminous beads improve bait visibility in turbulent white water. If targeting tailor or salmon from headlands Sliding Ball Sinker Rig – Ganged Hooks Ganged hook rigs present pilchards securely in moving wash and allow natural bait movement where predatory fish patrol along current edges near rock platforms. If targeting mulloway around deeper ledges Sliding Snelled Double Hook Rig – 2 × 6/0 Circle Hooks This setup presents larger baits such as whole pilchards or squid along deeper structure edges where mulloway move through tidal current zones after dark. If targeting larger pelagic species close to structure Slide bait rigs allow large live or whole baits to be positioned beyond the wash zone into deeper current lanes where mackerel, mulloway, and sharks patrol close to headlands and rock platforms. Prawns or cunjevoi → Paternoster rig Pilchards → Ganged hook rig Whole squid → Sliding snelled rig Live baitfish → Slide bait rig Kingfish are commonly encountered around pressure points, bait schools and current edges near headlands. See the Kingfish Rig Guide → See available rock fishing rigs here →

sections.heading: Offshore & Reef Fishing (Australian Conditions)
sections.text: Reef fishing requires stronger rigs than beach or rock fishing because fish are feeding close to structure where abrasion, reef edges, and vertical terrain increase failure risk. Rig choice depends on water depth, reef density, and the size of target species. Fishing heavy reef systems like Swains Reef requires reinforced rigs built to survive coral structure and powerful reef species. See the Swains Slayer Series → For a deeper breakdown of leader strength, sinker weight, and structure-specific setups used around coral reefs, see our Best Reef Fishing Rigs in Australia guide → Recommended rig for shallow reef and snapper Snapper Rig – 60lb Mono – Twin Hook Configuration See the full snapper rig guide here → Best snapper rigs in Australia This setup presents whole pilchards, squid, and slab baits naturally along shallow reef edges where snapper and reef species feed above broken ground. If targeting mixed reef species in deeper structure Heavy Duty Reef Paternoster Rig – 80lb Class When kingfish are holding above reef edges or bait schools, longer twin-hook snelled rigs or flasher paternosters improve hook placement on live and slab baits. See the Kingfish Rig Guide → This rig keeps bait positioned just above reef structure where species such as coral trout, emperor, cod, and larger snapper feed close to the bottom. See the full Best Reef Fishing Rigs in Australia guide for when to step up leader strength, sinker size and rig layout in heavier coral structure → If fishing remote reef systems or heavy coral country Swains Slayer Series Reef Rigs These rigs were developed specifically for high-abrasion reef environments where standard paternoster rigs fail quickly against coral structure. Heavier trace materials and reinforced components improve landing success when targeting larger reef species in demanding conditions.

sections.heading: Match the Shark Rig to the Fish and Deployment Method
sections.text: A shark rig must provide bite protection, withstand contact with rough skin and remain suitable for the way the bait will be sent into the water. The right setup depends on: • The size of shark being targeted • Whether the bait will be cast, slide baited or deployed • The size and weight of the bait • Whether fishing from a beach, rocks or a boat • The amount of reef, rock or other abrasive ground present • Whether a mono rub leader is required in addition to the wire bite trace Castable shark rigs must remain short and manageable enough to cast safely. Slide bait rigs use a trolley to carry the bait down an already anchored mainline, while drone and other deployed rigs can use longer and heavier leader systems because the bait is not being cast. Leader length, wire strength, hook size and connection method must work together as a complete system. Choosing only the heaviest available wire or largest hook does not automatically produce the right rig. This guide explains how castable, slide bait and deployed shark rigs differ, how leader length and bite protection affect the setup, and which features matter when targeting sharks in Australian conditions. Not sure which rig style suits your fishing method? Start with the Australian Fishing Rig Decision Guide → New to land-based shark fishing? Read the Land-Based Shark Fishing Guide →

sections.heading: Choosing Between Castable, Slide Bait and Deployed Shark Rigs
sections.text: These are not simply different strengths of the same rig. Each one uses a different method to get the bait into the fishing zone. Castable Shark Rigs A castable shark rig suits fish within normal casting range and baits that can be cast without excessive drag, tumbling or damage. Castable rigs are commonly around 1–2 metres long because the complete bait, sinker and rig must remain manageable during the cast. The wire trace must still provide suitable bite protection, but its length and weight are limited by what the fisho can cast effectively. Slide Bait Shark Rigs With a slide bait system, the breakaway sinker and mainline are cast first. Once the sinker is firmly anchored and the mainline is tensioned, the baited shark trace is attached to a slide trolley and worked down the line towards the stopper. Because the bait is not cast with the sinker, slide baiting allows larger live or dead baits to be sent beyond normal bait-casting range. For the complete setup and operating method, see: Slide Bait Rigs Explained → Deployed Shark Rigs Drone deployment, paddling a bait beyond the breakers or lowering a bait from a boat removes the practical length restrictions created by casting. This allows the use of: • Longer mono rub leaders • Longer or heavier wire bite traces • Larger hooks and baits • Heavier complete leader systems for bigger sharks The basic choice is straightforward: • Cast the complete rig when the bait and leader remain manageable • Use slide bait when the sinker can be cast but the bait cannot • Deploy the rig when longer leaders, heavier components or much larger baits are required

sections.heading: Why Shark Rig Length Matters
sections.text: A shark does not need to bite directly through the mainline for a short rig to fail. During the fight, a shark may roll, change direction or bring its body and tail across the leader. Its rough skin can abrade mono, while its teeth can cut any unprotected line that reaches the mouth. A complete shark leader system may therefore include: • A wire bite trace immediately ahead of the hook • A heavy mono rub leader above the wire • Strong connections joining the protected leader to the mainline The wire protects the section most likely to contact the shark’s teeth. The mono rub leader extends protection farther along the shark’s body without requiring the complete leader to be made from wire. When deliberately targeting larger sharks, the protected leader system should be at least as long as the shark expected and preferably longer. This helps keep the mainline beyond the shark’s mouth, rough skin and tail as it turns or rolls. Castable rigs are restricted by the length and weight that can be handled during the cast. Slide bait and deployed systems allow longer protected leaders to be used because the complete baited rig is not cast through the air. Rig length should therefore be chosen around the expected shark size and deployment method—not simply by using the same trace for every situation.

sections.heading: Wire Bite Traces and Mono Rub Leaders Do Different Jobs
sections.text: Wire and heavy monofilament are used in shark rigs for different reasons. The wire bite trace is positioned directly ahead of the hook. Its job is to prevent the shark’s teeth from cutting through the rig when it takes the bait, turns or becomes hooked. The mono rub leader extends above the wire and protects the mainline from contact with the shark’s rough skin, body and tail during the fight. A longer deployed shark rig will often combine both materials: • Wire nearest the hook for bite protection • Heavy mono above the wire for additional length and abrasion resistance • Mainline connected beyond the protected leader system Using heavy mono alone does not provide the same protection against teeth, while using a long wire trace does not automatically provide the most manageable complete rig. Castable rigs generally use a more compact protected leader because the complete rig must pass through the cast. Slide bait and drone-deployed rigs can use longer mono and wire sections because the baited trace is not being cast. After landing a shark, inspect the complete protected leader. Check mono for scuffing, flattening or cuts, and check wire for kinks, broken strands, damaged coating or corrosion. Replace any damaged section before using the rig again.

sections.heading: Why a Flemish Eye Loop Is Used at the Hook
sections.text: Some Wiggle ya Worm shark rigs use a Flemish eye loop to connect the circle hook to the wire leader. The wire passes through the hook eye and is twisted back around the main trace before the connection is secured. This creates a strong loop while allowing the hook to pivot and rotate independently of the heavy wire. A circle hook needs this freedom of movement to travel towards the corner of the shark’s jaw and turn into position as pressure comes onto the line. The Flemish eye loop provides: • Freedom for the circle hook to rotate • Better alignment between the hook and leader • Less restriction from the heavy wire trace • A reinforced connection directly in front of the hook Hook size must also suit the bait. After baiting up, the hook point and gape must remain exposed rather than being buried beneath thick bait or bait elastic. Allow the line to tighten and apply steady pressure instead of striking hard. This gives the circle hook time to move into position and roll into the corner of the jaw.

sections.heading: Why Heavy Shark Rigs Use Double-Crimped Connections
sections.text: Heavy wire shark leaders cannot be secured with conventional fishing knots. Each connection is formed by passing the wire through the hook, swivel or connection point, returning it through the crimp and mechanically compressing the crimp around the wire. Wiggle ya Worm crimps are secured using a mechanical crimping machine to apply firm, consistent pressure to each connection. On rigs built for larger sharks, two crimps are used to provide two separate holding points. This is particularly important around the hook, swivel and other terminal connections where the rig carries the full load of the fish. A properly built double-crimped connection provides: • Two secure holding points on the leader • Consistent compression around the wire • Additional security during long, powerful fights • A strong connection without restricting the hook or swivel Where fitted, heat-shrink tubing covers the completed connection, helps protect it against abrasion and creates a neat finish.

sections.heading: Why Some Shark Rigs Use a Twisted Bite Zone
sections.text: The section of leader directly in front of the hook receives the most contact from the shark’s teeth, mouth and rough skin. Some heavier Wiggle ya Worm shark rigs include an approximately 400mm twisted stainless-steel bite zone at the hook end. The wire is folded and twisted together, creating two strands of protection through the section most likely to contact the shark. The twisted bite zone provides: • Additional bite protection directly in front of the hook • Greater resistance to abrasion from teeth and rough skin • Extra durability while the shark rolls or changes direction • A compact reinforced section without doubling the complete leader The remainder of the leader stays as a single strand, while the reinforced section protects the part of the rig that works hardest during the fight.

sections.heading: Match the Circle Hook to the Bait and Shark
sections.text: Circle-hook size should be chosen for both the shark being targeted and the thickness of the bait. The hook must be large enough for its point and gape to remain completely exposed after the bait has been secured. If a thick bait fills the gape, the hook has less room to roll into the corner of the jaw. Across the Wiggle ya Worm range: • 6/0 and 8/0 hooks are used on gummy and school shark rigs with smaller baits • 10/0 and 14/0 hooks suit heavier rigs and larger fish, eel or flesh baits • 16/0 and 20/0 hooks are used with substantial baits when deliberately targeting much larger sharks The bait should be held firmly without covering the hook point or closing the space between the point and shank. Choose the bait first, then select a circle hook large enough to remain fully exposed once that bait is attached.

sections.heading: Choosing and Securing Shark Baits
sections.text: Shark baits need to release plenty of scent while remaining firmly attached during casting, deployment and time in the water. Useful shark baits include: • Eel sections • Tailor fillets • Whole mullet or bonito • Oily fish and flesh baits • Stingray wings • Other tough, scent-rich fish baits Match the bait size to how the rig will reach the fishing area. Castable rigs require a manageable, streamlined bait, while slide bait and drone-deployed rigs can carry much larger baits without having to cast them through the air. Pass the hook through a firm section of the bait and use bait elastic to secure loose edges. The bait should remain compact rather than spinning, folding or tearing in the current. Keep the circle-hook point and the complete gape exposed. Bait elastic should secure the bait—not bind it across the working area of the hook.

sections.heading: Prepare for Dehooking Before You Start Fishing
sections.text: Shark release equipment should be ready before the bait enters the water. Once a shark reaches the shoreline is not the time to start looking for pliers, cutters or a dehooking tool. Keep the following within reach: • Long-reach shark dehooker • Heavy-duty pliers • Suitable wire cutters • Gloves appropriate for handling heavy leader material All Wiggle ya Worm shark rigs are supplied with barbed hooks. When targeting larger sharks for release, experienced fishos may use pliers to crush the barb before fishing. This makes the hook easier and faster to remove while the shark is being handled. A long-reach dehooker allows the hook to be controlled from farther away without placing hands close to the shark’s mouth. Keep other fishos and bystanders clear while the hook is removed and the shark is prepared for release. For complete landing, handling and release guidance, see: Safe Shark Release Guide → Solid Stainless-Steel Shark Dehooker →

sections.heading: How to Safely Remove Hooks from Sharks – Land-Based Release
sections.text: Releasing sharks safely and efficiently is an important part of responsible land-based shark fishing. Using the correct technique and the right equipment helps reduce injury to the fish while keeping fishos at a safer working distance during hook removal. This guide explains a simple, practical release method used by experienced Australian land-based shark fishers. Using a long-reach stainless steel dehooker allows safer hook removal while maintaining distance from the shark’s mouth during release. Planning to target sharks from the beach? See our Land-Based Shark Fishing Guide for rig selection, deployment options and landing approach. If you're deploying baits by drone, our Australian Drone Fishing Guide covers payload management, bait deployment and practical drone fishing techniques. Keeping sharks in shallow surf during release reduces stress, prevents internal injury and improves release success.

sections.heading: Why Safe Shark Release Matters
sections.text: Large sharks are powerful animals, even when tired. Quick, controlled hook removal: reduces stress on the fish improves release success keeps hands clear of teeth and leader tension reduces the risk of tail strikes supports responsible catch-and-release fishing practices In many situations, sharks can be released without dragging them fully onto dry sand.

sections.heading: Recommended Tools for Safe Hook Removal
sections.text: For large shark release work, experienced fishers typically carry: long-reach stainless steel shark dehooker heavy gloves leader cutters (if hook removal is not possible) long-nose pliers as backup only A long-reach stainless steel dehooker is the safest primary option for removing hooks in the 8/0 to 20/0+ range while maintaining distance from the mouth.

sections.heading: 1. Keep the shark in shallow water where possible
sections.text: Working in shallow surf reduces stress on the fish and allows safer positioning during hook removal. Avoid dragging sharks high onto dry sand unless necessary.

sections.heading: 2. Maintain tension on the line
sections.text: Keeping the line tight helps hold the hook in position and makes it easier to engage with the dehooker.

sections.heading: 3. Engage the bend of the hook
sections.text: Slide the dehooker onto the bend of the hook as shown in product images. This provides the leverage needed for controlled removal.

sections.heading: 4. Apply steady rotation
sections.text: Use the handle of the dehooker to rotate the hook. Most circle hooks will roll free cleanly when steady pressure is applied.

sections.heading: 5. Step back once the hook is released
sections.text: Give the shark space to move off safely. Avoid standing directly in front of the head or tail during release.

sections.heading: Common mistakes when releasing sharks from the beach
sections.text: Dragging sharks fully onto dry sand This increases internal injury risk and stress. Keep the shark in shallow water whenever possible during hook removal. Not supporting exhausted sharks before release If a shark is slow to move off, hold it facing into the current so water flows over the gills until it swims away strongly. Using tackle that’s too light for the species Long fights increase exhaustion and reduce survival after release. Use appropriately strong rigs to shorten fight time and improve recovery. Whether you're casting from the beach or deploying baits by drone, matching your rig to the size of the shark you're targeting helps reduce fight time and improves release success. Trying to remove deeply embedded hooks instead of cutting the leader Cutting the leader close to the hook is often safer than forcing removal. Standing near the tail during hook removal A sudden tail strike can cause serious injury. Stay beside the mid-section of the shark whenever possible. Using short pliers instead of long-reach dehookers Short tools reduce control and increase risk. Long-reach dehookers allow safer hook removal while keeping distance from the mouth. Leaving barbs intact when catch-and-release is planned Flattening the barb before fishing makes hook removal faster and reduces handling time during release.

sections.heading: When It’s Better to Cut the Leader
sections.text: Sometimes removing the hook is not the safest option. Cut the leader as close to the hook as possible if: the hook is deeply swallowed the shark is still actively moving its head access to the hook is unsafe the leader is wrapped conditions are unstable Fast release is always better than perfect hook recovery.

sections.heading: Safety Tips for Land-Based Shark Fishers
sections.text: The safest working position beside a shark is around the middle of the body, away from both the mouth and the tail. This area moves less suddenly than the head or tail and reduces the risk of injury during hook removal. Never place hands near the mouth. Keep clear of leader tension under load. Watch tail movement at all times, as sudden strikes from the tail can cause serious injury. Avoid kneeling directly beside the head or tail especially during hook removal. Work with a second person where possible to maintain control and improve safety during release. Using a long-reach stainless steel dehooker allows safer hook removal by increasing distance from the shark’s mouth while maintaining control during release.

sections.heading: Why Long-Reach Dehookers Work Best for Sharks
sections.text: Standard short dehookers are designed for smaller species and lighter hooks. Large sharks require: increased working distance from the mouth leverage to rotate heavy hooks corrosion-resistant materials for surf conditions reliable control under tension Solid stainless steel long-reach dehookers are widely used by experienced shark fishers for these reasons.

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Rig Helps Safe Release
sections.text: Hook removal is easier when the rig is designed for controlled presentation and clean hook positioning. Circle hooks, appropriate leader length, and balanced rig setups all improve release outcomes and reduce handling time. See our Shark Fishing Rigs Guide for proven land-based shark rig designs, or explore the Drone Fishing System if you're deploying large baits by drone.

sections.heading: Built for Safe Shark Release
sections.text: The Wiggle ya Worm solid stainless steel shark dehooker is designed specifically for removing large hooks from powerful fish during land-based and offshore release situations. Its extended reach allows safer hook removal while keeping distance from teeth and leader tension during release work.

sections.heading: Responsible Catch-and-Release Shark Fishing
sections.text: Careful handling, correct positioning beside the shark, and efficient hook removal all help improve release outcomes for large fish. Working in shallow water where possible and using appropriate long-reach release equipment reduces stress on the shark and improves safety for fishers during the release process. Responsible catch-and-release practices allow land-based shark fishers to target large species confidently while supporting the long-term health of local shark populations. Good preparation starts long before the shark reaches the beach. Choosing the right rig, using suitable release equipment and planning your release before deploying your bait all contribute to safer outcomes for both fish and fishos.

sections.heading: Send Large Baits Beyond Casting Range
sections.text: Slide baiting allows you to cast the sinker and mainline first, then attach a separate baited trace and send it down the mainline using a non-return slide trolley. Because the bait is not cast with the sinker, large dead baits and livebaits can be placed much further from shore without being damaged, torn from the hooks or restricted by the weight and wind resistance of the bait during the cast. Once attached, the trolley travels down the tensioned mainline through gravity, water movement and controlled movements of the rod. It continues towards a stopper positioned near the sinker, carrying the bait into the fishing zone. The system is commonly used from beaches, rock ledges and headlands when targeting sharks, kingfish, mulloway and other large predators holding beyond normal bait-casting range. This guide explains how the complete system works, how to attach and operate it correctly, the difference between weighted and unweighted trolleys, and how the Wiggle ya Worm Anti Burn-Off Stopper controls trolley movement once the trolley reaches the stopper.

sections.heading: How a Complete Slide Bait System Works
sections.text: The first part cast into the water consists of: • The sinker • A separate section of sinker line • The stopper • The mainline The sinker is tied to one end of the sinker line, while the other end is tied to the stopper. The stopper is then tied directly to the mainline. Cast this setup into position and allow the sinker to take hold. Place the rod securely in a rod holder and keep the mainline tight. Next, bait up the hooks and attach the slide trolley to the mainline. Release the trolley and allow gravity and the line angle to carry the bait towards the sinker. Short, controlled flicks of the rod help move the trolley down the mainline. The trolley’s one-way design allows it to move towards the sinker while resisting movement back towards the rod. Continue until the trolley reaches the stopper. A standalone slide bait trolley is the reusable stainless-steel sliding component. It has a connection point so a fisho can attach a hook trace they have made themselves. A complete pre-rigged slide bait rig includes the trolley, wire hook trace and hooks already connected and ready to bait up.

sections.heading: Why Slide Baiting Can Reach Further Than Casting a Baited Rig
sections.text: With an ordinary cast, the sinker must also carry the bait, hooks and trace through the air. Large baits create considerable wind resistance. They can flap, spin or tumble during the cast, reducing distance and placing extra strain on the bait and hooks. With slide baiting, the baited trace is not part of the cast. The breakaway sinker leads the cast, with the sinker line, stopper and mainline following behind. There is no large bait or baited trace flapping, spinning or tumbling through the air. More casting energy to carry the sinker forward Less wind resistance during the cast A cleaner and more controlled flight The sinker to reach water beyond normal bait-casting range Very large baits to be used without attempting to cast them Once the sinker is firmly anchored, the baited trace is attached to the trolley and worked down the mainline. This means a large livebait, whole fish or other bulky bait can be sent into water that would be extremely difficult—or impossible—to reach by casting the complete baited rig.

sections.heading: Why Slide Bait Burn-Offs Happen
sections.text: All Wiggle ya Worm slide bait trolleys and complete pre-rigged slide bait rigs are supplied with the standard ring stopper traditionally used for slide baiting. The trolley travels down the mainline until it reaches and rests against the ring. It does not lock to the standard stopper and can be forced back along the mainline under load. When a fish is hooked, the mainline normally remains tensioned between the rod and the anchored sinker. If the fish swims across the direction of the mainline, the loaded trolley can slide or rub against the tensioned line. If the fish changes direction or disturbs the sinker, the trolley may travel back up the mainline. As the load changes, the trolley can become tangled around the line, suddenly pull tight or slide rapidly along it under pressure. The resulting friction can damage or cut the mainline. This failure is known as a burn-off . The Wiggle ya Worm Anti Burn-Off Stopper is an optional product available separately. Unlike the supplied standard ring stopper, the Anti Burn-Off Stopper physically engages with and locks onto the trolley. Once connected, the trolley remains locked to the stopper throughout the fight and cannot travel back along the mainline. This prevents the loaded trolley from sliding or rubbing against the mainline, eliminating the movement responsible for slide-bait burn-offs.

sections.heading: How to Attach a Slide Bait Trolley to the Mainline
sections.text: To attach the trolley: Unclip the spring mechanism. Slide the compression bead away from the spring. Wind the mainline through the gap and into the spring. Slide the compression bead back against the spring. Clip the spring mechanism back together. The video shows each step and how to wind the mainline into the trolley. No knots are needed, and the sinker setup remains connected.

sections.heading: Choosing a Weighted or Unweighted Slide Trolley
sections.text: The mainline angle, water movement and type of bait determine whether a weighted or unweighted trolley is the better choice. A weighted slide trolley has additional lead built into the trolley. This causes it to hang at a steeper angle on the mainline. Use a weighted trolley when: • The mainline angle is shallow • Rough weather, swell or wave action may push the trolley back • A livebait may try to swim back up the mainline On a shallow line angle, the bait must travel down a much flatter slope. The additional weight helps the trolley overcome friction and continue towards the stopper. The steeper hanging angle also makes it harder for swell, wave action or a livebait to move the trolley back up the mainline. An unweighted slide trolley is suited to steeper mainline angles and calmer conditions where the trolley and bait can travel down the line without the additional weight. The Wiggle ya Worm Slide Bait Trolley Pack includes one weighted trolley, one unweighted trolley and a matching standard fully welded stainless-steel stopper for each.

sections.heading: Standalone Trolleys and Pre-Rigged Slide Bait Rigs
sections.text: A standalone slide bait trolley is suited to fishos who prefer to build their own hook traces. The trolley’s rolling swivel provides the connection point for your chosen: • Monofilament or wire trace • Hook size and style • Single or twin-hook arrangement • Trace length A complete pre-rigged slide bait rig has the trolley, wire hook trace and hooks already connected. Pre-rigged rigs are available with weighted or unweighted trolleys and different hook arrangements. Twin-hook versions use: • One fixed bottom hook • One sliding snelled top hook The sliding top hook allows the hook spacing to be adjusted to match the length of the bait. Available twin-hook options include: • Weighted Slide Bait Rig – Twin 6/0 Circle Hooks / 120lb Stainless Wire • Weighted Slide Bait Rig – Twin 8/0 Octopus Beak Hooks / 110lb Wire For larger sharks, the Heavy-Duty Single-Hook Slide Bait Shark Rig uses one large hook rather than an adjustable twin-hook arrangement. Browse the complete Slide Bait Rig Range to compare the weighted, unweighted, single-hook and twin-hook options. All standalone trolleys and complete pre-rigged rigs are supplied with the conventional standard ring stopper. Use the slide bait system in this order: Cast the sinker, sinker line, stopper and mainline into position. Allow the sinker to take hold. Place the rod securely in a rod holder and keep the mainline tight. Bait up the hooks and attach the slide trolley to the mainline. Release the trolley and allow it to begin travelling towards the sinker. Hold the rod vertically and use short flicking movements to work the trolley down the mainline. Continue until the trolley reaches the standard ring stopper or locks onto an optional Anti Burn-Off Stopper. Loosen the drag and wait for a bite. Do not stop working the trolley partway down the mainline. If a fish takes the bait before the trolley reaches the stopper, the loaded trolley can slide or rub against the tensioned mainline and cause a burn-off. Work the trolley all the way down before loosening the drag and leaving the rig to fish.

sections.heading: Standalone Trolleys and Pre-Rigged Slide Bait Rigs
sections.text: Because the bait is slid rather than cast, large dead baits remain intact and livebaits avoid the impact of a full cast.

sections.heading: Choosing the Breakaway Sinker and Sinker Line
sections.text: A breakaway sinker is used because its spikes anchor firmly into the bottom and keep the mainline tight. This firm anchor is essential. The slide bait trolley cannot travel properly down a moving or slack mainline. A 168g breakaway sinker suits most situations. A heavier sinker may be needed when: Rough conditions make it difficult to hold bottom Strong tidal movement is pushing against the bait A larger bait creates enough resistance to pull the sinker free The sinker should be attached using a separate length of weaker line, usually 20–40lb , depending on the sinker and fishing conditions. The sinker line must: Be weaker than the mainline and the rest of the slide bait rig Be strong enough to cast and retrieve the sinker Break if the sinker becomes firmly snagged If the sinker catches in rocks or other rough ground during the fight, the weaker sinker line can snap, allowing the fisho to recover the fish and slide bait trolley rather than losing the complete setup.

sections.heading: Choosing the Bait and Hook Arrangement
sections.text: Slide baiting can carry large livebaits and dead baits that would be difficult to cast without damaging or tearing them from the hooks. Suitable baits include: Whole fish baits Large fish fillets Whole squid Large strip baits Livebaits Choose the hook size and arrangement to suit the bait rather than forcing a large bait onto hooks that are too small or poorly spaced. A single-hook trace provides a simple setup when one correctly positioned hook gives suitable coverage. An adjustable twin-hook trace allows the top hook to be moved to match the length of a longer bait. This helps keep the bait straight while placing both hooks in useful positions. Whichever arrangement is used: Match the hook size to the bait Keep each hook point properly exposed Secure the bait firmly without restricting a livebait’s movement Use bait elastic on large or softer baits to reduce twisting, tearing and wash damage as the bait travels down the mainline The bait must remain securely attached while the trolley is worked down to the stopper and while it fishes in the current.

sections.heading: Where Slide Baiting Works Best
sections.text: Slide baiting is most useful from land-based locations where large baits need to reach water beyond normal casting range. Common locations include: Surf beaches Rock platforms Coastal headlands Deep gutters and channels Reef edges accessible from shore The sinker must be able to anchor firmly, and the mainline needs to remain tight so the trolley can travel towards the stopper. A steeper mainline angle helps the trolley move down more easily. Where the angle is shallow, a weighted trolley can help overcome friction and carry the bait towards the stopper. The path of the mainline should also remain clear. Contact with rocks, reef or heavy weed can prevent the trolley from travelling properly and may damage the line. Slide baiting is particularly useful when sharks, kingfish, mulloway and other large predators are holding beyond the distance at which a large bait could normally be cast.

sections.heading: Common Slide Baiting Mistakes
sections.text: Most slide baiting problems begin before the trolley reaches the stopper. The breakaway sinker has not anchored properly If the sinker moves, the mainline cannot remain tight enough for the trolley to travel properly. Use enough sinker weight for the current, swell and bait size. Allowing the mainline to become slack The trolley needs a tight mainline to move towards the stopper. Keep the rod secure and maintain steady line tension while working the trolley down. Leaving the trolley partway down the mainline A fish taking the bait before the trolley reaches the stopper can place the moving trolley under heavy load against the mainline, creating a serious burn-off risk. Using the wrong trolley for the conditions An unweighted trolley may struggle on a shallow mainline angle, in rough weather or with an active livebait. A weighted trolley hangs at a steeper angle and is harder to push back up the line. Using sinker line that is too strong The sinker line should be weaker than the mainline and the rest of the rig. If the sinker becomes snagged during the fight, the weaker line can break so the fish and trolley can still be recovered. Failing to secure the bait properly Large or soft baits can twist, tear or wash out while travelling down the mainline. Keep the hook points exposed and use bait elastic where needed to hold the bait securely.

sections.heading: Species Commonly Targeted with Slide Bait Rigs
sections.text: Slide bait rigs are primarily used for large predators that take substantial livebaits, whole fish and other big dead baits. Common targets include: Sharks Kingfish Mulloway Large trevally Rays Other large coastal predators The species being targeted determines the hook arrangement, hook size, trace material and overall strength of the rig. Wire traces are commonly used where sharks or other toothy fish are expected. Mono may be suitable where additional bite protection is unnecessary. For more species-specific advice, see the: Kingfish Rig Guide Mulloway Rig Guide The bait and likely by-catch should always be considered when choosing between a single-hook rig, an adjustable twin-hook rig and the required trace strength.

sections.heading: Adjustable Hook Spacing for Longer Baits
sections.text: A sliding snell rig uses two hooks on the same bait trace: a fixed bottom hook and an adjustable top hook that slides along the leader. The top hook is repositioned each time the rig is baited, allowing the spacing between the hooks to match the length of the bait being used. This makes sliding snell rigs particularly useful for longer or variable-sized baits such as squid, pilchards, fish fillets, whole fish and livebaits. Both hooks can be positioned along the bait while keeping their points properly exposed. The two-hook arrangement also provides hook coverage towards both ends of the bait, making it useful when targeting fish that may strike at either the head or tail. Sliding snell rigs are used from beaches, rocks and boats for species including mulloway, snapper, kingfish and gummy sharks. This guide explains how the adjustable hook works, how to match the spacing to your bait and how to keep longer baits straight and securely rigged.

sections.heading: Why Hook Spacing Must Match the Bait
sections.text: Long baits vary considerably in length, shape and thickness. Using fixed hook spacing can leave the bait stretched between the hooks, bunched up or supported in the wrong places. With a sliding snell rig, the top hook can be moved until both hooks suit the natural length of the bait. Correct spacing helps: Keep the bait straight Support the bait at two points Position hooks towards different strike areas Keep both hook points properly exposed Reduce bait twisting or spinning in the current Fish may take a bait head-first, strike the tail or grab it across the middle. Placing hooks towards both ends of a longer bait increases the chance that one of the exposed hook points is in the area being struck. The hook spacing should be adjusted for every new bait rather than assuming that two baits from the same packet will be identical.

sections.heading: How the Sliding Top Hook Stays in Position
sections.text: The sliding top hook is held on the leader by the friction created through the snell. It takes deliberate hand pressure to move the hook, allowing it to be positioned to suit the bait and remain where it is set during normal baiting and handling. The hook is adjustable rather than permanently locked. If a fish takes the top hook and applies enough pressure, the hook may move along the leader towards the fixed bottom hook. Because every rig is hand tied, the amount of pressure required to adjust the top hook can vary slightly between rigs. For longer or softer baits, we recommend using bait elastic after both hooks have been positioned. Wrapping the bait and hooks together helps: Keep the bait straight Hold both hooks in the selected positions Prevent the bait moving along the hooks during the cast Keep the hook points properly exposed Bait elastic helps the bait and hooks remain together as one controlled unit during the cast and while fishing.

sections.heading: Baits Suited to Sliding Snell Rigs
sections.text: Sliding snell rigs are particularly useful when the length of the bait changes from one bait to the next. Suitable baits include: Whole pilchards Garfish Long fish fillets and strip baits Whole squid Squid strips Eels Livebaits such as yakka and slimy mackerel The sliding top hook can be moved to suit each bait while the fixed bottom hook provides a consistent lower attachment point. This allows both hooks to support the bait without stretching it or forcing it to bunch between fixed hook positions. Twin-hook arrangements are also useful when rigging longer baits for Flathead. See the Flathead Rig Guide . When using whole pilchards with ganged hooks rather than a sliding snelled pair, see the Tailor Rig Guide . For livebait rigging around reef edges and structure, see the Kingfish Rig Guide .

sections.heading: How to Bait a Sliding Snell Rig
sections.text: Lay the bait beside the rig and move the sliding top hook until the two hooks align with suitable positions towards each end of the bait. Attach the bait to both hooks, then check that: The bait sits straight between the hooks Neither hook is pulling the bait out of shape Both hook points and hook gapes remain exposed The top hook is positioned firmly against the bait No loose section of bait can fold or spin in the current For longer, softer or heavier baits, wrap bait elastic around the bait and hook shanks to hold everything together. Use enough elastic to secure the bait without covering the hook points or closing the hook gapes. The finished bait should remain straight and securely attached while leaving both hooks clear to make contact with the fish.

sections.heading: Matching the Hook Style and Size to the Bait
sections.text: Sliding snell rigs can be built with circle hooks or beak hooks depending on the bait, target species and how the rig will be fished. Whichever hook style is used, the hook must be large enough for its point and gape to remain clear after the bait has been attached. A hook buried deeply in a thick bait can prevent it from making proper contact with the fish. Circle-hook sliding snell rigs are commonly used when baits are left for the fish to take and move away with. Keep both hook gapes clear and apply steady pressure rather than striking aggressively. Beak-hook versions can be used where the fisho intends to set the hooks manually. The hook spacing and bait size must work together. Increasing the bait length without checking the hook positions can leave both hooks concentrated at one end of the bait. For more information about hook patterns and choosing a suitable size, see Choosing the Right Fishing Hook .

sections.heading: Choosing a Mono or Wire Bait Trace
sections.text: Sliding snell rigs can be built with either monofilament or wire. The correct material depends on the target species, the ground being fished and what else may take the bait. Mono sliding snell rigs are commonly used for: Mulloway Snapper Kingfish Flathead General surf, reef and inshore fishing Mono provides flexibility and allows longer baits and livebaits to move naturally. Wire sliding snell rigs are useful when: Tailor or other toothy fish are active Sharks may take the bait Fishing mixed-species water where bite-offs are a genuine risk Additional protection is needed around abrasive mouths Wire provides greater bite protection but should be selected for a clear reason rather than automatically being used for every sliding snell setup. Match the bait-trace strength to the target species, likely bycatch, bait size and ground being fished.

sections.heading: Species Commonly Targeted with Sliding Snell Rigs
sections.text: Sliding snell rigs are not restricted to one species. They are selected primarily because of the bait being used and the need for adjustable hook spacing. They are commonly used when targeting: Mulloway Snapper Kingfish Gummy sharks Flathead Other fish that take longer baits or may strike towards either end The required hook size, leader strength and bait-trace material will vary between these species, but the adjustable top hook performs the same job: matching the hook spacing to the bait.

sections.heading: Common Sliding Snell Rigging Mistakes
sections.text: Using the same hook spacing for every bait Baits vary in length and thickness. Reposition the sliding hook whenever the next bait requires different spacing. Stretching or bunching the bait between the hooks The hooks should support the bait in its natural shape. Incorrect spacing can pull the bait tight or force it to fold. Burying the hook points or filling the hook gapes Both hook points and gapes need to remain exposed after baiting and wrapping with elastic. Leaving the sliding hook away from the bait The top hook should sit firmly in the selected position against the bait rather than hanging loosely on the leader. Not securing longer or softer baits Bait elastic helps hold the bait and both hooks together during casting and while fishing. Wrapping bait elastic over the hook points Secure the bait around the hook shanks while keeping the points and gapes clear. Using hooks that do not suit the bait size The hooks must be large enough to remain exposed without being so widely spaced that the bait is stretched out of shape.

sections.heading: How Wiggle ya Worm Sliding Snell Rigs Are Built
sections.text: Most Wiggle ya Worm sliding snell rigs use: A fixed bottom hook An adjustable top hook secured with a sliding snell A mono or wire bait trace selected for the intended species and conditions Hook sizes and patterns matched to the baits the rig is designed to carry A swivel connection for attaching the rig to the mainline or fishing system The range includes different hook styles, hook sizes, leader strengths and bait-trace materials for surf, estuary, reef and offshore fishing. Wiggle ya Worm also makes a Snapper rig with two fixed hooks. That rig provides consistent, permanent hook spacing and should not be confused with an adjustable sliding snell rig. The important difference is simple: Sliding snell rig: one fixed hook and one adjustable hook Fixed twin-hook rig: both hooks remain in permanent positions Every rig is individually hand tied in Queensland. Explore the current Sliding Snell Rig range .

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Rig for Your Bait
sections.text: A sliding snell rig is most useful when bait length varies or when hook coverage is needed towards both ends of a longer bait. Choose the hook size, leader strength and bait-trace material for the target species and fishing conditions, then adjust the hook spacing to suit the individual bait.
